## Overview
Deprecates the tracking blocker in favor of script loading allowing for
full control over what is blocked and what is not.
In the React packages, the script loader can also conditionally render
React components based on the consent. For example if you wanted to load
a script with `Next/Script` or a React Provider instead.

We now also have pre-defined scripts for stuff like Google Tag Manager,
Meta Pixel & Posthog

feat(react): add frame component to conditionally render iframes etc (#420)

## Overview
Core: 
Render iframes based on consent via data-src and data-category tags.
This does not display fallback content.

React: 
Conditionally render components & elements based on the consent. 

We do this in the UI level with react as you want a UI fallback for your
iFrames, to prevent layout shifts and provide better UX. This component
is customizable similar to the other c15t components.

This is useful for iframes such as for youtube embeds as they set
cookies on load or play.

## Related Issue
Fixes #335 

## Type of Change
- [x] 🚀 New feature

## Usage
c15t:
```html
  <iframe
    width="560"
    height="315"
    data-src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/mQJ6q1ZCzsg"
    data-category="marketing" // Note: Not typesafe
  />
```

@c15t/react:
``` tsx
<Frame category="marketing" className="h-[300px] w-[500px]">
	<iframe
		title="Cool Duck Video"
		src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/mQJ6q1ZCzsg"
		width="100%"
		height="100%"
	/>
</Frame>
```

feat(translations): add automated translations with Lingo.dev CLI (#500)

## Overview

This PR:

- adds support for more EU languages to the `@c15t/translations` package
- sets up [Lingo.dev CLI](https://lingo.dev/en/cli) for easier
generation and maintenance of translations

This approach has a few benefits:

- the translations are generated with AI
- as the source content is updated, only the changes are retranslated
- support additional languages with just a couple of (small) changes

Some other possible enhancements (not in this PR) include:

- translating the documentation (either for all locales or just a
subset)
- setting up CI/CD integration that:
    - verifies if translations have been generated
- commits translations automatically to repo (directly to the main
branch, or via PR, etc)

**Note:** Based on the config in this PR, a Lingo.dev API key is
required. It's also possible to BYOK with a standard LLM provider though
(e.g., OpenRouter).

## Related Issue

Fixes https://github.com/c15t/c15t/issues/497

This PR:

- adds support for more EU languages to the `@c15t/translations` package
- sets up [Lingo.dev CLI](https://lingo.dev/en/cli) for easier
generation and maintenance of translations

This approach has a few benefits:

- the translations are generated with AI
- as the source content is updated, only the changes are retranslated
- support additional languages with just a couple of (small) changes

Some other possible enhancements (not in this PR) include:

- translating the documentation (either for all locales or just a
subset)
- setting up CI/CD integration that:
    - verifies if translations have been generated
- commits translations automatically to repo (directly to the main
branch, or via PR, etc)

**Note:** Based on the config in this PR, a Lingo.dev API key is
required. It's also possible to BYOK with a standard LLM provider though
(e.g., OpenRouter).

refactor(workflows): consolidate and update deployment workflows (#538)

- Removed outdated workflows for canary, preview, and production
deployments.
- Introduced a new unified deployment workflow to handle various
deployment scenarios including PR previews, scheduled checks, and manual
triggers.
- Enhanced the release workflow to support both canary and regular
releases with appropriate configurations for pnpm and Node.js.
- Improved permissions and concurrency settings for better workflow
management.
## Overview

This PR consolidates and enhances GitHub Actions workflows to improve
maintainability and add new capabilities:

1. **Merged release workflows**: Combined `canary-release.yml` and
`release.yml` into a single unified workflow that handles both canary
and production releases based on branch triggers.

2. **Added PR preview workflow**: Created a new workflow
(`pr-preview.yml`) that automatically detects changed packages in PRs
and publishes preview versions to `pkg.pr.new` for testing before
merging.

3. **Merged docs deployment workflows**: Combined
`deploy-docs-preview.yml` and `deploy-docs-production.yml` into a single
workflow with manual trigger support for both preview and production
deployments.

**Benefits:**
- Reduced workflow duplication and maintenance overhead
- Single source of truth for release and deployment logic
- Better developer experience with PR preview packages
- Manual deployment controls for production/preview environments
- Simplified npm trusted publisher configuration (only one workflow file
needed)

## Related Issue

Fixes # (issue)

## Type of Change

- [x] 🏗️ Refactor (no functional changes)
- [x] ✨ Enhancement (improves existing functionality)
- [x] 🚀 New feature

## Implementation Details

### Key Changes

1. **Unified Release Workflow** (`.github/workflows/release.yml`)
   - Merged `canary-release.yml` and `release.yml` into single workflow
   - Triggers on push to `main` or `canary` branches
   - Uses conditional steps to handle canary vs production releases
   - Maintains all existing functionality while reducing duplication

2. **PR Preview Workflow** (`.github/workflows/pr-preview.yml`)
   - New workflow for publishing preview packages from PRs
   - Automatically detects which packages changed in PR
   - Only publishes packages with `publishConfig` (published packages)
- Security: Only runs for repository members or PRs with
`deploy:preview` label
   - Publishes to `pkg.pr.new` with version `0.0.0-preview.<SHA>`
   - Adds install instructions as PR notices

3. **Unified Docs Deployment Workflow**
(`.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml`)
   - Merged `deploy-docs-preview.yml` and `deploy-docs-production.yml`
   - Supports automatic deployments on push to `main`/`canary`
   - Added manual `workflow_dispatch` trigger with options:
     - Deployment type: `preview` or `production`
     - Branch selection
     - PR number (for preview deployments)
   - Conditional steps based on deployment type

### Technical Notes

- **Release workflow**: Uses conditional steps with `if` conditions to
determine canary vs production behavior, avoiding duplicate code while
maintaining clear separation of concerns.

- **PR preview workflow**: Uses matrix strategy to build/publish
multiple changed packages in parallel. Package detection uses git diff
to identify changed packages and filters to only published packages.

- **Docs deployment workflow**: Uses a deployment info extraction step
to determine branch/PR context, then conditionally runs preview or
production deployment steps based on trigger type.

- **Workflow consolidation**: All merged workflows maintain backward
compatibility - existing triggers and behaviors continue to work as
before.

feat(backend): add OTel instrumentation and strip PII from spans (#582)

## Overview
feat(backend): add OTel instrumentation and strip PII from spans

Instrument DB, cache, external, and request operations with
OpenTelemetry
   spans and metrics across handlers, registries, and the GVL resolver.
Strip PII from span attributes by removing error.message, error.stack,
   and http.path; sanitize external URLs to drop query params; and use
hostname-only span names for external calls. Consolidate error handling
   into a shared exported handleSpanError function.

Add e2e test with real InMemorySpanExporter that enforces an attribute
key allowlist and blocks PII value patterns (IPs, emails, stack traces,
   query strings) across all span types.

refactor(core): rename gdprTypes to consentCategories, add debug logger, remove hardcoded  necessary checks (#584)

## Overview
Replace GDPR-specific naming with generic consent vocabulary throughout
the core package so the config works for any consent category, not just
GDPR presets. Add a gated debug logger (disabled by default) that
replaces bare console.log calls, and make save-consents use the
ConsentType config properties (disabled, defaultValue) instead of
checking for the literal string 'necessary'

saveConsents was mutating the consents object in place and setting the
same reference back. Now it spreads into a new object ({ ...consents }),
so he reference always changes.

has, hasConsented, getDisplayedConsents are wrapped in useCallback with
reactive deps like [consents]. When the consents reference changes,
useCallback returns a new function reference. React Compiler caches
based on function identity.

fix(react): react compiler compatability (#605)

## Overview
saveConsents was mutating the consents object in place and setting the
same reference back. Now it spreads into a new object ({ ...consents }),
so he reference always changes.

has, hasConsented, getDisplayedConsents are wrapped in useCallback with
reactive deps like [consents]. When the consents reference changes,
useCallback returns a new function reference. React Compiler caches
based on function identity.

hostname-only span names for external calls. Consolidate error handling

fix(react): react compiler compatability (#605)

## Overview
saveConsents was mutating the consents object in place and setting the
same reference back. Now it spreads into a new object ({ ...consents }),
so he reference always changes.

has, hasConsented, getDisplayedConsents are wrapped in useCallback with
reactive deps like [consents]. When the consents reference changes,
useCallback returns a new function reference. React Compiler caches
based on function identity.

fix: add NODE_AUTH_TOKEN for npm publish auth (#686)

## Summary

- Adds `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` env var (set to `NPM_RELEASE_TOKEN` secret) to
all three release steps (production, canary, RC)
- Fixes the E404 errors that caused all 7 packages to fail publishing at
v1.8.6

## Root Cause

`actions/setup-node@v4` with `registry-url` creates an `.npmrc` at
`$RUNNER_TEMP` that references `${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`, and sets
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` to point to it. The changesets action creates
`~/.npmrc` using `${NPM_TOKEN}`, but npm **ignores** it because
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` takes precedence.

Since the workflow only set `NPM_TOKEN` (not `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`), npm was
authenticating with an empty token — resulting in E404 for all publish
attempts.

The previous `npm install -g npm@latest` step (removed in #684) likely
reset the npm config chain, masking this issue. Once that step was
removed, auth broke.

## Test plan
- [ ] Merge to main → release workflow re-runs → 1.8.6 publishes
successfully to npm
- [ ] Verify `npm view @c15t/backend@1.8.6` returns package info after
publish

## Overview
feat(backend): add OTel instrumentation and strip PII from spans

Instrument DB, cache, external, and request operations with
OpenTelemetry
   spans and metrics across handlers, registries, and the GVL resolver.
Strip PII from span attributes by removing error.message, error.stack,
   and http.path; sanitize external URLs to drop query params; and use
hostname-only span names for external calls. Consolidate error handling
   into a shared exported handleSpanError function.

Add e2e test with real InMemorySpanExporter that enforces an attribute
key allowlist and blocks PII value patterns (IPs, emails, stack traces,
   query strings) across all span types.

fix(react): react compiler compatability (#605)

## Overview
saveConsents was mutating the consents object in place and setting the
same reference back. Now it spreads into a new object ({ ...consents }),
so he reference always changes.

has, hasConsented, getDisplayedConsents are wrapped in useCallback with
reactive deps like [consents]. When the consents reference changes,
useCallback returns a new function reference. React Compiler caches
based on function identity.

Fixes #604

feat: policy packs (#637) - Added policy packs for flexible backends, no hard coded values - Improved support for headless components > [!NOTE] > ### Add policy packs for jurisdiction-aware consent resolution with snapshot signing and offline fallback > - Introduces a `PolicyConfig`/policy pack system where ordered packs of rules are matched by country/region to produce a `ResolvedPolicy` with model, UI hints, categories, and proof settings; unmatched packs fall back to a `no_banner` policy. > - The `/init` route resolves a policy decision per request, creates a signed JWT snapshot token (`policySnapshotToken`), and gates IAB fields (GVL, translations) on the resolved model being `iab`. > - The `POST /subjects` handler verifies the snapshot token at write time, enforces policy category scope (strict/permissive), applies purpose allowlists, and persists a deduplicated `runtimePolicyDecision` record linked to each consent row. > - The client store detects material policy fingerprint changes and resets stored consent when the active policy changes, and seeds `policyBanner`/`policyDialog` UI hints into state. > - React components (`ConsentBanner`, `ConsentWidget`, `IABConsentBanner`, `IABConsentDialog`) now render only policy-allowed actions in policy-determined order/layout via new `useHeadlessConsentUI` and `useHeadlessIABConsentUI` hooks. > - Adds `policyPackPresets` with regional defaults (Europe opt-in/IAB, California opt-in/opt-out, Quebec opt-in, world no-banner) and a CLI codemod `offline-add-policy-packs` to inject starter packs into existing offline configs. > - DevTools gains a dedicated Policy tab showing resolved policy identity, UI surface config, proof settings, and match trace; the Location panel and panel footer show init source metadata. > - Risk: `POST /subjects` returns HTTP 400 for disallowed categories in strict scope mode, and stored consent is silently reset when the material policy fingerprint changes. > > > > Macroscope summarized 3dddfa6. > > --------- Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.6

## Main thread impact

### Before: style injection blocks the main thread

```
Main thread ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │ Parse JS (435 KB, includes 244 KB CSS strings)
  │ Execute JS
  │   ├─ createElement("style") × 9    ← synchronous DOM mutation
  │   ├─ textContent = "..." × 9       ← 244 KB of CSS strings
  │   ├─ head.appendChild() × 9        ← triggers style recalc each time
  │   └─ style recalculation × 9       ← browser recomputes all styles
  │ React render
  │ First styled paint                  ← styles only available AFTER JS runs
  ▼
```

### After: CSS loads off the main thread

```
Main thread ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │ Parse JS (361 KB, no CSS strings)   ← 74 KB less to parse
  │ Execute JS                          ← no DOM mutations for styles
  │ React render
  │ First styled paint
  ▼
Network ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │ Fetch styles.css (7.4 KB gzip)     ← parallel with JS, off main thread
  │ Parse CSS (native engine)           ← ~10x faster than JS string→DOM
  │ Single style recalculation          ← one pass, not 9
  ▼
```

from test jobs (turbo remote cache handles deduplication), adds bun
install + Playwright browser caching via a reusable composite action,
introduces path filtering to skip CI on docs-only changes, and adds
concurrency control to cancel stale PR runs. Bun is pinned to `1.3.11`
across all workflows to match the `packageManager` field.

encapsulates bun setup, dependency caching (`~/.bun/install/cache`),
`bun install`, and optional Playwright browser caching
(`~/.cache/ms-playwright`)

all jobs now run in parallel after a lightweight `changes` gate. Turbo

fix: resolve npm auth and upgrade issues in release workflow (#695)

## Overview

Ports the release workflow fixes from `main` to the `2.0.0` branch. The
release workflow was failing due to two issues: Node.js 22.22.2's
bundled npm has a corrupted `promise-retry` module that breaks `npm
install -g`, and `actions/setup-node`'s `.npmrc` uses `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`
(not `NPM_TOKEN`), causing E404 publish errors.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

## Implementation Details

### Key Changes
1. **Fixed npm upgrade order** — moved npm upgrade step before `bun
install` and added a `promise-retry` workaround for Node.js 22.22.2's
broken bundled npm
2. **Added `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`** to all three release steps (canary, RC,
production) — `actions/setup-node`'s `.npmrc` uses this env var via
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG`, taking precedence over `NPM_TOKEN`
3. **Updated bun-version** from pinned `1.3.11` to `latest`

### Technical Notes
- `actions/setup-node@v4` with `registry-url` creates an `.npmrc`
referencing `${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`. This config takes precedence via
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG`, so setting only `NPM_TOKEN` resulted in an
empty auth token.
- The old `npm install -g npm@latest` step was placed after `bun
install` and would fail on Node.js 22.22.2 due to a missing
`promise-retry` dependency. The fix installs `promise-retry` globally
first (with error suppression) before upgrading npm.

feat: simplify static prefetch consumption before 2.0 GA (#712)

## Overview
Replace the RC static-prefetch consumer flow with automatic
request-context matching so static routes only need to start `/init`
early while dynamic SSR continues to use `fetchInitialData()` unchanged.
This adds canonical request-context metadata to SSR and browser-prefetch
payloads, auto-consumes matching prefetched data during first hosted
store initialization, and updates docs/templates/examples to the smaller
GA API surface.

## Related Issue
Fixes #711

## Type of Change
- [x] ✨ Enhancement (improves existing functionality)
- [x] 📚 Documentation
- [x] 🏗️ Refactor (no functional changes)
- [x] ⚡ Performance

## Implementation Details
### Key Changes
1. Added request-context metadata and matching helpers for SSR and
browser-prefetch payloads, including canonical backend URL handling and
ambient GPC checks.
2. Switched hosted runtime initialization to auto-consume matching
prefetched data on first store creation, and changed SSR reuse to skip
only on `context_mismatch` instead of any override.
3. Removed the public RC prefetch consumer exports and updated docs,
templates, and benchmark/example providers to the automatic model.

### Before / After
Static route setup no longer needs a separate consumer API in the
provider.

```tsx
// Before
import { ConsentManagerProvider, getPrefetchedInitialData } from '@c15t/nextjs';

<ConsentManagerProvider
  options={{
    mode: 'hosted',
    backendURL: '/api/c15t',
    ssrData: getPrefetchedInitialData({
      backendURL: '/api/c15t',
      overrides: { country: 'DE', region: 'BE', language: 'de' },
    }),
  }}
/>

// After
import { ConsentManagerProvider } from '@c15t/nextjs';

<ConsentManagerProvider
  options={{
    mode: 'hosted',
    backendURL: '/api/c15t',
    overrides: { country: 'DE', region: 'BE', language: 'de' },
  }}
/>
```

SSR-prefetched data is now reused when the effective request context
matches instead of being invalidated by any override.

```ts
// Before
if (!ssrData || get().overrides) {
  set({ ssrDataUsed: false, ssrSkippedReason: 'no_data' });
  return undefined;
}

// After
if (!ssrData) {
  set({ ssrDataUsed: false, ssrSkippedReason: 'no_data' });
  return undefined;
}

if (data?.init && !shouldReuseSSRData(config, data)) {
  set({ ssrDataUsed: false, ssrSkippedReason: 'context_mismatch' });
  return undefined;
}
```

### Technical Notes
Dynamic SSR stays explicit and unchanged; browser-prefetch reuse is
internal-only and first-initialization-only, so cached runtimes do not
adopt newly discovered prefetched data later.

- Introduces manifest step types for `loadScript`, `setGlobal`,
`callGlobal`, `pushToDataLayer`, and `inlineScript`
- Splits manifest handling into compile and runtime phases:
- `compileManifest()` interpolates config and normalizes install/setup
artifacts
- `resolvedManifestToScript()` converts the resolved manifest into
runtime `Script` objects and lifecycle hooks
- Supports consent signaling for Google Consent Mode style integrations
via manifest metadata

resolves for the same manifest + config reuse the compiled manifest
- Keeps the manifest architecture while reducing repeated compile
overhead on hot paths
- Preserves room for targeted imperative overrides where a vendor needs
a more specialized runtime path

Moves policy-driven action resolution utilities into `c15t` core so
non-React runtimes can share the same logic:

Fi branding sizing across host pages (#730)

## Overview
The prebuilt consent surfaces treated the INTH full logo differently
from the c15t wordmark, which left the raw `svg` exposed to host-page
CSS and caused it to either balloon or collapse in consumer apps. This
change wraps the INTH wordmark in the shared internal container and adds
explicit sizing rules on the wrapper and nested `svg`, so the stock
branding path stays stable across docs, marketing pages, and other
embedded shells.

## Related Issue
Fixes #719

1. Wrap the INTH full logo in the shared LTR wordmark container in
`@c15t/react` so it uses the same internal structure as the c15t
branding path.
2. Add explicit flex, max-width, display, and aspect-ratio rules in
`@c15t/ui` so host-page `svg` rules cannot blow up or collapse the INTH
logo.

`@c15t/nextjs` is included because its styled surfaces consume the same
React/UI branding path and should ship aligned package versions with the
CSS hardening.

fix: add NODE_AUTH_TOKEN for npm publish auth (#686)

## Summary

- Adds `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` env var (set to `NPM_RELEASE_TOKEN` secret) to
all three release steps (production, canary, RC)
- Fixes the E404 errors that caused all 7 packages to fail publishing at
v1.8.6

## Root Cause

`actions/setup-node@v4` with `registry-url` creates an `.npmrc` at
`$RUNNER_TEMP` that references `${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`, and sets
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` to point to it. The changesets action creates
`~/.npmrc` using `${NPM_TOKEN}`, but npm **ignores** it because
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` takes precedence.

Since the workflow only set `NPM_TOKEN` (not `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`), npm was
authenticating with an empty token — resulting in E404 for all publish
attempts.

The previous `npm install -g npm@latest` step (removed in #684) likely
reset the npm config chain, masking this issue. Once that step was
removed, auth broke.

successfully to npm

Harden CI supply chain security (#853)

## Summary

This hardens the repository against the GitHub Actions cache-poisoning
and privileged-PR workflow class described in the May 2026 TanStack
incident.

Changes include:
- remove the docs deploy workflow
- replace remaining `pull_request_target` usage with safer PR/workflow
patterns
- prevent PR jobs from receiving Turbo remote-cache credentials
- replace write-capable cache usage with restore-only cache usage where
cache writes are not needed
- remove long-lived npm publish token env vars from release jobs so
publishing relies on OIDC trusted publishing
- pin third-party GitHub Actions and CI tools to fixed versions or
commit SHAs
- add a zizmor GitHub Actions security workflow
- add Bun install cooldown settings via `bunfig.toml`
- require CODEOWNERS review for `.github/` changes from both core
maintainers
- add `SECURITY_HARDENING.md` as a reusable guide and prompt for
bringing other OSS repos to the same baseline

## Validation

- `ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Dir[".github/workflows/*.{yml,yaml}",
".github/actions/*/action.yml"].each { |f| YAML.load_file(f) }; puts
"workflow yaml ok"'`
- `rg` risky-pattern scan for privileged PR workflows, write caches, npm
token env vars, direct Turbo secret env in PR jobs, floating Bun/tool
versions: no matches
- `rg` action-ref scan for non-SHA third-party action refs: no matches
- `bun install --frozen-lockfile --dry-run --ignore-scripts`

## Follow-up Admin Settings

After merge, confirm npm trusted publishing is configured for every
published package, remove stale npm publish secrets from repository/org
settings, and make CODEOWNERS plus the GitHub Actions security workflow
required in branch protection or rulesets.

feat(scripts): add daily live vendor script monitor (#903)

Closes #899

## Summary

Adds a Playwright-based **live vendor probe harness** for every built-in
`@c15t/scripts` integration, plus a daily GitHub Actions monitor that
opens/updates deduped issues when a vendor's live loader behavior breaks
— the class of failure static jsdom tests can't see (like the Microsoft
Clarity loader change).

### How it works

`packages/scripts/live-vendors/` contains a runner that bundles a
browser harness with `Bun.build`, serves it locally, and drives real
Chromium through five phases per vendor:

1. **consent** — with denied consent, the script must not load and no
loader request may leave the page
2. **bootstrap** — queue stubs/globals seeded by the manifest must exist
immediately after `loadScripts()`, before the network answers
3. **load** — the real vendor loader must respond (full tier requires a
2xx JavaScript response; `loader-only` accepts placeholder-id
rejections, including Chromium ORB-filtered error pages)
4. **runtime** — the real vendor SDK must initialize (full tier, polled)
5. **network** — every third-party request outside the loader allowlist
is answered with an empty 204, so probes never send real analytics data

Failed probes retry once; every run writes a JSON report. A registry
coverage test makes CI fail if a vendor is added to the registry without
a live probe config, so future integrations (#873–#881) must ship with
live coverage.

### Workflow

`.github/workflows/script-vendor-monitor.yml` — daily at 06:30 UTC +
`workflow_dispatch` with optional vendor filter. Separate from PR CI so
transient third-party failures never block PRs. Opens one deduped issue
per failing vendor (`[vendor-script-monitor] <vendor> live script
contract failed`), comments while it keeps failing, auto-closes on
recovery. Issue planning logic is pure and unit-tested. zizmor-clean.

### Results

Full sweep: **26/26 vendors pass** — 20 full tier (real SDKs boot from
vendor CDNs: gtag, PostHog, Meta Pixel, TikTok, Intercom, …), 6
loader-only with documented placeholder-id limitations (GTM 404s fake
containers, Clarity answers 204, etc.). Upgrading loader-only vendors to
full tier needs real test-account ids as repo secrets — tracked as a
follow-up.

**The first sweep found a real bug**: the live Mixpanel SDK rejects our
stub with `Mixpanel error: Version mismatch` and never initializes (our
manifest bootstrap lacks the snippet contract, e.g. `__SV`). Fix lands
as a stacked PR.

### Local usage

```sh
bun run --filter @c15t/scripts test:live-vendors
bun run --filter @c15t/scripts test:live-vendors -- --vendor microsoft-clarity
```

fix(scripts): implement Mixpanel snippet contract so the SDK initializes (#905)

Fixes #904. Stacked on #903 (the live vendor monitor that found this
bug).

## Summary

The `mixpanel-analytics` manifest seeded `window.mixpanel = []` with
queue methods but never implemented Mixpanel's snippet contract. The
live SDK checks the snippet version marker and bails with:

```
Mixpanel error: Version mismatch; please ensure you're using the latest version of the Mixpanel code snippet.
```

…so in production the SDK loaded but **never initialized, and queued
`track`/`identify` calls were silently dropped**.

### Fix

The manifest bootstrap now reproduces the official snippet contract
(verified against the unminified `mixpanel-2-latest.js` source):

- `mixpanel.__SV = 1.2` — without it `init_from_snippet` refuses to boot
- `mixpanel._i = [[token, initOptions, 'mixpanel']]` — the pending init
tuple `init_from_snippet` consumes at load. The explicit `'mixpanel'`
instance name is load-bearing: `create_mplib` resolves the queue stub
through `mixpanel_master[name]`, so a two-element tuple makes the SDK
create an orphan instance and leave the stub in place (silently — no
console error)
- the `afterLoad` `mixpanel.init(...)` call is removed; init happens
through the snippet registry like the official snippet

Queued calls already used the right format (`[method, ...args]` arrays),
so they replay correctly via `_execute_array` once init actually runs.

The live probe for mixpanel is upgraded back to **full tier** with a
runtime assertion that the real SDK reports `__loaded` — the monitor now
guards this contract daily.

(unit + e2e contract tests updated to assert the snippet contract)

- [x] Live probe against the real CDN: `test:live-vendors -- --vendor
mixpanel-analytics` → ✅ full tier, SDK reports `__loaded`, no

Closes #914. Stacked on #913 (Heap) — continues the monitor/integration

## Summary

The live vendor monitor previously skipped the consent phase for
`alwaysLoad` vendors with "manages consent internally; not asserted".
That left our riskiest trust assumption unverified: GTM and Mixpanel run
for **every** visitor, including users who denied consent.

The consent phase now runs a **denied-consent egress assertion** for
these vendors in an isolated browser context (so warmed caches never
contaminate the granted-consent probe):

1. Load the vendor with denied consent through the production script
loader
2. Let the real SDK initialize and attempt collection (4s quiet window)
3. Assert **zero requests to the vendor's collection endpoints** — a
blocked attempt is still a violation, the attempt proves intent
4. Assert **zero vendor cookies/localStorage** (per-vendor prefixes;
consent-state markers like Mixpanel's `__mp_opt_in_out_*` are legitimate
and excluded)

Consent-safe traffic is excluded via explicit per-vendor allow/violation
lists — Google Consent Mode's cookieless pings are safe by design, so
GTM's violation list names real collection endpoints (`/g/collect`,
doubleclick) and ad-storage cookies (`_ga*`, `_gcl*`) only.

## Summary

- remove the pre-load `window.clarity.v` marker from the Microsoft
Clarity stub so Clarity's own loader no longer treats c15t as a
duplicate install
- switch c15t's Clarity synchronization to Consent V2 with `ad_Storage`

## Context

Microsoft's current `clarity-js` queue processor exits early when

`clarity.js`, no collect calls, and no dashboard data.

Microsoft's implementation sets `window.clarity.v` only after the real
runtime replaces the queued stub, so the c15t stub should only queue
calls. This also updates the helper to use Clarity Consent V2 instead of
the older boolean consent API.

fix(backend): support drizzle-orm 0.45.x (#900)

## Summary

Fixes #867

Installing `@c15t/backend` alongside `drizzle-orm@0.45.x` fails with an
unmet peer dependency error:

```
└─┬ @c15t/backend 2.1.0
  └─┬ fumadb 0.2.2
    └── ✕ unmet peer drizzle-orm@^0.44.0: found 0.45.2
```

`@c15t/backend` pins `fumadb@0.2.2`, whose optional peer range is
`drizzle-orm@^0.44.0`. The drizzle coupling lives entirely inside fumadb
— `@c15t/backend/db/adapters/drizzle` is a thin re-export of
`fumadb/adapters/drizzle` and the repo never imports `drizzle-orm`
directly.

## Changes

- **Bump `fumadb` 0.2.2 → 0.3.0** in `packages/backend`. This widens the
optional peer ranges to `drizzle-orm@^0.44.0 || ^0.45.0`, `prisma@6.x.x
|| 7.x.x`, and `mongodb@6.x.x || 7.x.x`. The upstream 0.2.2 → 0.3.0 diff
touches only the Prisma adapter (Prisma 7 support) plus dep/tooling
bumps — no changes to the drizzle/kysely/mongo/typeorm adapters, schema
builder, or migration engine.
- **Bump `kysely` 0.28.15 → 0.28.17** in `examples/demo`. fumadb 0.3.0
requires `kysely@^0.28.16`, so the stale pin created a duplicate kysely
copy and a nominal `Kysely<unknown>` / `#private` type clash in the demo
build; aligning dedupes back to a single copy.
- Add patch changeset for `@c15t/backend`.

### Why not fumadb 0.4.0 (latest)?

0.4.0 has the same widened drizzle range but bumps the optional typeorm
peer from `0.x.x` to `^1` (typeorm 1.0.0 just went stable) and moves to
kysely 0.29. That would hand typeorm 0.3.x and kysely 0.28.x users the
exact same class of peer/type conflict this PR fixes for drizzle users.
0.3.0 fixes the reported issue while breaking no one; 0.4.0 can be a
deliberate follow-up bump later.

Fix consent dedupe race without a schema change (#863)

## Summary

Fixes #861 by making consent creation idempotent for concurrent
identical `POST /subjects` requests, without a database schema change or
migration.

The issue's reproduction uses the same subject, domain, policy, and
`givenAt`. Those requests now derive the same `consent.id`, so the
existing primary-key constraint rejects the losing insert and the
handler returns the winner.

## Scope: identical requests and double taps

The backend deduplicates the issue's exact case: identical request
bodies with the same `givenAt`. Requests with different timestamps
remain distinct consent events.

c15t's client store now also coalesces concurrent saves with the same
intent while the first save is in flight. This covers a real double tap
through the banner/headless store even though two independently
generated requests would otherwise receive different `Date.now()`
values. Direct API callers, separate tabs, or separate processes that
intentionally submit different `givenAt` values are not merged.

Network retries and offline-queue replay already preserve the request
body, so they are protected by the deterministic primary key.

## What changed

- Derive `consent.id` from tenant, subject, domain, policy, and
`givenAt`.
- Recover unique conflicts outside the transaction, because PostgreSQL
aborts the transaction after a failed statement.
- Coalesce concurrent identical banner and policy-consent saves in the
core store.
- Use one indexed primary-key lookup for current submissions.
- Retain a field-based compatibility lookup only when the submitted
timestamp could belong to a row written by a pre-deterministic-ID
process.
- Remove the redundant in-transaction consent re-check; the primary-key
insert and bounded retry loop provide the exclusion.
- Reject timestamps outside JavaScript's representable `Date` range
before calling `toISOString()`.

## Why not a `dedupeKey` column

FumaDB schemas are immutable and migrations are generated by diffing
versions. Editing schema `2.0.0` in place generates no DDL for a
database already at `2.0.0`, while the runtime then queries a column
that does not exist. Existing deployments would fail consent reads and
writes.

The primary key already exists and is uniquely enforced on every
supported database, so using it avoids a migration and a production
index build.

## Compatibility and ordering notes

- Existing rows retain random IDs. Old, backdated, and future-skewed
submissions use the compatibility lookup after an ID miss.
- The time-ordered portion of a deterministic consent ID reflects client
`givenAt`, not server insertion time. Pre-2023-11-14 timestamps share
the zero timestamp prefix. No current consent handler orders or
paginates by ID; this should be revisited before introducing ID-based
cursors.
- Fractional epoch-millisecond values remain accepted. Only values that
cannot be represented by `Date` are rejected.

## Validation

- PostgreSQL/PGlite HTTP integration: real FumaDB migration, real
`23505` primary-key conflict, rollback recovery, concurrent submissions,
retry, and distinct timestamps.
- Core store unit coverage for concurrent banner and policy-consent
double taps.
- Backend unit coverage for the one-read hot path, legacy fallback,
bounded retries, and conflict recovery.
- Schema unit coverage for representable bounds, including fractional
and negative timestamps.
- `c15t`: 507 tests passed.
- `@c15t/backend`: 546 tests passed.
- `@c15t/schema`: 95 tests passed.
- Type checks and Biome passed for all affected packages.

No database migration is required.

Clamp future consent time to server time (#862)

## Summary

Clamp `POST /subjects` consent `givenAt` timestamps that are more than
five minutes ahead of server time to the server's current time.

This PR is stacked on #863 and should merge after it. It does not close
a GitHub issue; the future-clock-skew bug was found during review of the
consent deduplication path.

## Why

`givenAt` comes from the client's clock. A skewed device can report
consent arbitrarily far in the future, distorting the audit record and
pushing `validUntil = givenAt + expiryDays` out indefinitely.

Rejecting the request would prevent the affected user from recording
consent, so the backend records server time instead.

## Interaction with #863

The recorded timestamp changes on every retry because it uses current
server time. Consent identity therefore derives from the client's
original claim, while the clamped value is stored and returned. This
keeps a skewed client's retries idempotent.

#863 now independently rejects timestamps outside JavaScript's
representable `Date` range, so merging #863 first cannot turn `givenAt:
1e18` into a new `toISOString()` 500.

## What changed

- Clamp timestamps more than five minutes ahead of server time before
deriving `validUntil`.
- Preserve the original client claim as `metadata.clientGivenAt`.
- Derive identity from the original claim so retries remain stable.
- Read conflict winners by deterministic primary key.
- Synchronize local `consentInfo.time` from the timestamp returned by
the server, avoiding disagreement between local state and the returned
consent.
- Continue accepting fractional, negative, and past timestamps when they
are representable by JavaScript `Date`.

## Deferred scope

Past timestamps remain unbounded because choosing a lower bound requires
a product/compliance decision about legitimate offline replay.
Follow-up: #936.

The deterministic ID's time prefix reflects the client's claimed
timestamp rather than server insertion time. No current consent endpoint
orders by ID.

- Handler unit coverage for clamping, the tolerance boundary, past
replay, metadata, `validUntil`, stable retry identity, and conflict
recovery.
- Core store unit coverage that local consent time follows the
server-recorded value.

passed.

fix(react): apply CSP nonce to injected styles and scripts (#949)

Closes #948

## Problem

c15t injects its theme tokens as `<style id="c15t-theme">`, and that
element carried no nonce. Under a nonce-based Content Security Policy
the browser refuses it:

```
Refused to apply inline style because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "style-src-elem ..."
```

The only workaround was allowing `'unsafe-inline'`.

It was worse than a missed prop: `nonce` was not part of the provider
options at all — not in `CoreOptions`, `UIOptions`,
`CommonInlineStoreOptions`, or `ConsentManagerContentOptions` — so a
value passed there was dropped at the type boundary before it could
reach a DOM node.

## Fix

A single top-level `nonce` option, forwarded to everything c15t injects.

```tsx
<ConsentManagerProvider options={{ mode: 'offline', nonce }}>
  {children}
</ConsentManagerProvider>
```

**Theme stylesheet**
- `nonce?: string` on `CommonInlineStoreOptions` (public,
framework-facing — the options reference table renders from it) and on
`StoreConfig` in core. The core declaration is enough on its own for
three things: `StoreOptions extends Partial<StoreConfig>` accepts it,
`StoreRuntimeState extends StoreConfig` exposes it in state, and the
existing `...storeConfigOptions` spread populates it with no extra
wiring.
- The provider passes it to the `<style>` element.

**Script loader**
- `nonce` added to the shared `ScriptLoaderOptions` bag and resolved at
the single element-creation site as `script.nonce ?? options?.nonce`, so
a per-script value still wins.
- Threaded from state at both call sites (`updateScripts` and
`reloadScript`), which covers scripts declared in provider options *and*
scripts registered later via `setScripts`.

Without this second part a strict-CSP app hits the identical wall on
`script-src` the moment it uses the script loader, and today's only
answer is repeating the nonce on every script entry.

## Tests

- `provider-nonce.test.tsx` — the original issue repro (verified failing
before the fix) plus a negative case. Asserts via `styleEl.nonce` rather
than `getAttribute`, since browsers hide the content attribute once a
policy is live.
- 6 script-loader tests: 3 unit (loader default, per-script override,
neither set) and 3 store-level integration proving `options.nonce`
reaches the injected element.

`check-types` passes repo-wide. Full suites green: core 519, react 397,
plus ui and nextjs.

## Docs

A shared "Content Security Policy" section imported into the React and
Next provider pages, including a Next-specific middleware → `headers()`
→ provider example. The stale per-script CSP advice in
`next/script-loader.mdx` now points at the provider option.

## Notes for review

- The `nonce` option covers elements c15t injects. It does not cover
inline `style="..."` attributes, which CSP governs through
`style-src-attr` — a directive that ignores nonces entirely. Documented
as a caveat, since the reporter's policy sets `style-src-attr 'self'`.
- Unrelated and not addressed here: `noStyle: true` does not currently
suppress the theme `<style>` element; the provider renders it
unconditionally. Happy to file that separately.

ci: cache Playwright browsers and the Turborepo local cache (#953)

Stacked on #952 — both PRs rewrite overlapping parts of `ci.yml`. Base
retargets to `canary` automatically once #952 merges.

## Why

Measured on CI run `30625455595`, nothing in this repo's CI is cached:

- `Remote caching disabled`, `Cached: 0 cached, 47 total` — every turbo
task cold on every PR.
- `actions/cache/restore` for Playwright is the **only** cache action in
the repo. Nothing saves it, so it reported `Cache not found for input
keys` and re-downloaded Chromium — **32s** of the test job's 171s.
- No `.turbo` persistence to substitute for the disabled remote cache.

Note this is unrelated to Turborepo's Git worktree cache sharing, which
is already working — that redirects a linked worktree's cache to the
main worktree and is local-only. CI does a fresh clone, not a worktree,
so it contributes nothing here.

## Changes

**Playwright.** `actions/cache/restore` → `actions/cache`, so the
post-step actually writes the key. Re-keyed on the resolved Playwright
version instead of `hashFiles('bun.lock')` — browsers only change when
Playwright does, and lockfile churn was invalidating them on every
unrelated dependency bump (this repo bumps the lockfile often;
affected-scoping in #952 makes lockfile changes a full run anyway).

**Turborepo local cache.** All three jobs restore `.turbo/cache`
read-only. The **test job is the single writer** — it builds every
package as a dependency of `test`, so its cache is the most complete,
and one writer avoids concurrent-save conflicts on the same key.

Saves are gated to `push` only. PR runs restore read-only, which keeps
them from churning the 10GB repo budget and matches the posture already
chosen for `TURBO_TOKEN`. GitHub scopes caches per branch, so a PR
cannot write into canary's scope regardless.

**Pruning.** Restored entries carry into each save, so the cache would
grow without bound across pushes and evict everything else. It's pruned
newest-first to a 1GB ceiling before saving.

## Testing

- actionlint clean, including its shellcheck pass over the prune script.
- Prune pipeline tested against real files: 20 x 100KB with staggered
mtimes and a 1MB limit → exactly 10 survivors, the 10 newest. Correct
ordering and cutoff.
- Verified the resolved step graph: 3 read-only restores, save gated to
`push`, prune non-fatal.

**Not verified locally:** the prune uses `find -printf` and `xargs -r`,
which are GNU-only — no GNU findutils or working container runtime on
this machine, so only the `sort | awk | xargs` half ran here. Two
deliberate mitigations: the prune runs on **every** event rather than
only on pushes, so this PR's own CI exercises it; and it is
`continue-on-error: true`, so a failure means a larger cache, never a
failed build. Worth reading its log line on this PR before merge.

The **save** path still cannot be exercised until this is on a push to
`canary` — check the first post-merge run.

## Expected effect

~32s from Playwright plus cold-build savings on the test job. Roughly 3
min → ~2 min. Modest, because the repo is already fast; the point is
that both were straightforward gaps.

## Separately

`Failed to restore: Cache service responded with 400` appears in **Setup
Bun** on all three jobs. That is `oven-sh/setup-bun`'s own bundled
cache, not `actions/cache` — the pinned `actions/cache` v4.3.0 reported
a clean miss with no 400. Not touched here.

ci: fix coverage reporting and dedupe the coverage workflow (#955)

Stacked on #953 (which is stacked on #952). Bases retarget automatically
as each merges.

## The bug

Coverage reporting has failed on **every run since at least
2026-07-27**. I traced it: it is a typo, not a path or artifact problem.

The `report` job succeeds and produces a perfectly correct matrix —
verified against a real run:

```
coverage-artifacts/packages/logger/coverage/coverage-summary.json
"summary_path": "coverage-artifacts/packages/logger/coverage/coverage-summary.json"
```

All 11 matrix jobs then fail at the reporting action with `ENOENT` on
`/home/runner/work/c15t/c15t/coverage/coverage-summary.json` — the
action's **default** path. The workflow passed:

```yaml
json_summary_path: ...   # underscores
json_final_path: ...
```

but reading `action.yml` at the pinned SHA, the inputs are
**hyphenated**:

```
json-summary-path
json-final-path
```

GitHub Actions silently discards unknown inputs, so the action never
received the paths and fell back to its default. `name` happens to be a
real input, which is why the job titles looked correct and masked it.

## Changes

- **Fix the input names.** The actual bug.
- **Pass `pr-number` explicitly.** `workflow_run` carries no
`pull_request` payload, so the action cannot work out which PR to
comment on — its `pr-number` default is empty. Resolved from
`workflow_run.pull_requests`, with a fallback lookup by head SHA because
fork PRs arrive with that array empty.
- **Replace the blanket `continue-on-error`** on the artifact download
(added in #952) with an explicit existence probe. CodeRabbit's point on
#952 was fair: unconditional tolerance masks genuine download failures.
Now an absent artifact skips cleanly and a real failure still fails
loudly.
- **Declare the scopes both jobs need.** Specifying `permissions` sets
every unlisted scope to `none`, and the jobs need `actions: read` to
reach the triggering run's artifacts and `contents: read` for the
head-SHA lookup.
- **Delete `ci-coverage.yml`** — byte-identical to `coverage-report.yml`
apart from one stale comment. Both were named "Report Coverage" and both
fired on every CI completion, doubling compute and PR comments.
- Fix the "afterwards" spelling static analysis flagged on #952.

## Testing

- actionlint clean across all workflows, including its shellcheck pass
over the two new script steps.
- **Every input we pass validated against the action's real
`action.yml`** at the pinned SHA: `name`, `json-summary-path`,
`json-final-path`, `pr-number` all ✓. This is the check that would have
caught the original bug.
- Confirmed `canary` has no branch protection, so removing a workflow
drops no required check.
- Confirmed the two coverage workflows differed only by one comment line
before deleting one.

## Caveat on verification — please read before merging

**None of this can be exercised by CI on this PR.** `workflow_run`
workflows always run the **default branch's** copy of their own
definition, so any change here only takes effect once it is on `canary`.
That is also why the #952 artifact fix still shows red on these PRs.

Because each iteration costs a full merge cycle rather than a push, I
front-loaded robustness rather than fixing only the typo and seeing what
happened next — hence resolving `pr-number` and the permission scopes in
the same change.

**After merge, check the first coverage run for:** `Resolved pull
request: <n>`, `Matching artifacts: <n>`, and an actual coverage comment
on the PR. If the comment still does not appear, `pr-number` resolution
is the next thing to look at.

fix(scripts): seed PostHog snippet init queue so array.js installs (#982)

Fixes #981.

## What broke

PostHog JS 1.410.2 added a duplicate-loader guard. When `window.posthog`
already exists, `array.js` only installs its runtime if `posthog._i` is
an array. The c15t bootstrap stub had no `_i`, so the CDN script
returned successfully but left the noop stub installed and every event
was dropped.

## Minimal fix

Seed the pending-init registry as `{ _i: [] }`. This is the smallest
change that satisfies the upstream loader guard while preserving the
existing c15t lifecycle: the real SDK installs first, then the existing
load callback calls `posthog.init(...)`.

This PR intentionally contains only the hotfix, its regression test, and
a patch changeset. The unrelated Turbo cache change was moved to #994.

in flight.

- use PostHog root array queue with a complete `[token, config,
instanceName]` tuple in `_i`

Origins such as `capacitor://localhost` (the default iOS Capacitor origin),
`ionic://localhost`, and custom `iosScheme` values could not be used as
trusted origins.

`http://`, so `capacitor://localhost` parsed as the hostname `capacitor`.
That collapsed every `capacitor://` origin onto a single host, meaning a
trusted `capacitor://localhost` also trusted `capacitor://evil.com`. The
two origin matchers additionally disagreed, since `isOriginTrusted`
ignored schemes entirely while the CORS layer collapsed them.

Add a shared `app-scheme` helper used by both matchers. An entry naming a
non-web scheme is pinned to it and matched on scheme and host; entries
with no scheme or an http(s)/ws(s) scheme stay protocol-agnostic and match
exactly as before, so existing configurations are unaffected.

`www.` was stripped from both sides of the exact-hostname comparison
regardless of scheme, so a trusted `capacitor://localhost` also matched
the distinct origin `capacitor://www.localhost`. That contradicted the
exact scheme-and-host guarantee and disagreed with `createCORSOptions`,
which already rejected it.

Apply the `www.` equivalence only to entries with no app scheme, leaving
the web-domain convention unchanged.

fix(backend): correct www handling in CORS origin matching (#1013)

> 📚 Stacked on #1012. Review that one first — this branch contains only
the `www` fix.

## Overview

Two trusted-origin configurations silently failed to match the origins
they should. Both are pre-existing and unrelated to #1012; I confirmed
them against an unmodified `origin/canary` worktree.

| Trusted entry | Origin | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `*.example.com` | `https://www.example.com` | **null** | allowed |
| `*.example.com` | `https://api.example.com` | allowed | allowed |
| `*.example.com` | `https://example.com` (apex) | null | null |
| `www.example.com` | `https://example.com` | **null** | allowed |
| `www.example.com` | `https://www.example.com` | **null** | allowed |

So `*.example.com` allowed every subdomain *except* `www` — the one
people hit first — and a schemeless `www.example.com` entry matched
nothing at all, not even itself.

Both trace to one line: `normalizeOrigin` stripped `www.` off the
**incoming origin**. That turned `www.example.com` into the apex
`example.com`, which a `*.` wildcard deliberately excludes. And because
the schemeless branch returns before that strip, a schemeless trusted
entry kept a `www.` prefix the normalized origin could never carry.

## Related Issue

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

## Implementation Details

### Key Changes

1. **`normalizeOrigin`** — no longer strips `www.`; returns
`host[:port]` as-is. The catch-branch fallback strips only the protocol.
2. **`expandWithWWW`** — adds both the apex and the `www.` form of every
entry, whichever was configured. Wildcard entries are skipped: they
already cover every subdomain, and a `www.*.example.com` entry could
never match anything.

### Technical Notes

Moving the equivalence entirely onto the trusted list is what makes both
cases work from one change. The origin is now compared verbatim, so
wildcard matching sees the real hostname.

`isOriginTrusted` already handled both cases correctly, so this also
removes a disagreement between the two matchers.

## Summary

Rebuilds `examples/demo` for customer calls and fixes the bugs it
surfaced — two of them real library bugs that made IAB TCF unusable in
offline mode.

### Library fixes (with changesets)

- **`@c15t/iab`**: the `iab()` factory never injected `fetchGVL` into
its runtime module, so offline mode (and the hosted fallback path) could
never load the Global Vendor List — the IAB banner silently never
rendered. The GVL is now also requested with the resolved language
(`Accept-Language`), so purpose/feature names are localized.
- **`c15t`**: `setOverrides`/`setLanguage` re-initialized without the
IAB config, so the store kept a stale GVL after a language or location
change (e.g. English purpose names after switching to French).
- **`@c15t/ui` + `@c15t/react`**: new `consentActions.primary` theme
key. Themes could only pin treatments to specific actions, which fought
the policy's `primaryActions`. Now the policy decides *which* action is
primary and the theme decides *how* primary looks. The IAB banner
previously hardcoded its button variants and bypassed `consentActions`
entirely; it now resolves through the same helper with stock treatments
as the fallback.

- **Offline-first**: offline mode is the default and the only mode shown
on the sales-facing page (policy simulation only works offline). The
Offline/Hosted toggle remains on the `/self-host` dev page.

chore: add GitHub issue label taxonomy (#1019)

## Overview

Adds a `labels.yml` source of truth for GitHub labels and points the
issue templates at names that actually exist.

The old set mixed emoji kind labels (`✨ feature`, `🐛 bug`) with template
names that did not match (`enhancement`, `documentation`,
`needs-triage`). New issues often landed unlabeled. This replaces that
with:

- **Kind:** `bug`, `feature`, `docs` — applied by the matching template
- **Area:** product surface (`area:react`, `area:nuxt`, `area:scripts`,
…), not package folder. v3 is one kernel plus thin adapters; Nuxt lives
in `packages/vue`, React Router is Remix not TanStack.
- **State:** maintainer-applied (`needs-repro`, `needs-approval`, `help
wanted`, …)
- **Unlabeled** means untriaged — there is no `needs-triage` label

`from_name` records the emoji renames so a labeler action can migrate
existing issues in place.

fallback in hosted mode), activeUI stays 'none' — no surface renders

finalizes it: applied response derives the real activeUI; an empty
response or a failed init promotes the placeholder to the effective
policy (compliance fallback — a missing banner is worse than a
default-copy one when the backend is unreachable).

policies (prefetch/SSR/manifest/offline config) are untouched and still
render in first paint/HTML.

React provider now dispatches init at kernel creation (client render)
instead of a post-hydration effect — the backend latency overlaps
hydration (-43ms at condition B); InitMount skips its first pass for

feat(v3): window.c15t debug object installed on client hydration by every adapter (#924)

## What

v3 successor to v2's `window.c15tStore`. Every framework adapter
installs a tiny, frozen `window.c15t` object on client-side hydration so
anyone can validate c15t is on a site and see what it's running:

```js
window.c15t
// { version: "2.1.0", pkg: "@c15t/vue", mode: "manifest" }
```

- `version` — c15t core version (same source as the `x-c15t-version`
header, #920)
- `pkg` — installed adapter package: `@c15t/react`, `@c15t/nextjs`,
`@c15t/vue`, `@c15t/svelte`
- `mode` — resolved transport: `hosted | offline | custom | manifest`

Deliberately **not** exposed: the store/kernel (unlike v2), backend URL,
or any consent state.

## How

The v3 kernel must stay pure (window exposure is pinned as an opt-in
adapter concern by the correctness gate in
`v3-correctness-gates.test.ts`), so this is a new core module —
`c15t/v3/modules/window-debug` — following the persistence/script-loader
create→dispose pattern:

- inert handle on SSR, identity-checked `dispose()` (an unmounting old
provider can't clobber a newer one's object), last-writer-wins
- no global `Window` type augmentation (exported `C15tWindowDebug` type
instead)

Adapter wiring at each client-boot spot:

- **React**: `WindowDebugMount` — `useEffect` + dynamic import (zero SSR
bytes, off the hydration path; chunk-load failure caught as
best-effort). `mode: 'c15t'` reports `hosted`;
`transport`/`endpointHandlers` report `custom`
- **Next.js**: `ConsentBoundary` passes internal `__debugPkg:
'@c15t/nextjs'`
- **Vue/Nuxt**: wired in `startVueConsentRuntime` behind the existing
`typeof document` gate; reports `manifest` vs `hosted`. Nuxt reports
`@c15t/vue` because that is the package users actually install — there
is no `@c15t/nuxt`
- **Svelte**: `onMount` disposer chain
- **Vanilla**: exported from `c15t/v3` + the new subpath for
self-composition

Also in this branch: the Nuxt plugin now registers the runtime disposer
via `nuxtApp.vueApp.onUnmount(...)`, mirroring the plain Vue plugin
(matters for hosts that explicitly unmount the app — tests,
microfrontends).

## SSR impact

None. All wiring is effect/mount/document-gated and the module itself is
inert without `window`; client cost is a single frozen 3-field object
assignment (no kernel subscription, no network).

(install shape, frozen, dispose identity, SSR no-op)

fix(ui,react,vue,svelte): cross-framework a11y parity + conformance enforcement (#929)

## Summary

The new Vue consent surfaces had diverged from React on accessibility —
focus states, focus snatching, what gets focused when, Escape handling,
and focus indicators. This PR converges focus management, keyboard, and
ARIA behavior across **React, Vue, and Svelte** (React as the reference,
per RFC 0003), and locks it in with a new **a11y conformance suite**
that runs for every framework so it can't drift again.

## Why

Vue shipped its own hand-rolled focus trap + `@vueuse` scroll lock
instead of the shared `@c15t/ui` utilities that React and Svelte use.
Every divergence flowed from that. Along the way the review surfaced
real bugs affecting **all** frameworks (invisible focus rings, a
focus-trap escape, a clipped accordion ring).

## Changes

**Focus management (`@c15t/ui` shared utils — all frameworks benefit)**
- Vue now consumes shared `setupFocusTrap` / `setupScrollLock`; initial
focus target, Tab/Shift+Tab wrapping, and focus restore now match
React/Svelte.
- Shared trap wraps correctly when Shift+Tab would leave the focused
container, guards restore with `isConnected`, and re-targets a
**remounted opener** (e.g. the floating dialog trigger unmounts while
the dialog is open) by `id`/`data-testid` so keyboard focus is never
dropped to `<body>`.

**Keyboard + ARIA**
- React `ConsentDialog` now closes on `Escape` (WAI-ARIA modal pattern,
matching Vue/Svelte); banners never close on Escape.
- Consistent `role="dialog"` / conditional `aria-modal`, decorative
overlay (`role="presentation"`, no click-to-dismiss), heading semantics
on titles.
- Modal containers are `tabindex="-1"` — programmatic focus target only
(so screen readers announce the surface on open), never a keyboard tab
stop, so they don't flash a focus ring on open.

**Focus indicators**
- Fixed missing keyboard focus rings on `stroke` / `lighter` / `ghost`
button variants — a v3 CSS specificity bug that silently crushed the
`:focus-visible` ring in every framework.
- Stopped the accordion item focus ring from being clipped by the
dialog's scroll container (inset the ring so overflow can't cut it).

**Test coverage / compat suite**
- New `a11y` conformance suite in `@c15t/conformance` that runs against
real renders for React/Vue/Svelte via the existing `TestDriver` (dialog
semantics, initial focus, trap wrapping both directions, Escape rules,
focus restore, visible focus indicators).
- Wired the previously-dormant contract / focus / keyboard play
functions into all four storybook apps.
- Canonical `data-testid`s on the Vue manager/dialog surfaces (`bun run
lint:testids` green).
- Vue storybook animations left on to match React/Svelte (parity-runner
freezes animation itself, so screenshots stay stable).

## Verification

- Unit/conformance: `@c15t/ui` 287, `@c15t/react` 807 (+1 pre-existing
expected fail), `@c15t/vue` 55, `@c15t/svelte` 180 — all green.
- Storybook play suites (run in real Chromium): React 22/22 suites (57
tests), Vue 10/10 (33 tests), Svelte at baseline (3 pre-existing
unrelated IAB/primitive failures).
- `check-types` green across all touched packages; `lint:testids` green.
- Parity-runner: verified against a clean checkout at the merge-base —
the 8 remaining diffs (widget DOM/CSS, IAB a11y trees, stale screenshot
baseline) are **pre-existing upstream**; this PR introduces zero new
parity regressions.
- Behavior spot-checked in-browser across React/Vue/Svelte (focus ring
visibility, Escape, trap wrapping, animation).

- Parity screenshot baselines for the new stories are intentionally

Brings v3 up to date with `canary`, which it last took on 2026-06-19
(`1e111b40`). That is 47 commits and ~6 weeks of drift. Opened against
`v3`, which has not moved — this fast-forwards cleanly.

Three commits: the merge itself, the breaks the merge surfaced, and a
TypeScript/dependency pass.

## What v3 was missing

| Gap | |
|---|---|
| Clamp future consent time (#862) | `handlers/subject/consent-time.ts`
did not exist on v3 |
| CSP nonce on injected styles/scripts (#949) | 4 files reference

backend-only, no v3 equivalent |

cuts v3's own CI time |

It also brings canary's agent surface, which v3 did not have at all:
root `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` as `@AGENTS.md`, `skills-lock.json`, and
the `.agents/skills/` consolidation that turns
`.claude`/`.cursor`/`.github` into symlinks. Skill count goes 4 → 10
with none of v3's dropped.

## Conflict resolutions

32 files conflicted, but the two sides only overlapped on 70 files, so
most were mechanical. The judgement calls:

- **Kept v3's architecture** — the conformance package, the Nuxt module,
the demo's `ConsentManager` wrapper, `waitForStoredValue` in the IAB
tests, `svelte` as a peer dependency — and took canary's dependency
bumps on top.
- **Backend edge CORS** — unioned canary's `x-c15t-version` into v3's
GPC/geo allow-list. v3 shipped the version header in #920 but never
allowed it on the edge init path, so this fixes a live bug rather than
just resolving a conflict.
- **`ci.yml`** — canary's affected-scoped tests, turbo cache prune/save
and version-keyed Playwright cache; v3's `parity` and `e2e_consent` jobs
and root-script tests. Corrected the parity job's Playwright pins to the
versions that actually resolve (1.61.1 root, 1.62.0 `@playwright/test`).
- **Dropped** `internals/storybook-tests` (removed on v3 in #760) and
the unused demo `select.tsx`; **kept** the demo policy files v3 still
imports.

Worth knowing for review: `examples/demo/app/(main)/layout.tsx`
auto-merged *cleanly* to canary's version while silently dropping v3's
`ConsentManager` import and four Geist pixel fonts. A clean auto-merge
hid a broken build there, so the demo files got checked by hand rather
than by conflict markers.

## Breaks the merge surfaced

Each fixed and re-verified by running the affected task:

- **`@c15t/svelte` build** — `@sveltejs/package` loads the TypeScript JS
API, which TypeScript 7 does not ship.
- **`@c15t/vue` typecheck** — `packages/vue` moved to `^3.5.39` while
the nuxt bench pinned `3.5.38`; two Vue copies made every
`Ref<HTMLElement>` fail structurally.
- **`react-browser-bench` build** — Playwright 1.61 resolves
`addInitScript` to a `Disposable`, not `void`.
- **`example-demo` build** — canary's main-sync (#926) deleted the
demo's consent-manager provider and `/policy` route, which v3's layout
imports.
- **`@c15t/scripts` tests** — v3's 85% coverage ratchet met canary's
`live-vendors` monitor and fell to 65%. That monitor drives real vendor

still run. Coverage is 93%.

## TypeScript and dependencies

TypeScript 7 is stable, so **every published package now pins `7.0.2`
explicitly** — 15 packages, including nine (`c15t`, `react`, `schema`,
`scripts`, `iab`, `cli`, `logger`, `translations`, `dev-tools`) that had
no `typescript` entry at all and were silently using whatever root
resolved.

The **root pin stays on `6.0.3`**, deliberately. TypeScript 7 ships no
JS compiler API — its only `"."` export is `lib/version.cjs` — so
`import('typescript')` yields a version string instead of
`transpileModule`/`ts.sys`/`convertCompilerOptionsFromJson`. That breaks

and this is why `@c15t/svelte` and `@c15t/vue` sit on 6.0.3 despite
being published: their build tools are the JS-API consumers, not their
sources.

feat(examples/nuxt): self-hosted consent manifest demo + manifest-mode fixes (#958)

## What

A production-deployable **Nuxt example** that exercises the v3 consent
manifest end to end on a single origin — and the package fixes that
building it surfaced.

## The demo (`examples/nuxt`)

- Self-hosts `@c15t/backend` at `/api/self-host`
(`server/api/self-host/[...all].ts`), so the whole demo including the
manifest is served from one origin.
- Real `policyPacks` (EU opt-in / California opt-out / world fallback)
so the manifest carries fingerprints + matching rules and `POST
/subjects` exercises recompute-on-write.
- `manifest: true` — `@c15t/vue` resolves init locally from the
CDN-cacheable manifest with **no consent-backend round trip on the
request path**; banner is server-rendered into the first HTML.
- Region preview via `?country=US&region=CA`. The page shows the
resolved jurisdiction, policy pack, model and UI mode, so you can see
the manifest re-resolve — two of the three packs legitimately render no
banner.

### Storage

Both modes speak Postgres through the same `pg` driver and Kysely
dialect; only the destination changes.

- **Local dev** — [PGlite](https://pglite.dev) (Postgres compiled to
WASM) in-process behind a unix socket in `.pgdata/`. Gitignored, created
and migrated on first request, so `bun run dev` needs zero setup.
- **Deployed** — Postgres via `DATABASE_URL`. A production build without
it fails with an actionable error rather than crashing at request time.
Migrate with `bun run db:migrate`.

PGlite rather than SQLite deliberately: SQLite ships with `PRAGMA
foreign_keys` off, so a consent row referencing a non-existent policy
inserts happily locally and only fails once deployed — which is exactly
the bug below.

## Fixes surfaced while building it

- **backend** — manifest recompute wrote the runtime pack id into
`consent.policyId`, an FK into `consentPolicy`. Every manifest-mode save
500s on an FK-enforcing database. Now anchors the consent row to a real
`consentPolicy` via `findOrCreatePolicy`; pack identity + fingerprint
stay on `runtimePolicyDecision`. *(Mocked tests asserted on arguments
passed to a fake `db.create`, so they stayed green; SQLite accepted the
row too.)*
- **core** — manifest transport no longer asserts partial decision
inputs when the manifest resolved no policy pack, which the backend
rejects as incomplete (`422 STALE_POLICY`).
- **vue** — manifest server route forwards the backend's `Cache-Control`
+ `ETag` verbatim instead of nitro's `max-age=1` + `Vary:
Accept-Language`, so the geo-independent manifest is genuinely
CDN-cacheable.
- **vue** — `Vary` is no longer forwarded at all. The body is a pure
function of the request URL, and the backend's `Vary: Origin` is paired
with an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` this route never passes through,
so it only fragmented the edge cache.
- **vue** — backends serving `/manifest` without an `s-maxage` are
deduped in-process for a short floor, replacing the dedupe that
`defineCachedEventHandler` used to provide. An explicit
`no-store`/`no-cache`/`private` still disables reuse.
- **vue** — relative `backendURL` routed through nitro's in-process
`localFetch` (`globalThis.fetch` rejects relative URLs), enabling
same-origin self-hosting. Absolute URLs are unaffected.
- **vue** — branding `?ref=` link resolved after mount to fix an

docs: backend rewrite (#960)

Design document for rewriting `packages/backend` on Effect, plus the
tooling the work needs. No production code in this PR.

This is the bottom of a stack that builds the replacement as a parallel
package and measures it against the shipped one. The summary below
covers the stack as a whole, so the argument and the results sit in one
place.

## The problem

`packages/backend` has zero joins anywhere — `create` ×43, `findFirst`
×31, `findMany` ×22, and not one join — because fumadb targets a lowest
common denominator that includes MongoDB. That shows up as sequential
per-item loops in `consent-enrichment.ts` and hand-rolled chunked
batching in `list.handler.ts`.

Three of the five documented database adapters have never had a working
migrator: `migrator/index.ts` only runs migrations for kysely and mongo,
and prints schema code at Drizzle/Prisma/TypeORM users to apply
themselves.

## Why MongoDB goes

It is the constraint, not a casualty of one. Supporting a document store
means the query surface has to be expressible without joins, so *every*
SQL user pays for it: `GET /subjects?externalId=` costs one query for
the subjects, one per hundred subject ids for their consents, and one
more per distinct policy type — sequentially, in a loop that is not even
`Promise.all`. The round-trip count grows with the data.

Dropping it is a hard break, and there is no DDL path from Mongo to SQL,
so it would need an export/import script rather than a migration. **That
script is not being written.** A 2.x deployment on MongoDB therefore has
no supported upgrade path to 3.0 — those users stay on 2.x, or reshape
their data themselves against `db/schema.ts`. This is a stated break for
the release notes rather than an omission, and it is the one drop here
that removes capability from an existing user instead of relocating it.

The Drizzle/Prisma/TypeORM adapters also go. Those users keep their
database and lose the shared connection pool, since c15t opens its own
`SqlClient` against the same server. In exchange they get a migrator
that actually runs, which they have never had.

## Measured results

`benchmarks/backend-bench`, 1000 subjects against 20k background rows,
PGlite. Three arms: the real `@c15t/backend` data layer, the same query
pattern against a bare SQL client, and the rewrite — the middle arm
exists to stop an indexing win being attributed to Effect.

**Read path** (`GET /subjects?externalId=`):

| arm | indexed | queries | median ms |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `@c15t/backend` (real fumadb) | no | 9 | 16.516 |
| chunked fan-out (pattern only) | no | 9 | 8.513 |
| joined (rewrite) | no | 2 | 4.337 |
| `@c15t/backend` (real fumadb) | yes | 9 | 11.927 |
| chunked fan-out (pattern only) | yes | 9 | 4.489 |
| joined (rewrite) | yes | 2 | 3.273 |

Like-for-like — same schema, same indexes, different implementation — is
**3.64×**. Decomposed: fumadb's own overhead is about half the v2 cost
(16.5 → 8.5 ms for the *identical* nine queries against identical data),
the join a further ~1.96×, the indexes ~1.35×.

PGlite is in-process, so nine sequential round trips cost almost nothing
here. Against a networked Postgres the gap widens.

**Write path** (`POST /subjects`): new writes 0.447 ms against 0.557 ms.
Retries are at parity — 0.130 ms against 0.127 ms — and that is the
honest result: the rewrite's win on writes is correctness, not speed. A
retry is answered by one indexed primary-key lookup rather than by
attempting an insert and string-matching the adapter's error code to
decide whether the failure was a duplicate.

`/manifest` does no database work in either backend, so there is nothing
to compare.

## Testing

The old package's suite could not have caught most of what this stack
found, so the testing changed shape rather than just growing:

- **Migration fixtures generated from real published releases** —
`internals/migration-fixtures` installs `@c15t/backend` 1.0.0, 1.4.2,
1.8.6 and 2.1.0 into throwaway workspaces, runs their actual migrators,
and captures the resulting schema. 5 shapes × 3 engines. Two of those
record a *failure*: fumadb cannot migrate MySQL at all, in either era.
- **A cross-backend HTTP conformance suite** —
`internals/backend-conformance` holds 15 cases that neither package
owns, run against both. Expectations were written by reading v2 and then
executed against it, so each one is a characterisation of real behaviour
rather than a description of what the rewrite assumes v2 does. Recorded
gaps carry a `knownGap` and still run, so a gap that closes gets
noticed.
- **Every behaviour asserted on every engine** — PGlite, real Postgres,
SQLite and MySQL. Both Postgres engines are in the matrix deliberately:
PGlite runs a single in-process connection and so cannot exhibit
anything pool-shaped. This is the one that mattered most; see below.
- **A tenant isolation suite** seeding two tenants with deliberately
colliding data and asserting every read and write sees only its own.
- **The published artifact, not just `src/`** — every export-map entry
resolved the way npm resolves it. Two subpaths added during this rewrite
had never once been loaded that way.
- **The migrator end to end**, driven by a connection description rather
than a Layer — the form a deploy script writes.

**576 tests across four engines; 96.8% statements, 94.8% functions.**
349 of them run without Docker, on PGlite and SQLite alone.

Postgres and MySQL run in CI as service containers. They did not at
first: Turborepo's default `envMode` is strict, so the database URLs
were filtered out before vitest started and the whole MySQL arm skipped
silently behind a green suite (#992).

## What the tests found

Worth stating plainly, because it is the argument for the shape above.
At 180 passing tests and ~95% coverage, the package **could not execute
a single statement against MySQL and could not write to SQLite at all.**
Every test used PGlite; SQLite was covered only for DDL, MySQL not at
all.

Seven defects, including two that fail silently rather than loudly:
adoption read `information_schema` unaliased, and MySQL uppercases those
labels — so it saw an empty database, added no columns, and stamped the
ledger as baseline anyway. And MySQL timestamps were mapped to a type
that stops at 2038 and shifts through the session time zone, on a legal
record's `givenAt`.

Widening the matrix later kept finding things, which is the argument for
having done it at all:

- **A 2.x `tablePrefix` database classified as `Empty`** (#979). Not a
harmless wrong answer — `migrate` was not blocked, and would have
created a full parallel schema beside the real one, leaving every
existing consent record orphaned while the deployment came up looking
healthy. On a consent platform that is a compliance incident: the audit
trail is still there and the backend can no longer see it.
- **Adoption's foreign-key introspection was database-wide, not
schema-scoped** (#992) — so with a second installation in another schema
it would conclude this one already had its foreign keys and skip both
adding them and the orphan check that guards them. It surfaced only once
two suites shared one server.
- **Two tests passing for the wrong reason** — one on suite ordering,
one counting scans that Postgres had not yet flushed.

Also found, and live on `v3` today rather than caused by the rewrite: no
foreign key column is indexed in any shipped version, and the legacy
migrator emitted foreign keys on Postgres and SQLite but none on MySQL.
Full list in RFC §11.

## Decisions taken

- **MongoDB support is dropped**, for the reason above.
- **Effect v4**, pinned exactly. v4 puts `SqlClient` and `Migrator` in
core with all three dialects published; the cost is no
`@effect/sql-kysely`, so queries are typed template-literal SQL.
- **The 2.0.0 schema is frozen** until cutover. That is what makes the
rewrite provably behaviour-preserving and the benchmarks comparable.
- **Indexes ship as migration 2, with v3** — not backported to 2.x, and
kept out of the baseline so a fresh install still matches an adopted
database.

Open decisions are listed in §10; what implementation changed against
this design is §11.

## The cutover is in this stack

It was not when this was first written. #979 renames
`@c15t/backend-next` to `@c15t/backend`, deletes the old package, and
takes the linked version group to 3.0.0 with a major changeset. The
three example apps and the CLI move across with it.

Two things dropped along the way, both deliberate and both worth naming
in the release notes:

- **`@c15t/backend/edge`** does not ship in 3.0. The capability survives
— `resolveInitFromManifest` in `@c15t/schema` is the resolver the edge
handler was built on, and a host that wants edge resolution calls it
directly. What goes is the packaged handler.
- **MongoDB**, for the reason above, with no export/import script.

## Not in this stack

Docs and the upgrade guide, which land before the 3.0 release.
`tablePrefix` support in 3.0 is still an open question — the migrator
refuses such a database rather than corrupting it, so nothing is blocked
on deciding.
