fix: block network requests sent before the network blocker loads (#1202) ## Summary The React provider loaded the network blocker in a mount effect (`NetworkBlockerMount`). Children's mount effects run before their parent's, and the blocker is a lazy chunk, so every `fetch` or XHR matching a rule that was sent at mount went out with no consent check. That happened on first visits, for visitors who had rejected, and when the policy request failed or hung. Only requests sent after the chunk loaded were blocked. This PR holds matching requests from the point where c15t first knows the rules, and has the blocker decide them once it loads: - **`@c15t/core/modules/network-hold`** (new, about 0.8 KB gzip): `holdNetworkRequests(rules)` patches `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` synchronously and queues only requests that match a rule. `createNetworkBlocker()` ends the hold and replays the queue through its own patches. Everything else passes straight through. - **React**: `NetworkBlockerMount` calls the hold during its first render. It renders before `children`, so the hold is in place before any child renders or runs an effect, and before effects in components rendered next to the provider. Nothing runs on the server (`typeof window` guard). If the provider unmounts before the blocker loads, the hold is released; StrictMode's effect re-run is detected so it doesn't release early. - **Consent unknown**: while the policy is pending and hasn't failed, a request the blocker would block now waits instead of getting a 451. It is sent if the resolved policy and stored choice allow it and blocked otherwise. A failed policy load blocks it, matching the existing "optional categories stay denied" behaviour. If the policy request hangs, the request is never sent. This keeps saved-accept visitors' mount-time requests working now that they are caught before persistence hydrates. - **Vue** had the same defect (the blocker is installed in the root's `mounted`, after every child's). The hold now starts in `createVueConsentKernelContext`. - **`createConsentRuntime()`** (used by `@c15t/svelte` and the `c15t` browser client) installs the blocker in `start()`, which Svelte calls from the provider's `onMount` after its children. The hold now starts at construction. `@c15t/solid` doesn't expose the network blocker. Apps that don't pass `networkBlocker` still never download the blocker chunk. The hold code is in first-load JavaScript for every provider app. ## What c15t can't cover These are documented on the new Next.js and React network blocker pages: - Code that runs before the provider renders: inline scripts, tags in ``, `beforeInteractive` scripts, and client modules evaluated before the root renders. **Webpack evaluates a route's client component modules when its chunk loads, so module-level requests still leak under webpack builds** (the Next 15 compat cell pins this). Turbopack evaluates a client module when its first element renders, so a module used inside the provider is covered. - Code that saved its own reference to `fetch` before the provider rendered; `sendBeacon`, WebSocket, EventSource, element-initiated requests, and workers. - The standalone `useNetworkBlocker` hook still installs after mount. Its render-purity contract is tested ("abandoned render does not patch fetch"), so I left it alone; the docs point to the provider option. The docs recommend sending tracking calls from effects or event handlers rather than at module top level, loading SDKs through `scripts`, and checking `useConsent()` in your own code, with the blocker as a backstop. ## Before / After Packed tarballs installed into a Next 16.3.4 App Router production consumer (Turbopack) using the documented streaming layout (`resolveConsent` promise → `ConsentRoot`) and a `networkBlocker` rule for `tracker.test`. Requests: (a) at client module evaluation of a page component, (b) in a `useEffect` of a component rendered next to (before) `ConsentRoot`, (c) in a child's mount effect by fetch and by XHR, (d) 1.5 s after mount. fix: close consent surfaces without waiting for the backend save (#1205) In v3, Save in the preference dialog kept the dialog open until `POST /subjects` answered. `saveConsentUI` reopened the dialog after the kernel committed the receipt, then closed it only on `result.ok`. Vue's `ConsentManager` and Svelte's `saveConsents` copied the same logic, and the browser client did it for the banner too. v2 closes on the click. The kernel already records the choice, updates permissions, schedules the storage write and queues failed saves for replay before the transport runs. So this PR drops the wait: every save path closes its surface in the click task and leaves the request to finish in the background. The request's outcome never reopens anything. ## Save paths found and what changed | Framework | Path | Before | Change | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | React, Next.js, TanStack Start | `saveConsentUI` (`packages/react/src/ui-save.ts`), used by `ConsentButton` (banner, dialog, set-consent), `useHeadlessConsentUI().performAction` / `saveCustomPreferences`, `useConsentManager().saveConsents` | Reopened the dialog, closed on `ok` | Closes when the save recorded a new receipt or vendor map. A save that recorded nothing closes when it resolves. The navigation guard stays for that case. | | React IAB | stock `IABConsentBanner` / `IABConsentDialog` via `component-hooks/use-headless-iab-consent-ui.ts` | Closed when the IAB commit landed, after TC string encoding, which can wait on the TCF chunk | New `saveIABConsentUI`: closes on the click, restores the surface only if nothing was recorded locally | | React IAB, public hook | `hooks/use-headless-iab-consent-ui.ts` | Already closed on the click | Unchanged | | Next.js, TanStack Start | no own close logic (`root.tsx` only wraps the transport) | | Covered by React | | Vue, Nuxt | `ConsentManager` `onAction` (`manager.vue`) | Reopened the manager, closed on `ok` | Closes on the local record, as React | | Vue IAB | `iab-prompt.vue`, `iab-panel.vue` | Closed on the IAB commit | Close on the click through `utils/save-iab-choice.ts` | | Vue banner | `prompt.vue` | Already closed through the kernel commit | Unchanged | | Svelte | `saveConsents` (`context.svelte.ts`), used by `ConsentButton` and `performAction` | Reopened the dialog, closed on `ok` | Closes on the local record. Bulk actions reset the draft at record time. `ConsentButton` no longer leaks an unhandled rejection when the request fails. | | Svelte IAB | `iab-prompt.svelte`, `iab-panel.svelte` | Closed on the IAB commit | `saveIABChoice`, as React | | Astro | delegated banner handler (`client.ts`) | Already closed through the kernel commit | Unchanged. Dialog islands render the React, Vue or Svelte surfaces, so they get those fixes. | | Browser client / global | `saveSelection` (`client.ts`), used by `acceptAll`, `rejectAll`, `save`, the banner and dialog | Restored the banner or dialog, closed on `ok` | Closes on the local record | | Browser IAB | `saveIAB`, `iab/surface.ts` | Closed after `handle.save()` resolved | Closes on the click, restores only if nothing was recorded. The "Unable to save" message only shows on a restored surface. | | Core kernel | `commands.save` | Commits synchronously, then yields one task before the transport | Unchanged | | `@c15t/ui`, `@c15t/solid` | no close logic | | Unchanged | `ConsentGate`'s button opens the dialog, so it follows the dialog path. ## Failure and retry I kept the existing kernel queue rather than adding one. A failed request emits `command:error`, which reaches `onError` in React, Next.js, TanStack Start and Svelte, and the `error` event on the browser client. Vue has no `onError` option, so there the kernel event is the only signal. The kernel also queues the payload in localStorage (`c15t-v3-pending-consent-saves:v1`). It replays after the next successful init and on `online`, for up to 10 attempts over 7 days. The UI no longer reopens and the choice is not rolled back. Backend contract for late saves: the queued payload keeps `givenAt` from the click and the `policySnapshotToken` from init. The backend records the visitor's time, not the replay time. The consent id covers tenant, subject, domain, policy and `givenAt`, so a retry of a save that did land returns the existing record. One limit I didn't change: the self-hosted backend's snapshot tokens expire after 30 minutes, so a replay after that gets a 422 and the save stays browser-only. This isn't new. The old dialog kept the same choice locally after a failed save. ## Callback timing Unchanged, now documented in `docs/guides/consent-state.mdx`: 1. Click task: receipt commit, `onChoiceRecorded`, `onPermissionsChanged`, script loader, iframe and network blockers, then the surface leaves the active state. 2. Next task: cookie and localStorage write. 3. Then `POST /subjects`. 4. When it settles: `command:save:completed`. The promises from `kernel.commands.save()`, `performAction()`, Svelte's `saveConsents()` and the browser client's `save()` settle here, as before. Svelte's `saveConsents()` still rejects on failure. ## Before / After Next.js 16.3.4 App Router production consumer built from packed tarballs, the `combined-v2-v3` consumer with the v3 guide shape (`ConsentRoot`, `manifestURL`, awaited `resolveConsent`). fix(react): prerender pages that render ConsentGate (#1209) With Next.js 16 `cacheComponents: true`, `next build` fails on any page that renders `ConsentGate` in its prerendered shell: ``` Error: Route "/embed": Next.js encountered the unstable value `Date.now()` in a Client Component. ``` It fails on alpha.2 and on current `v3`. #1195 tells users to wrap the gate in its own `Suspense` as a workaround. This PR removes the need for that. ## Cause `ConsentGate` decided consent with `evaluateConsent({ category }, snapshot)`, whose `now` parameter defaults to `Date.now()`. It ran during render, including the server render. `useVendorAllowed` had the same call. I checked the other gates too. Vue's `ConsentGate` already evaluates at `snapshot.evaluatedAt`. Svelte reads `effectivePermissions` and renders nothing until mount. Astro has no gate component. Nothing else in the React gate's render path reads the clock, `Math.random()`, cookies or storage. ## Change - `hooks.ts` gets an internal `useGateSelector`. Its server snapshot evaluates at the snapshot's own `evaluatedAt`, so server rendering and hydration never read the clock. The browser snapshot still evaluates at `Date.now()`, so a grant that expired before the kernel's deadline timer fired still denies. That is the same enforcement as before. - `ConsentGate` uses it through `useCategoryAllowed`. So does `useVendorAllowed`. - The Next.js `ConsentGate` page says the gate needs no `Suspense` of its own. With the fix, a static page stays `○` and its prerendered HTML contains the placeholder. With the `Suspense` workaround, Next.js bails the gate out to client rendering. The HTML has only the fallback, and the placeholder appears after hydration. ## Tests - `next-16-cache-components` compat cell: two new routes render a marketing `ConsentGate` straight from the page with no `Suspense`. One uses a client-init layout (`/gate`, static) and one uses the promise layout (`/gate-stream`, partial). Without the fix the cell's `next build` fails with the error above. The new test also checks, from browser network requests, that the placeholder is in the first HTML, nothing requests the embed before Accept, Accept loads it once, a returning visitor who accepted loads it once, and one who rejected never loads it. - `consent-gate-placeholder.test.tsx`: server-renders the gate with `Date.now` stubbed to throw, granted and denied. Both fail without the fix. ## Before / After Integration baseline: local merge of the 12 open perf PRs (`integ/all-perf` at `c05270016`, on `v3` `9993ae578`). After: that plus this PR. This is an intended breaking change for the v3 alpha. The hook read the whole consent snapshot plus the draft, so every caller re-rendered on every change. With 50 components subscribed to a category that never changes, one saved toggle re-rendered all 50. c15t's own dialog, preference rows, vendor lists, dialog trigger, overlay and `ConsentGate` used it too, so they paid the same cost. - **Stock components** now read only the values they render. Draft state is read through an internal slice selector (`useConsentDraftSlice`), and the accordion renders one row component per category, so a staged toggle re-renders only that category's row and vendor list. - **Removed:** `useConsentManager` and the undocumented `useConsentManagerDraft` on `@c15t/react/draft`, which existed only for it. - **Added to the main entries:** `useSubscribeToConsentChanges()` and `useRegisterConsentCategories()`, already public on `@c15t/react/hooks`. perf!: stop a slow or failing consent backend from holding server renders (#1212) > **Stack:** layer 20 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1210, above #1195; the `timeoutMs` wording is applied to #1195's restructured `app-router.mdx`. Server-side consent resolution waited for the manifest cache's 10 second fetch timeout when the backend hung, and every request after a cold failure went back to the backend. This PR gives server rendering a 500 ms budget, caches cold failures with a short backoff, and reads the manifest in Next.js `resolveConsent` through the in-process cache. ## Cause - `resolveConsent` (Next.js, TanStack Start) and Nuxt's server render had no budget of their own. With the awaited layout, a hanging backend on a cold cache kept the page blank until `MANIFEST_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (10 s) fired. - The manifest cache remembered nothing after a failed fill with nothing cached. Stale entries had a 5 s retry floor; cold keys had none, so sequential requests each hit the backend. - Next.js `resolveConsent` fetched `manifestURL` with a plain `fetch`. Pointed at the manifest route it paid a loopback hop on every render; pointed at the backend it skipped both caches. ## Changes - `@c15t/core` manifest cache: - `timeoutMs` bounds how long a call waits, counted from the start of the upstream request, so a call joining a slow request gives up at once. The request keeps running, fills the cache, and goes to `onBackgroundRevalidate`. - A failed fill with nothing usable cached is recorded. That key is not retried for 1 s, doubling to 5 s. Calls in between reject with `ManifestUnavailableError` (`reason: 'backoff'`, `retryAfterMs`, `cause`). Coalescing and stale-while-revalidate are unchanged. A stale copy is still never served past its window. - The upstream request timeout drops from 10 s to 5 s, so the cache notices a recovered backend sooner after a hang. - Non-2xx errors carry `status`. - New exports: `withResolutionBudget` and `DEFAULT_RESOLVE_TIMEOUT_MS`. - `@c15t/nextjs` `resolveConsent`: new `timeoutMs` option (default 500, `false` to disable). It covers the manifest read, the backend `/init` call (`AbortSignal.timeout`) and local resolution. The manifest is read through the in-process cache for any `manifestURL`. `waitUntil` also receives the request that the render stopped waiting for. - `@c15t/tanstack-start` `resolveConsent`: same `timeoutMs`. - `@c15t/vue` (Nuxt): - New `timeoutMs` config. The server render sends it to the in-process init route as `x-c15t-timeout-ms`, because an abort signal does not reach Nitro's local fetch. It also passes `timeout` to `useFetch` for an absolute backend `/init`. - The init route no longer falls back to backend `/init` on every request while the manifest backs off. It still falls back when the backend has no `/manifest` (404). - The awaited and streamed layouts behave the same way. The awaited one paints after at most the budget. The streamed promise resolves to the baseline within the budget. Neither renders consent UI without a policy. - Docs: App Router guide, Next.js fetching reference (new "Slow or unavailable backends" section), TanStack Start and Nuxt quickstarts. Tegami note with a migration section. - The seven-day CDN TTL is unchanged. A `manifestURL` pointing at the backend is now routed through the cache rather than rejected. fix(react)!: hold useNetworkBlocker requests from the first render (#1216) > **Stack:** layer 23 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1214 (#1202 is further down), so its diff now shows only this PR's commit. Stacked on #1202 (`fix/react-network-blocker-early-install`), which adds `@c15t/core/modules/network-hold`. This PR changes that module and uses it from the hook, so it can't land without #1202. Review only the top commit. ## Cause #1202 made `ConsentProvider`'s `networkBlocker` option hold matching requests from its first render. The standalone `useNetworkBlocker` hook still installed the blocker from a mount effect. React runs children's effects before their parent's, and earlier siblings' effects before later ones, so every matching `fetch` or XHR sent from those effects went out before the hook did anything. #1202 left the hook alone because a test required that "abandoned render does not patch fetch". ## Fix - `useNetworkBlocker` now starts a hold during its first render in the browser, as the provider does. Nothing runs on the server. - **Holds are tracked per caller.** `holdNetworkRequests(rules)` now returns a `NetworkHold`, and `createNetworkBlocker({ hold })` takes over only that caller's requests. Before, the first blocker to load (or the first unmount) ended every hold, so on a page using both the provider option and the hook, the provider's blocker loading would release the hook's held requests unchecked. `createNetworkBlocker()` without `hold` still ends every hold; Vue and `createConsentRuntime()` use that. - **Renders React throws away.** A render that never commits has no effect cleanup to end its hold, so each render-time hold expires after 10 s unless its component commits. A component that commits also ends any uncommitted hold for the same rules. That covers a retry after suspending: without it, the discarded attempt's hold made requests that consent allows wait 10 s. When a hold expires, its requests are sent, as they would have been without the hook, because its rules never took effect. - The provider's `NetworkBlockerMount` uses the same helper (`module-hooks/network-hold.ts`), so it gets per-caller release and the expiry too. StrictMode's effect re-run is still handled: the cleanup defers the release and a re-mount cancels it. ### Breaking change: the hook's render has a side effect The test "abandoned render does not patch fetch" is removed. It required the hook's render to leave `window.fetch` alone, and that is why requests leaked: nothing can be held before the effect if the render may not patch anything. The new contract, tested in `use-network-blocker-early.test.tsx`, is that a discarded render's hold ends on its own and sends what it held. Tests that assert `window.fetch` is untouched after rendering a component that calls the hook need updating. App code needs no changes. The tegami note has a migration section. ## Before / After The network-level harness from #1202 (Playwright records what leaves the browser), with the provider's `networkBlocker` option removed and `useNetworkBlocker({ rules })` called by a component inside `ConsentRoot` that wraps the page. Packed tarballs installed into a Next 16.3.4 App Router production consumer (Turbopack, `reactStrictMode: true`), rule `{ category: 'measurement', domain: 'tracker.test' }`. Requests: `module` at client module evaluation of the page component; `sibling` from an effect of a component rendered before `ConsentRoot`; `provider-sibling` from an effect of a component inside `ConsentRoot` rendered before the hook's component; `mount` / `mount-xhr` from a child's mount effect; `late` 1.5 s after mount. Before = #1202 head `400decc31`. After = this branch's working tree before the final lint-only edits (runtime logic matches `23e2e7299`). Arms interleaved; load average 6.99 at start, 3.93 at end. Cells: runs in which the request left the browser, with the median send time after navigation. | Condition | Visit | Runs | Before: module, sibling, provider-sibling, mount, mount-xhr | After | `late` before → after | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | | Healthy | Fresh | 5 | 5/5 each, 52–61 ms | 0/5 each | 0/5 → 0/5 | | Healthy | Saved reject | 5 | 5/5 each, 50–58 ms | 0/5 each | 0/5 → 0/5 | | Healthy | Saved accept (control) | 5 | 5/5 each, 50–57 ms | 5/5 each, 54–56 ms | 5/5 → 5/5 | | Manifest 503 | Fresh, reject, accept | 3 each | 3/3 each, 48–63 ms | 0/3 each | 0 → 0 | | Manifest hangs | Fresh, reject, accept | 3 each | 3/3 each, 47–55 ms | 0/3 each (held, never sent) | 0 → 0 | | Cold manifest (1.5 s) | Fresh, reject | 3 each | 3/3 each, 90–100 ms | 0/3 each | 0 → 0 | | Cold manifest (1.5 s) | Saved accept | 3 | 3/3 each, 89–94 ms | 3/3 each, 1,564 ms (sent once the policy resolved) | 3/3 → 3/3 | `module` is covered because Turbopack evaluates the page's client module when its first element renders, which is inside the hook's component. Under webpack it would still leak, as #1202 documents for the provider. ## Tests - `@c15t/react` `use-network-blocker-early.test.tsx`: - requests from a child's and an earlier sibling's mount effects are held and blocked (fails on #1202: both are sent), and the same under StrictMode (fails); - held requests are sent when stored consent allows them; - after a retry following a suspend, an allowed request doesn't wait (fails with the same-rules cleanup disabled: it waits for the 10 s expiry); - a discarded render's hold ends on its own and sends its request (fails on #1202). - `@c15t/core` `hold.test.ts`: releasing one caller sends only what no other caller holds; a blocker given one caller's hold leaves the other hold in place; releasing after the blocker took over does nothing. - Package tests for core, react, vue, svelte, nextjs and tanstack-start (browser tests headless), `check-types` for core and react, `bun run lint`, `bun run fmt`. ## Docs `docs/shared/react/network-blocker.mdx` now covers when blocking starts with the hook, what happens to a discarded render's hold, and the narrower limit (requests sent before the calling component renders). ## Review fixes - A blocker with `enabled: false` no longer ends other callers' holds, and `createConsentRuntime()` and the Vue plugin now hold per caller too, so disposing one before it starts ends only its own hold and answers the requests it held as blocked instead of sending them (`@c15t/vue` added to the release note). - A render hold that ends unclaimed (a discarded render after 10 seconds, or an unmount before the blocker loads) now fails its requests as blocked instead of sending them. > [!NOTE] > ### Make `useNetworkBlocker` hold requests from first render with per-caller holds > - `useNetworkBlocker` now patches `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` during its component's first render, so requests from earlier effects are held before the blocker loads. The loaded blocker takes over the hold; an uncommitted or prematurely unmounted hold expires after 10 seconds (`UNCOMMITTED_HOLD_MS`) and fails its unchecked requests as blocked. > - `holdNetworkRequests` now returns a `NetworkHold` handle. Each caller owns its own rules and queue, so blocking or releasing one caller no longer affects another caller's held requests. A `NOT_HELD` sentinel covers disabled and server-side callers. > - `createNetworkBlocker` accepts an internal `hold` option on `NetworkBlockerOptions`; a supplied hold is released and replayed through the blocker's patches, while omitting it keeps the whole-active-hold takeover. Runtime and Vue kernel code ([index.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1216/files#diff-3a1fc27e345ff5cfacf0557fc8f132d407202255ba8598557cc44791512b93ff), [kernel.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1216/files#diff-f1ebcbf60f8f8be12f5cddc6872d9612cd9e919658f96dfc30445783d41be2ba)) now create, claim, and dispose per-context holds. > - Risk: breaking change — callers of `holdNetworkRequests` and `blockHeldRequests` ([hold.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1216/files#diff-27ef55dacaa0e26b1b84ad0d9aac193165960b0653d174f3342ccbfc2b5db43a)) get new per-owner semantics; requests matched by a removed caller now fail as blocked instead of replaying, and only requests sent before the hook's component renders remain uncovered. > > > > Macroscope summarized 7409b74. > > ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Matching network requests are now held from the first browser render when using the React network blocker, helping prevent requests from being sent before consent checks run. - Holds are isolated per caller: disabling or disposing one blocker no longer releases another caller’s requests. Requests released without a consent check are blocked. - If a render is discarded before the blocker takes over, held requests are sent after 10 seconds. - **Documentation** - Updated network-blocker guidance to describe early request holding and its limitations.

fix(backend,core)!: record consent saves replayed after the policy token expired (#1219) > **Stack:** layer 24 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1216, above #1205 and #1206; the `saveFailure` change moved into `hosted-records.ts`, where #1206 put the hosted save. Follow-up from #1205. Based on `v3` (`9993ae578`): the save queue and snapshot tokens are both on `v3`, so this doesn't depend on #1205, but #1205 makes the queue the normal path for a failed save. ## Cause When a save fails, the kernel queues it in localStorage and replays it after the next successful init and on `online`, for up to 10 attempts over 7 days. The replay keeps the click time as `givenAt` and the `policySnapshotToken` from the `/init` the visitor saw. The self-hosted backend's tokens expire 30 minutes after `/init`, and `POST /subjects` verified them against the arrival time, so any replay after that got `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` and the choice stayed browser-only. The client couldn't tell that refusal from a transient one and retried it until its attempts ran out. Only hosted mode is affected. Manifest mode asserts decision inputs, which the backend recomputes against the current manifest at any time. ## Fix **Backend** (`policy-snapshot.ts`, `consent-submission.ts`): a token that expired before the request arrived is verified again with `givenAt` as the clock. The late save is accepted when: - signature, issuer and tenant audience verify (jose only reports expiry after the signature checks out); - `givenAt` is within the token's `iat`…`exp`, with 10 minutes of slack for the visitor's clock; - the request arrives within `policySnapshot.replayWindowSeconds` of `exp` (new option, default 7 days to match the client queue, `0` turns late acceptance off); - the manifest still has the policy the token names under the same fingerprint and model. The record keeps `givenAt` as sent, `createdAt` is the arrival, and `runtimePolicySource` is `snapshot_token_replayed`. The wide event gets `consent.decisionSource`. Saves that arrive while their token is valid take the same path as before. I picked this over refreshing the token on the client before replay. A refreshed token reflects the visitor's location and the manifest at replay time, not at the click, so it can name a different policy for reasons that have nothing to do with the policy changing, and it costs an `/init` per replay. The original token already is the evidence of what was shown; the question is only how long to honour it. **Refusals are now specific:** | Case | Response | | --- | --- | | Choice made after the token expired, or replay after the window | `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRED` (the code already existed in `@c15t/schema` but was never sent) | | Token names a policy that changed since | `422 STALE_POLICY`, reason `policy-changed` (was `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID`), live or late | | Token doesn't verify | `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID`, unchanged | **Client** (`@c15t/core`): `saveFailure()` turns those four codes (plus `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_REQUIRED`) into a `ConsentSaveRejectedError`, thrown by the hosted and manifest transports (the browser package reuses `hosted.save`). The kernel doesn't queue a live save refused that way, and the replay queue drops such an entry at once instead of spending its 10 attempts. `save:replayed` carries `rejected: `, and devtools shows it. Other failures (network, 5xx, 400) stay retryable. A custom transport can throw the error too. **Schema**: `runtimePolicySource` accepts `snapshot_token_replayed`. ### What the integrity check still guarantees A late save is recorded only against a token this backend signed for this tenant, for the policy the visitor was shown, which must still be current, with a decision time inside that token's lifetime. It can't be recorded against a policy the visitor never saw. What it can't prove: `givenAt` comes from the client, so within the token's lifetime a chosen time and a genuine click time look the same. Live saves already had that property, with no lifetime bound at all. Late records are flagged, so audits can treat them separately. `docs/self-host/api/endpoints.mdx` has a new "Late saves" section with these semantics. ### Breaking changes - New `runtimePolicySource` value `snapshot_token_replayed` on consent records. - A token naming a changed policy returns `422 STALE_POLICY` / `policy-changed` instead of `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID`. Expired tokens return `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRED`. - Replays that used to be refused inside the 7-day window are now recorded. `replayWindowSeconds: 0` restores the old behaviour. - The hosted and manifest transports throw `ConsentSaveRejectedError` (still an `Error`) for these codes, and the kernel no longer queues them. The tegami note has a migration section. ## Before / After `POST /subjects` on a fake clock (`vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['Date'] })`), PGlite, signing on, default 30-minute tokens. `/init` at T, click at T+5 min unless noted. Before = `v3` `9993ae578`; after = this branch. The probe was a temporary test in `packages/backend`; the committed tests cover the same cases. | Case | Before | After | Row flagged `snapshot_token_replayed` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Live save, T+5 min | 200 | 200 | no | | Replay at T+31 min | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 200 | yes | | Replay at T+2 days | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 200 | yes | | Replay at T+6.9 days | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 200 | yes | | Replay at T+8 days (past the window) | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRED` | — | | Click at T+45 min (token already expired) | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRED` | — | | Replay at T+1 day, policy changed | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 422 `STALE_POLICY` / `policy-changed` | — | | Live save, policy changed | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 422 `STALE_POLICY` / `policy-changed` | — | | Replay at T+1 day, tampered token (`exp` pushed out) | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | — | | Live, tampered token | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | 409 `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` | — | Client queue, same refusal replayed on each load: before, the entry stayed queued and was re-sent on every init or `online` event until 10 attempts; after, it leaves the queue after the first refusal. ## Tests - `@c15t/backend` `snapshot-replay.test.ts` (PGlite and SQLite, fake clock): live save unchanged; replay after expiry recorded at the click time and flagged; replay after the window, click after expiry, and a click claimed an hour before the token was minted all get `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRED`; changed policy gets `STALE_POLICY` / `policy-changed` with no row written; tampered token refused live and late; `replayWindowSeconds: 0` refuses late saves. Through the core hosted transport against the same app: a replay inside the window saves, one past it throws `ConsentSaveRejectedError`, a 503 stays a plain retryable error. On `v3`, 8 of these fail (the replay is refused; every refusal is `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID`). - `@c15t/core` `transport.test.ts`: a live save refused for good isn't queued (choice still recorded locally); a queued save refused on replay leaves the queue with `rejected` on `save:replayed` and isn't sent again; a replay failing for another reason stays queued; the hosted transport maps each code to a refusal and keeps 400/409-other/500/503 retryable. - Package tests for core, backend, schema, dev-tools, react and browser (browser tests headless); `check-types` for backend, core, schema and dev-tools; `oxlint`, `bun run fmt`, `lint:docs`. ## Docs `docs/self-host/api/endpoints.mdx` (late saves, audit semantics, refusal table), `configuration.mdx` (`replayWindowSeconds`), `guides/observability.mdx` (`consent.decisionSource`). ## Review fixes - A save the backend refuses for good now also drops older queued saves for the same categories, so a grant queued offline can't replay after a newer choice was refused. `ConsentSaveRejectedError` and `isConsentSaveRejection` are also exported from `@c15t/core/transports`. --- Need help on this PR? perf!: mount collapsed preference content on first open (#1220) > **Stack:** layer 25 of 25 (top) in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1219. Merge the PRs below it first. ## Summary Opening the preferences dialog mounted every collapsed category's content, including every vendor card in it. With 100 declared vendors that is 1,625 React components and 1,811 DOM nodes for a dialog that shows 5 rows. Almost none of it is visible, and all of it is `inert` and `aria-hidden`. `PreferenceItem.Content` now keeps its content element but mounts the children the first time the item opens, then leaves them mounted. The dialog opens with 112 components and 103 DOM nodes whatever the vendor count. React, Vue and Svelte change together so the parity runner still sees the same DOM: - **React:** the `PreferenceItem.Content` primitive. This covers category rows, vendor cards and the IAB purpose, stack and vendor rows. - **Svelte:** the same primitive. Its preferences and vendor list use it. - **Vue:** the `PreferenceItemContent` primitive (used by the IAB items), plus the inline category and vendor-card markup in `preferences.vue` and `vendor-list.vue`. Accessibility is unchanged. The content element keeps its id, so each trigger's `aria-controls` still resolves. Collapsed content was already `inert` and `aria-hidden`, so it was never in the tab order or the accessibility tree. Opening a row with the keyboard mounts its content the same way a click does. The close transition still has content to collapse, because content stays mounted once opened. **Breaking:** collapsed content is empty until its row first opens. Tests or custom CSS that read it earlier break. The content part gets a `forceMount` prop in all three frameworks to opt out (`PreferenceItem.Content` in React and Svelte, `PreferenceItemContent` in Vue). The release note (`.tegami/2026-09-26-lazy-preference-content.md`, major for `@c15t/react`, `@c15t/vue`, `@c15t/svelte`) has a migration section. Independent of the open performance PRs. The TanStack Start quickstart awaits the consent server function in the root loader. TanStack Start runs every matched loader before it renders, so no byte of the response goes out until `resolveConsent()` returns. With a warm manifest cache that is a few milliseconds. On a cold cache (the first request after a server starts) it adds the backend's latency to TTFB and first paint, and when the backend stops answering it holds the page until the manifest cache's request timeout fires (10 s on `v3`). #1195 and #1215 moved Next.js to the streamed form, where `ConsentRoot` gets the pending `resolveConsent` promise. TanStack Router can stream a promise the loader returns unawaited, but `@c15t/tanstack-start`'s `ConsentRoot` typed `state` as a resolved `ConsentState`, so the streamed form didn't type-check. ## Change - `ConsentRoot`'s `state` is `ConsentState | Promise`. `ConsentProvider`'s `prefetch` already takes a promise: the server render and the first client render have no policy, and the resolved state answers the first init without a request. A promise that resolves without a policy (the server gave up on the manifest) falls back to the init route. The server-state decision seed for the same-origin init route is only built from a resolved state; after a streamed state resolves, saves carry the decision the kernel applied, so the route's assertion still accepts them. - The quickstart gets a "Stream the page while consent resolves" section with the loader (`loader: () => ({ consent: getConsentState() })`), the banner trade-off and when to pick which. The awaited loader stays the default: unlike the Next.js layout in #1195, it has no warm-cache paint penalty here, and it puts the banner in the server HTML. - The CLI boilerplate needs no change: its generated `Consent` component types `state` as `ConsentRootProps['state']`, so it takes the promise as soon as a user switches the loader. `examples/tanstack-start` keeps the awaited loader. The runtime path was already there; without this change the streamed loader only compiled with a cast. fix(core): isolate consent listeners and keep nested transitions ordered (#1221) ## Problem Checked against `9993ae578`, the current `v3` head. Snapshot notification called subscribers without isolation and passed the live snapshot cell. - A throwing subscriber stopped the subscribers after it. The exception rejected `commands.save()` before `choice:recorded`, so persistence never wrote the denial, even though the in-memory permission had already changed. - A subscriber that saved a grant while being notified of a denial ran a nested notification. The outer loop then resumed with the new snapshot, so later subscribers saw `[true, true]` and missed the denial. `permissions:changed` arrived newest first, and the outer save's `choice:recorded` carried the nested snapshot. ## Change Snapshot subscribers and the event bus now share one dispatcher (`packages/core/src/kernel/dispatch.ts`). - Each listener call is isolated. Errors go to `reportError` where the platform has it, and to `console.error` otherwise. The reporter's own failures are swallowed, so reporting cannot recurse into delivery. - `commit()` delivers the frozen snapshot it produced, not the live cell. - Delivery stays synchronous and reentrant, but deliveries share cursors. When a listener commits, the deliveries in progress first finish for their remaining listeners, then the new one runs, all before the nested commit returns. Every listener sees commits in order. A listener that is mid-work, such as the script loader mounting a script, still learns about a revocation it caused. - Commands and setters batch a commit together with its follow-up event (`choice:recorded`, `init:applied`, `overrides:set` and so on). The event carries its own snapshot and is delivered before any transition a listener starts. `save()` builds its payload and records generation from its own commit. - A listener added during delivery first receives the next change. A listener removed during delivery is skipped. - Feedback loops stop after 100 nested deliveries and report an error. Before, they overflowed the stack. I first tried a FIFO queue that deferred nested deliveries. It broke `@c15t/dev-tools`' "does not insert a later target after synchronous consent revocation" test: the loader mounted a body script after the visitor had revoked consent. Reentrant delivery with shared cursors keeps that guarantee. Docs: added "How listeners are notified" to the kernel API overview. Release note: `.tegami/2026-09-27-isolate-consent-listeners.md` (`@c15t/core`, `c15t` patch). ## Tests - `kernel/__tests__/listener-isolation.test.ts`: throwing subscribers before, between and after the others; throwing event listeners; `reportError` and a throwing reporter; setters; nested regrant with each registration order; event order and snapshots; synchronous nested delivery; subscribing and unsubscribing during delivery; the feedback cutoff; frozen committed snapshots. - `modules/persistence/__tests__/listener-failure.test.ts`: real `createPersistence` with throwing consumers registered before and after it, and a nested regrant. - Before the fix, 11 kernel cases and both throwing-consumer persistence cases failed. - `bun run --cwd packages/core test`: 1,313 tests pass. Core `check-types` and `lint` pass. - `TURBO_SCM_BASE=origin/v3 bun run test --continue`: every affected package passed except these: - `@c15t/svelte` `iab-lazy` timed out once under full parallel load, and the full Svelte suite passes on its own. - The `example-nextjs` and `next-compat-16-static-export` builds need `NEXT_PUBLIC_C15T_BACKEND_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_COMPAT_BACKEND_URL`, which aren't set locally. - Not verified locally: Playwright browser groups. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? fix(core): reconcile consent that other tabs store (#1223) ## Problem A running runtime kept a grant after another runtime stored a denial in the same browser. `kernel.refresh()` only re-evaluates records already in memory, and `runtime.reinit()` only reruns transport init. Neither reads storage again, and the runtime did not expose its persistence handle. I reproduced this in jsdom through `createConsentRuntime`: grant, start a second runtime, deny from a third, then refresh and reinit the second. It still reported the grant. ## Change **API.** `createPersistence` gets `reconcile()`, `ConsentRuntime` gets `reconcileStorage()`, and React's `usePersistence()` handle gets `reconcile()`. Each returns whether any in-memory record changed. The new persistence option `sync` defaults to `true`. With it on, the module schedules one coalesced reconciliation on a `storage` event for its own keys (including custom `storageKey`s and `localStorage.clear()`), on `visibilitychange` to visible, and on window `focus`. Reconnecting does not trigger a read, since going online changes nothing in storage. `dispose()` removes the listeners and cancels a scheduled run. Every adapter that mounts persistence (React, Next.js, TanStack Start, Vue, Svelte, Astro, the script tag and the runtime) gets this without code changes. **What a reconciliation applies.** Only records whose stored value changed since this runtime last read or wrote them are considered. A record held only in memory is not touched, for example a receipt merged from the server after `identify()`. Each changed record is then handled as follows: - A stored record at least as new as the one in memory replaces it. The comparison uses the record's own times: category `confirmedAt`, `dismissedAt`, vendor `confirmedAt` and directive `recordedAt`. - An older stored record is ignored. - A record removed from readable storage is cleared, so the active policy decides again. - Blocked storage and bytes that do not decode change nothing. There is a new `readStoredRecordsForReconcile`, because the existing read treats undecodable bytes as absent, which under an opt-out policy would turn a denial into a grant. Changes go through `kernel.hydrate()`, so they are validated and never written back. The existing evaluator decides expiry at read time. Subscribers and `permissions:changed` fire once. **Ordering.** Reconciliation first flushes this runtime's queued writes, so it never reverts the visitor's latest action in this tab. Writes are now guarded: a queued write skips when storage holds a newer record. The rewrite triggered by `subject:resolved` only lands on a record that still holds this runtime's decisions. That also fixes a pre-existing race where a slow save response could overwrite another tab's newer denial or recreate records another tab had cleared. As with any hydration, a save still in flight when another tab's choice is applied is fenced by the records generation, so this tab neither sends it nor queues it for retry. I didn't restructure `notify()` or `commit()` in `kernel/runtime.ts`. ## Tests - `packages/core/src/runtime/__tests__/storage-reconciliation.test.ts` (jsdom, public runtime API) covers the reproduction plus notification, clearing under opt-in and opt-out, a custom storage key, blocked and undecodable storage, memory-only records, the queued-write-first order, an older queued write versus a newer stored denial, a late subject acknowledgement versus a newer denial or a clear, the event triggers and key filtering, `sync: false`, and disposal. I checked that the ordering tests fail when the write guards, the flush-before-read, the undecodable-read handling or the change fingerprints are removed. - `packages/browser/src/__tests__/storage-sync.browser.test.ts` runs in real Chromium through the existing Vitest browser project. It opens two pages with `window.open` against a fixture page served by the Vitest server. A denial saved in one page reaches the other and notifies it, and clearing in one returns the other to the opt-in default. It fails without the listeners and passed six times in a row with them. Commands run: - `TURBO_SCM_BASE=origin/v3 bun run test --continue`: every package test task passed (core 1307, react 719, browser 206, vue 345, svelte 480, astro 318, nextjs 283, tanstack-start 299, and the rest). Two example builds failed only because `NEXT_PUBLIC_C15T_BACKEND_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_COMPAT_BACKEND_URL` are unset locally. - `bun turbo run check-types --filter=...@c15t/core` passed, and so did core's `tsconfig.test.json`. - `bun run fmt`, `bun run fmt:check`, `bun run lint:docs` and `bun run lint:testids` passed. `bun run lint` and `lint:repo` fail on `no-barrel-file` in `packages/react/src/preferences.ts` (104 modules). That file is unchanged here, and the count stays at 104 with the new module removed from `dist`. ## Not verified - Cross-origin iframes, Safari and Firefox. Only Chromium was exercised. - Whether Chromium ever delivers the `storage` event before another renderer can read the new cookie. The cookie is read first. If it lags, the next event, focus or visibility change picks the record up. I did not see this in six runs. - IAB/TCF state across tabs. The kernel resets the TC string when records are cleared, but I didn't test the `@c15t/iab` module with two tabs. - Saves already in the pending-replay queue still replay with their original `givenAt`. I didn't check how the backend orders a replayed older grant against a newer denial from another tab. - Bundle cost: bundling the persistence module with `bun build --minify` measures about +1.3 kB gzip. I didn't run the repo's bundle benchmarks. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Storage, visibility, and focus browser events schedule one coalesced reconciliation in `createPersistence`; `sync: false` in `persistence.PersistenceOptions` disables it. New `reconcile` and `ConsentRuntime.reconcileStorage` APIs allow manual reconciliation. > - Adds clear epochs in `persistence.writeStoredClearEpoch`. fix(iab): encode, decode and enforce publisher restrictions (#1222) Publisher restrictions were declared in the public types (`TCFConsentData.publisherRestrictions`, `TCData.publisher.restrictions`) but dropped at every stage of the TCF pipeline. ## What was broken I reproduced this with hand-built TC strings before changing anything. `packages/iab/src/__tests__/fixtures/publisher-restrictions.ts` writes and reads the core segment from the field table in the IAB spec, including NumPubRestrictions, PurposeId(6), RestrictionType(2), NumEntries(12) and the range entries. It shares no code with `@iabtechlabtcf/core`, so it can check the encoder's bit layout independently. Against `9993ae57`: - **Encode:** `generateTCString` ignored `publisherRestrictions`. The PubRestrictions section was always `[]`. - **Decode:** `decodeTCString` had no restrictions field. It returned `undefined` for the type 0, 1 and 2 fixtures. - **CMP API:** `getTCData().publisher.restrictions` was always `{}`. - **Authority and gates:** `KernelIABAuthority` had nowhere to put restrictions, and `hasIABConsent` granted a vendor whose purpose was prohibited. - **Unsupported input:** the codec already rejects type 3, purpose ID 0 and inverted ranges on decode. Vendor ID 0, LI required for purpose 3 and conflicting types for one vendor decoded without error. On encode, the library silently drops any restriction its vendor list does not allow. ## Contract `publisherRestrictions` is accepted by `createIAB`, `IABProvider` and the runtime's `iab` options. It is documented in a shared include used by the JavaScript, React and Next.js IAB pages. | Type | Meaning | Allowed when the vendor | | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | Purpose not allowed | declares the purpose for consent or LI | | 1 | Consent required | declares it for LI and lists it in `flexiblePurposes` | | 2 | LI required | declares it for consent and lists it in `flexiblePurposes`, and the purpose is not 1, 3, 4, 5 or 6 | Restrictions require a service-specific string. Unsupported input throws `PublisherRestrictionError`, a subclass of `TypeError`. This covers reserved type 3, IDs out of range, a vendor or purpose missing from the list, a restriction that does not match the vendor's declarations, conflicting types for one vendor and purpose, and a non-service-specific string. `whenReady()` rejects, `save()` and `generateTCString()` reject, and no TC string or consent is written. ## Change - `tc-string.ts` validates restrictions against the vendor list, then encodes them. It checks that the library kept each one, and decodes and validates them on read. - `cmp-api.ts` reports restrictions decoded from the current TC string as `{ [purposeId]: { [vendorId]: type } }`. - `authority.ts` puts decoded restrictions on `KernelIABAuthority`. A stored string whose restrictions differ from the configuration for listed vendors is not restored, so the visitor is asked again. - `has.ts`: in `hasIABConsent`, type 0 denies. Type 1 moves an LI purpose to consent, and type 2 moves a consent purpose to LI. A move only applies when the vendor list marks the purpose flexible for that vendor; otherwise the vendor is denied. - `acceptAll` sets the vendor signal a restriction moves a purpose to, such as LI for a vendor that declares no LI purposes. - Core threads the option through `IABConfig`, the runtime factory options and the save-authority guard. ## Tests - `publisher-restrictions.test.ts`: decodes the spec fixtures and rejects invalid ones. Checks the encoder's bit layout with the independent reader and round-trips through decode. Covers 14 encode rejection cases and the CMP API map. - `authority.test.ts`: full save flow with configured restrictions (gating, the `getTCData` map, the LI signal from accept all). Unsupported restrictions reject `whenReady` and `save`. Stored authority must match the configuration. fix(core,react): keep v3 iframe blocker running past unreadable nodes and invalid categories (#1249) ## Overview This is the v3 counterpart to #1248, which fixes the same bug on canary. The v3 iframe blocker was rewritten, so the fix is separate. One bad node can make the blocker let consent-gated iframes load. On v3 this happens in two ways: 1. **A node page script can't read.** The observer in `modules/iframe-blocker` reads `node.nodeType` without a guard, for both added and removed nodes. Firefox throws `Permission denied to access property "nodeType"` for some nodes, most likely ones inserted by extensions. v3 collects every iframe in a batch before reconciling any, so the throw skips all of them, including iframes added before the bad node. The on-demand watcher in `@c15t/react` (`isIframe` / `collectIframes`) has the same unguarded read. 2. **An iframe with an invalid `data-category`.** `determineCategory` throws. `registerIframes` reads every gated iframe's category before any iframe is reconciled, so one invalid category: - makes `createIframeBlocker` throw on startup, and no observer is attached; - stops every later pass early. Revoking consent updates the permissions but leaves the other gated iframes loaded. The kernel catches subscriber errors, so consent saves still work on v3. The damage is limited to iframes. ## Related Issue Fixes #1168 for v3. #1248 fixes it on canary. ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) ## Implementation Details ### Key Changes 1. `isIframe` and `addIframes` in `modules/iframe-blocker/index.ts` read each node inside a try/catch, for added nodes, removed nodes, and attribute targets. An unreadable node is skipped, and the rest of the batch is gated. 2. `determineCategory` returns `null` for an unknown category instead of throwing. `reconcileIframe` keeps that iframe blocked and logs a console warning. `registerIframes` already skipped falsy categories, so it needs no change. 3. The React on-demand watcher gets the same guard in `isIframe` and `collectIframes`. 4. The sentence in `docs/integrations/granular-consent.mdx` that said an unknown category always throws now names the iframe blocker as the exception. 5. A Tegami note bumps `@c15t/core` and `@c15t/react` (patch). ### Technical Notes - An iframe with an invalid category is kept **blocked**. The React on-demand watcher already does this (`isClearlyAllowed` returns `false` for a category it can't read), so the watcher and the loaded blocker now agree. The canary fix in #1248 leaves such an iframe unchanged, to avoid changing behavior on the stable line. - Behavior change: `createIframeBlocker` no longer throws for an invalid `data-category`, and the on-demand path no longer produces an unhandled rejection. The tests that asserted those errors now assert the iframe stays blocked and a warning is logged. ## Testing ### Test Plan - [x] Core (`iframe-blocker.test.ts`, `reconcile.test.ts`) covers: - an invalid category at startup, and during a revoke; - an unreadable node between two iframes in one batch; - an invalid-category iframe inside a batch; - `determineCategory` returning `null`; - an invalid-category iframe staying blocked even with every category granted. All 6 new tests fail on `v3` and pass with the fix. The full core suite passes (1490 tests). - [x] React (`iframe-blocker-on-demand.test.tsx`, real Chromium) covers an iframe added in the same batch as an unreadable node, and an invalid category staying blocked with a warning. Both fail on `v3` and pass with the fix; all 11 tests in the file pass. - [x] I ran a browser repro against `v3`, before and after the fix. The try/catch wraps reads that were already happening. - [x] Security: this closes a gap where consent-gated iframes loaded, or stayed loaded, without consent. feat: share consent and script controls across frameworks (#1204)

Blume needs c15t to own script loading and consent lifecycle while
allowing an existing CMP to remain the consent authority. This adds that
support to c15t's shared core and native framework APIs, plus
consent-aware application event dispatch in the scripts SDK.

`consentSource` works through React (including Next.js and TanStack
Start), Vue/Nuxt, Svelte/SvelteKit, the browser client, and Astro.
Headless JavaScript and Solid use the same core runtime. No framework
depends on Astro for these controls. React uses a lightweight controls
entrypoint to preserve lazy script loading. When the source withdraws a
granted category, the page reloads through the existing
`reloadOnConsentRevoked` option and `onBeforeConsentRevocationReload`
callback.

External permissions start denied and follow the provider's current
decisions. c15t skips its backend initialization, persistence, and IAB
setup, and never turns provider booleans into choice receipts. Save
commands reject before recording. Native preference controls delegate
through a shared kernel event while c15t's own choice surfaces stay
hidden. Preference failures reach lifecycle error callbacks. Nuxt skips
consent prefetch and record hydration for an external source and
subscribes after mount.

`createEventDispatcher` delivers only to configured integrations whose
current gates permit analytics, discards denied events, isolates vendor
errors, and deduplicates explicitly configured SPA pageviews. The SDK
additions preserve Google tag config, custom GTM queues with denied
defaults before container initialization, and Segment load options. The
scripts package declares its core dependency.

Validation:
- 4,018 tests passed across core (1,297), React (720), Vue/Nuxt (347),
Svelte (481), browser (205), Astro (319), Next.js (283), TanStack Start
(299), and DevTools (67). Applicable coverage gates passed.
- The scripts SDK's 434 tests passed for the initial SDK changes; this
follow-up changes the framework wiring and shared controls.
- Builds, typechecks, and lint passed for all affected runtime/framework
packages and the umbrella package, using Node 24.
- Framework regressions cover external grants, withdrawal, preference
delegation, listener disposal, React StrictMode, lazy script loading,
and Nuxt initialization boundaries.
- Canonical shared documentation added, package docs regenerated, and
umbrella exports regenerated.
- Blume refreshed local packages passed targeted consent/analytics
tests, uncached workspace typechecks, and production browser checks for
both offline GTM and Osano external consent, including events,
preferences, navigation, and withdrawal/reload. The initial integration
also verified Fides and ejected sites. Vendor requests were intercepted.

Draft companion to https://github.com/BurnedChris/blume/pull/1. The
external CMP remains responsible for records, expiration, privacy
signals, and category mapping; the bridge does not certify compliance.
Blume's temporary file dependencies must be replaced with the published
v3 alpha before release.

fix(astro): restore stored consent on prerendered pages (#1178) Stack for Astro static builds: #1177 → #1178 → #1179 → #1180 → #1182 → #1183 → #1184 → #1185 → #1186 → #1187 → #1188 → #1189. On a prerendered page, a visitor's consent choice was lost on every reload. `readInitialConsentConfig` ran at build time even with `skipPrefetch`. It read the build request's empty cookie header and inlined `initialRecords: { choice: null }` and a build-time `now` into `__c15tAstroConfig`. The core runtime skips reading storage whenever the inlined config carries `initialRecords`, so the stored `c15t` cookie was never read back. ## Changes - `resolveConsentContext` takes a new `prerendered` option. It ignores the request headers and leaves `initialRecords`, `now` and `initialPrivacySignals` out of the inlined config, so the browser reads the visitor's own cookie. GPC is still detected in the browser. - The middleware passes `prerendered` and hands prerendered routes an empty `Headers`. That removes Astro's warning about reading `Astro.request.headers` on a prerendered page. - The client fills in `now` at boot when the inlined config has none. - `Astro.locals.c15t` gains a `prerendered` flag. #1179 uses it. This PR doesn't make the banner appear on static pages. That's #1179. ## Testing - New `prerender.test.ts`: a prerendered request whose `headers` getter throws, the inlined config with no visitor state, and hosted mode making no request at build time. - New `prerender.dom.test.ts`: a stored rejection is restored on a prerendered page, and a first-time visitor is asked. feat(astro): show the prerendered banner at first paint when nothing is stored (#1185) Stack for Astro static builds: #1177 → #1178 → #1179 → #1180 → #1182 → #1183 → #1184 → #1185 → #1186 → #1187 → #1188 → #1189. A prerendered offline banner ships hidden, because the same HTML serves visitors who have already chosen. It stayed hidden until the page's module scripts loaded. An inline script right after the hidden banner, and after the IAB banner, now checks the cookie and `localStorage` for the consent keys: `c15t` (or the configured `storageKey`), its `-notice` sibling and the legacy `privacy-consent-storage`. If none exist, the visitor cannot have chosen, so it shows the banner and its overlay straight away. Anyone with a stored record still waits for the runtime, which validates it. The builder is exported as `buildBannerRevealScript` from `@c15t/astro/server`. A first-time visitor with GPC under a policy that owes them no banner would see it briefly, until the runtime hides it. fix(astro): stop dialog islands shipping a second copy of the stylesheet (#1188) Stack for Astro static builds: #1177 → #1178 → #1179 → #1180 → #1182 → #1183 → #1184 → #1185 → #1186 → #1187 → #1188 → #1189. With `ui: 'svelte'`, every page of the Astro 5 demo linked a 72 KB dialog stylesheet on top of the injected full stylesheet, which already has those rules. The dialog islands import `@c15t/ui` class maps. In the browser those modules also import their component CSS, and Astro links every stylesheet a page script can reach on every page. When the integration injects the full stylesheet, a new Vite plugin resolves browser-side `@c15t/ui/styles/components/` imports to the `.node.js` variant, which has the same class names and no CSS import. The server build already uses that variant through the `node` condition. With `styles: false` the plugin is not added, so the islands keep their own CSS. ## Astro bug: lazy chunk CSS deleted Since Astro 5.16.12, CSS imported by modules that are reachable only from an `injectScript('page', ...)` script is deleted from the build, whether the import is static or dynamic. The cause is the orphan check in `astro:rollup-plugin-inline-stylesheets` ([withastro/astro#14607](https://github.com/withastro/astro/pull/14607)): it looks for the sheet in a chunk's `importedAssets` but not in `importedCss`, where Vite records it. The same thing happens on Astro 7.3.5. This PR does not change that. With `styles` on, the injected stylesheets cover every rule. On the published alpha, which relies on the islands' own CSS, the IAB dialog surface loses about 120 of its classes. #1180 and this PR close that gap by injecting `@c15t/astro/iab/styles.css` whenever `iab` is set, and by leaving IAB class maps alone otherwise. ## Testing - Unit tests for the resolver: it points browser class maps at the no-CSS variant, and leaves the server build, `.css` subpaths and class maps without a variant alone. Another test checks the plugin is added only when `styles` is on. - `astro-demo` (Svelte, Astro 5) now emits one stylesheet, and pages no longer link `panel-surface.css`. - Both Astro example targets pass all journeys. > [!NOTE] > ### Fix duplicate stylesheet in Astro dialog islands via `c15t:class-maps-without-css` plugin > - Adds a Vite plugin `c15t:class-maps-without-css` in [class-map-plugin.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1188/files#diff-3c904e381e1432696ff3fa49add7fc3091cd774879c6865c4bc0358e0bd4e5db) that redirects browser class-map imports to their `.node.js` variant, avoiding the CSS-bearing module when the full stylesheet is already injected. > - The plugin skips SSR/server resolution, direct `.css` imports, missing variants, and IAB class maps unless the IAB stylesheet is also injected. > - [integration.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1188/files#diff-b33047facc2c2c36ae72893d968e153c5658f06e67f34d8b339cf191ac064931) registers the plugin in `buildVitePlugins` when styles are enabled; it is omitted when `styles: false`. > - Behavioral Change: eligible browser imports of `@c15t/ui/styles/components/` now resolve to the `.node.js` variant instead of the CSS-bearing module; check `createClassMapPlugin` matchers if other components rely on the original resolution. > > > > Macroscope summarized b7a4098. > > ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Performance** * Astro integrations with styles enabled now avoid loading unnecessary dialog CSS, reducing the amount of CSS sent to the browser. * Disabling styles continues to preserve the islands’ CSS. * **Compatibility** * The Astro integration now selects the appropriate client-side class-map variant while leaving server-side imports unchanged.

fix(benchmarks): measure real saved-consent visits and separate banner milestones (#1190) Several browser-bench labels described something other than what they measured. This fixes the definitions, adds a production consumer built from packed artifacts, and marks the superseded parts of the July gate report. No SDK package changes. ## What was wrong - **`repeat-visitor` measured first-time visitors in five of six harnesses.** React, Next.js and TanStack Start opened a new browser context without the stored choice. SvelteKit and Astro seeded a cookie stamped `i.t:1800000000000` (January 2027), which the cookie reader rejects as a future consent time. Only Nuxt measured a returning visitor. - **`bannerInFirstHtml` read the finished document.** It could not tell the first streamed chunk from a banner that arrives after an awaited consent resolution. - **Banner milestones were blurred.** `bannerPaintMs` fell back to a different reading, arms without a banner reported `bannerReadyMs = 0`, and nothing recorded FCP or LCP. - **Cold labels didn't say which caches were cold.** The Nuxt `--cold-manifest` token was only read at build time, so it never changed the URL of an existing build. ## Changes - `saved-consent-accept` and `saved-consent-reject` replace the fresh-context `repeat-visitor` arms (React, Next.js, TanStack Start). A fresh visit clicks accept or reject and its `storageState()` seeds a new context. Every sample fails the run if the banner shows in the DOM or server HTML, or if no stored choice is restored. Fresh visits must show the banner. SvelteKit and Astro use `createRepeatVisitorCookie()` and the same assertion. - `bannerInFirstChunk` and `bannerInServerHtml` come from a raw `accept-encoding: identity` HTTP read with the visit's cookies, plus arrival times for the first chunk and the banner markup. - The shared observer records `bannerDomMs`, `bannerFirstFrameMs`, Element Timing `bannerPaintMs`, `fcpMs` and `lcpMs`. `bannerReadyMs` stays the hydrated reading. Visits without a banner report `null`. - Every result carries `cacheBrowser`, `cacheSdkManifest`, `cacheFrameworkProcess`, `cacheCdnEdge: not-measured` and a `cacheSetup` sentence. - `bench:production-consumer` (in `nextjs-browser-bench`) packs c15t with `bun pm pack`, installs the tarballs into a Next.js 16 app outside the workspace, and runs interleaved arms. The app uses the aggregate stylesheet, a custom theme, `resolveConsent` under a Suspense boundary, and the deferred dialog. It reports stylesheet count, bytes and cross-stylesheet class overlap per route, and separates fresh, warm-browser-cache, cold-SDK-manifest and cold-process visits. - `benchmarks/reports/visit-definitions-2026-09-25/README.md` has the details. `gate-2026-07-05.md` now says which rows and gate claims are superseded, including the placeholder-driven hosted-client banner win from Addendum D. - Ports are configurable (`--port` / `C15T_BENCH_PORT`) in every harness. - **The React `C15T_CSS=styles` arm hasn't built since `bbfcc04bb`.** Its shim and extras imported `*.module.css` specifiers that now resolve to JavaScript class maps. Turbopack failed with `missing VAR_MODULE_GLOBAL_ERROR in template` and webpack with `Selector ":root" is not pure`. The shim also dropped `rights`, `rightLink` and the overlay classes the banner reads. The shim and aliases are gone because v3 class maps already are CSS-module maps. The default build imports `@c15t/react/styles.css`. The `C15T_CSS=styles` build imports the banner's five component stylesheets explicitly and builds into `.next-css-styles`. Component stylesheets carry no default tokens, so `banner-css` passes the full default theme in both builds. Without it, the component-CSS banner renders with a transparent card and square corners. Each `banner-css` sample now fails if the banner card is unstyled. ## Before / After Old harness (`v3` at `40032552c`) against this branch, same c15t build, same machine. Condition A (no throttle, no injected latency) unless noted. 7 measured samples after 1 warm-up. Medians with ranges. Load averages were 5 to 18 because other benchmark jobs shared the machine; the label findings don't depend on timing. | Harness | Before arm | Banner shown | Banner ready | After arm | Banner shown | Choice restored | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | | React | `repeat-visitor` | 7/7 | 50.9 (50.2–57.8) ms | `saved-consent-accept` / `-reject` | 0/7 / 0/7 | 7/7 / 7/7 | | Next.js | `repeat-visitor` | 7/7 | 57.3 (53.3–66.0) ms | `saved-consent-accept` / `-reject` | 0/7 / 0/7 | 7/7 / 7/7 | | TanStack Start | `repeat-visitor` | 7/7 | 58.6 (57.0–69.7) ms | `saved-consent-accept` / `-reject` | 0/7 / 0/7 | 7/7 / 7/7 | | SvelteKit | `repeat-visitor` | 7/7 (server HTML) | 38.0 (32.5–45.2) ms | `repeat-visitor` | 0/7 | 7/7 | | Astro | `repeat-visitor` | 7/7 (server HTML) | 26.6 (23.2–29.5) ms | `repeat-visitor` | 0/7 | 7/7 | The old Next.js arm also made one browser `/init` per visit; the saved-consent arms make none. Replaying the old flow through the new assertion fails: ```text old repeat-visitor (new context, no storage): a saved-accept visit carried a stored choice but still showed the consent banner (dom=1, activeUI=banner, serverHtml=n/a). The stored consent was not carried over. ``` First chunk against full server HTML (the old metric reported the second column): | Route | Condition | First chunk | Server HTML | First chunk at | Banner markup at | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Next.js bench `manifest-ssr` | A | 7/7 | 7/7 | – | – | | Astro bench `ssr-manifest` | A | 0/7 | 7/7 | 2.0 ms | 2.0 ms | | Production consumer `/` fresh | A | 0/7 | 7/7 | 4.8 ms | 7.7 ms | | Production consumer `/` cold SDK manifest | B | 0/7 | 7/7 | 2.9 ms | 209.5 ms | | Production consumer `/` saved consent | A, B | 0/7 | 0/7 | – | – | Condition B is 4× CPU, 170 ms latency, 1,125,000 B/s down, 187,500 B/s up, and 200 ms on the consent origin. docs(benchmarks): decompose the cold-start cost of a new Next process (#1196) The alpha.2 docs-site run showed a new `next start` process at 629 ms TTFB against 3 ms for a second request, with 7/7 origin `/manifest` calls. This PR adds a report and a runnable harness that measure the cache states separately. It changes no package code. Report: `benchmarks/reports/cold-start-decomposition-2026-09-25/README.md` ## Findings - **Why the site called the origin on every restart, and #1190's consumer did not:** the site passes `manifestRevalidateSeconds: 0` to `createNextConsentRouteHandlers`, which turns off the Next Data Cache and leaves only the SDK's in-process cache. That cache is empty in a new process. The handler default (300 s) writes the manifest to `.next/cache/fetch-cache`, which survives a restart. The consumer reproduces both: 9/9 origin calls on restart with the site's setting, 0/9 with the default. - **The 626 ms TTFB gap:** the manifest fetch contributes nothing. On the site build, the origin request leaves 110 ms (97–133) after the response headers; the brief's own samples show 106–212 ms. Loading c15t's share of the server chunks takes 3.3–4.2 ms before the first byte (and 2.4–2.8 ms after it), and no c15t code runs before the first byte. The rest comes from Next.js loading the site's route entries and modules on the first request. - **In a small app,** c15t adds about 25 ms to a cold first byte: about 14 ms for its modules in the page graph and about 11 ms for the first loopback to the manifest route. - **Manifest cache:** - 5 concurrent cold requests make 1 origin call, in a warm process and in a new one. - Stale-while-revalidate and the 5 s retry floor behave as documented. - With a cold failure (503) or a hang, the tracker stays blocked and the browser shows no banner. - **Not changed, for an owner to decide:** - A hanging backend on a cold cache holds page content for the route's 10 s fetch timeout. - A cold failure is not remembered, so each later request retries the origin. - Pointing `resolveConsent`'s `manifestURL` at the backend (off the documented path) bypasses both caches. - **Not measured:** the CDN edge, and Vercel's shared Data Cache. The seven-day CDN TTL was not tested. ## Before / After No fix, so "before" is the brief's combined measurement and "after" is the same cost split by state. fix(ui): load each component stylesheet rule once (#1191) The `@c15t/ui/styles/components/` class maps imported their own stylesheet, and `styles.css` carries the same rules. A Next.js 16 Turbopack production build of the documented setup (`@import 'c15t/react/styles.css'` plus prebuilt components) therefore shipped the same component rules twice, as separate CSS assets. This PR removes the CSS import from the class maps, so each rule loads once. ## CSS-loading contract - **React, Next.js, TanStack Start, Svelte, Astro:** the app imports `styles.css` (or `styles.tw3.css`) once. It holds every component rule, the default tokens and the shared primitive styles. Components load no CSS of their own. A component rendered without the stylesheet is unstyled. That was already true in practice: removing the aggregate on alpha.2 left the dialog broken because tokens and primitive rules only live in the aggregate. - **Vue / Nuxt:** components include their styles, as the Vue quickstart says. Vue components now import `@c15t/ui/styles/components/.css` next to each class map instead of relying on the class map to do it. Vue apps emit the same CSS files as before, byte for byte. Default tokens come from the Vue plugin config at runtime, as before. - **Per-component `.css` exports** stay published for hosts that assemble their own stylesheet. They hold one component's rules and no tokens or primitive rules. - **Class maps** (`.js` and `.node.js`) are now identical and CSS-free under every export condition. The `node` condition and `*.node.js` subpaths stay for compatibility. ## Cause `packages/ui/scripts/generate-style-artifacts.ts` kept `import "./.css"` in `.js`, which the `import` condition serves to bundlers. `packages/react` (and Svelte, Astro) import those class maps, for example `components/prompt/prompt.js` → `@c15t/ui/styles/components/consent-banner` → `prompt.js` → `prompt.css`. Next's client graph turned each of those side-effect imports into its own stylesheet, next to the global one that already inlines `styles.css`: | Extra asset (alpha.2) | Contents | Pulled in by | | --- | --- | --- | | `0r84qk585kd6s.css`, 18,278 B | `prompt.css` | `ConsentBanner` | | `26wn2-vv6-4op.css`, 25,916 B | `consent-actions.css`, `branding.css`, `button.css` | banner actions | | `10m2etv5psngl.css`, 1,459 B | `legal-links.css` | banner legal links | | `3bphc3-q_ba9v.css`, 2,093 B | `frame.css` | `ConsentGate` re-export | | 3 more on dialog open | `panel.css`, `panel-trigger.css`, accordion/switch/preference-item/vendor-list | deferred dialog | Three of these have the same content hashes as the extra stylesheets on the c15t docs site. Primitive class maps already had their CSS import stripped for the same reason, and 2.x stripped both. The duplicates also change the cascade. If a layout imports a consent component before its global CSS, the component stylesheets load first and declare `@layer components` before Tailwind 4 declares `theme, base, components, utilities`. Tailwind's preflight then outranks c15t, and the banner buttons lose their background and radius. See the second screenshot table. ## Before / After Minimal Next.js 16.3.4 App Router consumer, Turbopack production build, installed from packed tarballs (not workspace links). It mirrors the docs site: Tailwind 4 + `@import 'c15t/react/styles.css'`, the site's colour-only custom theme (light/dark via `next-themes`), a page-wide `Suspense` around `await resolveConsent()` from `c15t/next/server` resolving a captured manifest, `ConsentBanner` rendered on the server, the deferred `ConsentDialog`, and a `ConsentGate` re-export. Before: `origin/v3` `40032552c` (alpha.2). After: this branch `7eadda5b1`. Chromium 1223 (Playwright), 1280×720. ### Emitted CSS (both `/` and `/docs`) | | Before | After | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Stylesheets on first load | 5 | 1 | | First-load CSS, raw / gzip | 184,028 B / 24,948 B | 136,282 B / 18,122 B | | Stylesheets after opening the dialog | 8 | 1 | | CSS after opening the dialog, raw / gzip | 231,029 B / 32,949 B | 136,282 B / 18,122 B | | CSS rules present in more than one asset | 399 | 0 | | CSS transfer on first load (resource timing) | 26,729 B | 18,649 B | The global stylesheet is byte-identical in both builds (same hash). ### First contentful paint Interleaved ABAB, one warm-up per arm and route, fresh browser context and disabled cache per sample. Medians, range in brackets. | Conditions | Route | n per arm | Before | After | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | CDP 4× CPU, 170 ms, 1,125,000 B/s down, 187,500 B/s up, **HTTP/2** (local TLS proxy) | `/` | 11 | 504 ms (500–508) | 496 ms (488–500) | | same | `/docs` | 11 | 520 ms (512–548) | 504 ms (492–524) | | same profile, **HTTP/1.1** direct to `next start` | `/` | 11 | 436 ms (432–444) | 468 ms (464–476) | | same | `/docs` | 11 | 444 ms (440–456) | 480 ms (472–492) | | Lighthouse 13.5.0 mobile, simulated throttling | `/` | 7 | 1,204 ms (1,054–1,206) | 904 ms (903–905) | | same | `/docs` | 7 | 1,203 ms (1,053–1,212) | 904 ms (903–905) | The HTTP/1.1 row got slower, and the stylesheet itself did not cause it. Request timing shows why: with alpha.2, the four extra render-blocking stylesheets hold five of Chrome's six HTTP/1.1 connections, so the low-priority async scripts wait, and the global stylesheet gets the throttled pipe mostly to itself (done at 402 ms). With one stylesheet, the scripts download alongside it and CDP throttling splits bandwidth evenly regardless of priority, so the same 18,740-byte file finishes at 430 ms. Over HTTP/2, which is what a CDN serves, the fix is 8–16 ms faster. Lighthouse's model, which charges a round trip per render-blocking request, shows about 300 ms. Machine load averages (1 min) during runs: HTTP/2 11.4 → 9.8, HTTP/1.1 6.9 → 8.5, Lighthouse 9.9 → 10.4. fix(nextjs,tanstack-start): keep offline-mode presets out of the ConsentRoot initial bundle (#1192) ## Summary The c15t docs site's initial route JS grew by 22,030 B gzip and CSS by 12,945 B between 2.2.1 and 3.0.0-alpha.2, but that comparison mixed in other site changes. This PR measures the payload in one Next.js 16 consumer where only the consent setup changes, attributes it to packages and modules, and fixes the one SDK cause it found in the initial bundle. **Fix.** `ConsentRoot` in `@c15t/nextjs` and `@c15t/tanstack-start` picks its transport at runtime and imported `offline()` statically. Offline mode's default rule pack (`policy-rule-presets`, `legacy-preset-material`, `policy-runtime` and the offline transport) shipped in the initial bundle of every app that renders the root, including apps with a backend or manifest URL, where offline mode never runs. Both roots now load offline mode with a dynamic import on first init, as the Next.js root already did for the manifest transport.
