fix(react): load the consent dialog before its first open (#1193) ## Summary The deferred `` downloads its chunk (10 KB gzip) on first use. Before this PR, only `ConsentBanner.PolicyActions` started that download early, so the stock banner and every other dialog opener waited for the chunk after the click. This PR makes the dialog load before the first open in three ways: - **Hover and focus.** `ConsentButton` warms the dialog on focus and pointer enter when `action="open-consent-dialog"`. That covers the stock banner's Customize button, `PolicyActions`, `ConsentDialogLink`, the `ConsentGate` button and the widget's Customize button. `ConsentDialogTrigger` does the same. Handlers passed as `onFocus` or `onPointerEnter` still run. - **Idle time.** A tap, or focus and Enter together, leaves no lead time for hover or focus. While the banner is shown or a dialog opener is mounted, the dialog now loads in the first idle period after the page's `load` event (`requestIdleCallback`, or 200 ms after `load` in Safari). It's skipped with Save-Data, on `2g`/`slow-2g` and offline, where hover and focus still load it. `preloadDialog: 'intent'` in the provider options (or `ConsentRoot`'s `options`) turns idle loading off. A saved-consent visit with nothing on the page that opens the dialog downloads nothing extra. - **Failed preloads retry.** A preload that failed used to be cached, so the later open threw the same error. With the first commit's focus warming, a failed chunk request on focus left the dialog unopenable until reload. Only a rendered export caches a failure now, so after a failed preload the next hover, focus or open retries the import. The dialog still isn't part of first-load JS. ### Eval at idle, or download only? I measured both. The network-only arm preloads the same chunk at idle with `` and evaluates it on open. - Evaluating at idle costs 2.6 ms of `EvaluateScript` at 4× CPU (3.2 ms of task time in all, longest task 2.8 ms), well below the 50 ms long-task threshold. - Deferring the evaluation to the open saves nothing measurable: focus and Enter 3 s after load takes 38.4 ms evaluated at idle and 39.1 ms network-only (B, 4×). - A library can't portably learn a bundler's chunk URL without importing the chunk. perf(nextjs): send the first manifest-mode save without loading the resolver (#1194) With `ConsentRoot` and a `manifestURL` config (the documented App Router setup), the first Accept, Reject or Save downloaded the manifest resolver chunk before `POST /subjects` went out. That chunk is 63,877 B gzip, mostly all-locale translations. When the server has already resolved the visitor's state, the browser never runs init, so nothing in that chunk is needed to save. This PR makes `ConsentRoot`'s lazy manifest transport send saves, identity links, subject reads and privacy directives through the hosted transport until init starts loading the resolver. Both transports send the same request to the same route. Once a browser init loads the resolver, every call goes through it as before. ## Why the backend check is unaffected The backend recomputes the decision from `policyId`, `fingerprint`, `country`, `region`, `language` and `gpc` on `POST /subjects` and rejects a mismatch with `STALE_POLICY`. The kernel puts those values on every save payload from the server-resolved snapshot (`saveDecisionInputs`), and `buildDecisionAssertion` prefers them over anything the transport remembered. The manifest transport only has its own remembered inputs after a browser init, which this path never runs. Checked in a production consumer: the POST path, header names and body (subject id and timestamps masked) are identical between alpha.2, this branch, and `hosted()`. One visible difference: if the save fails, the `onError` message says `c15t hosted transport` instead of `c15t manifest transport`. ## Before / After Production Next.js 16.3.4 consumer installed from packed tarballs (issue 3's App Router guide arm: `ConsentRoot`, `manifestURL`, SSR `resolveConsent` inside ``, custom theme, animations on). Before is alpha.2 (`40032552c`), after is this branch (`08659da9c`), `hosted()` is the site-shaped arm for reference. 7 measured samples plus 1 warm-up per cell, arms interleaved with rotating order. A: native CPU, no throttling. B: 4× CPU, 170 ms latency, 1,125,000 B/s down, 187,500 B/s up. Busy: a 40 ms long task every 160 ms. Load average 8.2 at start, 6.7 at end (other benchmarks were running on the machine). Times are ms from the click event's `timeStamp`, median [min–max]. | Flow | Condition | Measure | alpha.2 | This PR | `hosted()` | | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Accept | A idle | POST starts | 31 [30–37] | 26 [22–30] | 25 [24–30] | | Accept | B idle | POST starts | 279 [272–281] | 40 [33–41] | 40 [34–50] | | Accept | B busy | POST starts | 287 [280–294] | 39 [36–57] | 39 [35–79] | | Reject | B idle | POST starts | 276 [272–288] | 40 [33–55] | 43 [35–52] | | Save (dialog) | A idle | Dialog closed | 24 [23–32] | 16 [15–16] | 15 [14–20] | | Save (dialog) | B idle | Dialog closed | 464 [449–474] | 216 [210–218] | 213 [209–224] | | Save (dialog) | B busy | Dialog closed | 473 [444–489] | 209 [208–241] | 212 [207–234] | | Any first save | all | JS downloaded after the click | 63,877 B gzip | 0 B | 0 B | | Page load | — | Initial JS (gzip) | 209,763 B | 209,786 B | — | The banner itself closes on the first frame in every arm (Accept, B idle: 36, 35 and 36 ms), since the kernel commits the choice before the transport runs. The dialog numbers are larger because a v3 dialog stays open until its save request returns. A Chrome trace of Accept under B shows the chain on alpha.2: chunk requested at 35.7 ms, received at 269.6 ms (64,314 B), evaluated from 270.3 ms for 8.1 ms, POST sent at 277.9 ms. On this branch the POST is sent at 45.4 ms with no chunk request. ## Other packages Only `@c15t/nextjs` has this problem. I checked the other packages that resolve a manifest in the browser: - **`@c15t/vue` / Nuxt.** No change needed. In `manifest: 'server'` mode (the default with `manifestURL`), the browser uses the hosted transport and never loads the resolver. In `manifest: 'client'` mode there is no server-resolved state; the resolver loads at page start because the browser resolves init itself, and `save` uses the hosted transport until that resolver exists, so it never waits on the chunk. Measured on a Nuxt 4.5.1 production build of `benchmarks/nuxt-browser-bench` (workspace packages at `08659da9c`, condition B, 7 samples + 1 warm-up): | Route | POST starts | POST done | JS after the click | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `/ssr-manifest` | 34 [33–38] | 217 [207–222] | 0 B | | `/client-manifest` | 37 [34–39] | 217 [209–220] | 0 B | | `/ssr` (no manifest) | 39 [34–41] | 216 [210–226] | 0 B | - **`@c15t/browser`.** No change needed. `manifest()` imports its resolver statically with English translations only, and `save` is the hosted transport's. - **`@c15t/tanstack-start`.** No change needed. `ConsentRoot` picks `hosted()` or `offline()` and has no client manifest transport. - **Svelte and Astro.** No change needed. They use `manifestURL` only in server routes. ## Merging with #1192 #1192 also edits `packages/nextjs/src/root.tsx`. `git merge-tree` reports one conflict hunk in that file, in either merge order. This PR deletes the old lazy manifest block, and #1192 adds `lazyOffline` directly below it. To resolve it, delete the old block and keep `lazyOffline`. Every other change in both PRs, including the import lines, merges on its own. I tested that resolution in a scratch copy: `tsc` passes and `@c15t/nextjs` tests pass (16 files, 287 tests, including #1192's `root-offline-mode.test.tsx`). ## Tests - `packages/nextjs/src/__tests__/lazy-manifest-transport.test.ts` (new). A kernel seeded with a server-resolved state saves through the transport with an injected loader. The test asserts the loader is never called, the request goes to `/subjects`, and the body carries `policyId`, `fingerprint` and `country`. It fails on the alpha.2 behavior. A second test checks that saves use the resolver once init has loaded it. - `bun run --cwd packages/nextjs test`: 15 files, 285 tests pass. - `bun turbo run check-types --filter=@c15t/nextjs` passes. `bun run fmt` makes no changes. - `bun run lint`: every package passes. The repo-wide `oxlint .` step reports `no-barrel-file` on `packages/react/src/preferences.ts` (104 modules). This branch changes nothing reachable from that file. ## Related findings This came out of checking why the React acceptance speedup reported in #860 doesn't reproduce consistently. None of the findings below changes code in this PR: - #860's "v3 accepts 43% faster" comes from callback timing, not render speed. v2's `onConsentSet` fires after a `setTimeout(0)` that runs after the first frame. v3's `onChoiceRecorded` fires inside the click handler. Playwright's rAF polling needs one more frame for v2 (A idle: 49 vs 23–25 ms). The banner disappears on the same frame in both versions, and Event Timing's click duration is 24 ms in every arm. - The site's 3–8 ms "v3 slower from click to recorded" did not reproduce in this consumer. - Selector hooks do reduce renders. With 50 subscribers to a category that doesn't change, one saved toggle re-renders 100 components in v2, 50 through v3's `useConsentManager`, and 0 through `useConsent`. perf(react): load the iframe blocker when a gated iframe is on the page (#1201) > **Stack:** layer 10 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1200. Merge the PRs below it first. ## What was loading `ConsentProvider` mounts `IframeBlockerMount` unless `iframeBlocker: false`. It called `useIframeBlocker`, which imports `@c15t/core/modules/iframe-blocker` in a mount effect. So every page downloaded and ran the blocker right after hydration, iframes or not. In the documented App Router setup that was one extra request of 4,725 B raw (2,007 B gzip): `iframe-blocker/index.js`, `reconcile.js` and `consent-types.js`. On a page with no gated iframe, all it did was scan the DOM and subscribe. ## Change The provider now uses `useIframeBlockerOnDemand`: - If an iframe with `data-category` or `data-vendor` is on the page at mount, the blocker loads at once. That is the same timing as before. - Otherwise a small `MutationObserver` waits for the first one and loads the blocker then. - Until the blocker runs, a gated iframe that arrives with a `src` the current snapshot does not allow gets paused. The watcher moves `src` to `data-src` and sets `data-c15t-paused`, the same state the blocker leaves a denied frame in, so the blocker restores it once consent allows it. A frame the snapshot allows (checked with core's `evaluateConsent`, which is already in the first-load bundle) is left alone. - `iframeBlocker: { disableAutomaticBlocking: true }` and the public `useIframeBlocker()` hook still load the blocker at mount. The docs paragraph on iframe blocking now says the blocker loads on demand. It also says to write gated iframes with `data-src`, because the network test below shows a `src` is requested before any blocker can pause it. ## Regression tests `packages/react/src/__tests__/iframe-blocker-on-demand.test.tsx` counts loads of the blocker module, and can hold the module back: - A page without gated iframes never loads it. This fails on `origin/v3`. - A denied frame inserted before the chunk arrives loses its `src` while the chunk is held back. It stays paused after the blocker loads and gets its `src` back after a save grants the category. - An allowed frame inserted before the chunk arrives never loses its `src`. - A gated frame on the page at mount loads the blocker, which pauses it. The first, second and fourth tests fail with the old provider. ## Before / After Next.js 16.3.4 App Router consumer built from packed tarballs (`benchmarks/bundle-test-app/client-payload`). fix: block network requests sent before the network blocker loads (#1202) ## Summary The React provider loaded the network blocker in a mount effect (`NetworkBlockerMount`). Children's mount effects run before their parent's, and the blocker is a lazy chunk, so every `fetch` or XHR matching a rule that was sent at mount went out with no consent check. That happened on first visits, for visitors who had rejected, and when the policy request failed or hung. Only requests sent after the chunk loaded were blocked. This PR holds matching requests from the point where c15t first knows the rules, and has the blocker decide them once it loads: - **`@c15t/core/modules/network-hold`** (new, about 0.8 KB gzip): `holdNetworkRequests(rules)` patches `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` synchronously and queues only requests that match a rule. `createNetworkBlocker()` ends the hold and replays the queue through its own patches. Everything else passes straight through. - **React**: `NetworkBlockerMount` calls the hold during its first render. It renders before `children`, so the hold is in place before any child renders or runs an effect, and before effects in components rendered next to the provider. Nothing runs on the server (`typeof window` guard). If the provider unmounts before the blocker loads, the hold is released; StrictMode's effect re-run is detected so it doesn't release early. - **Consent unknown**: while the policy is pending and hasn't failed, a request the blocker would block now waits instead of getting a 451. It is sent if the resolved policy and stored choice allow it and blocked otherwise. A failed policy load blocks it, matching the existing "optional categories stay denied" behaviour. If the policy request hangs, the request is never sent. This keeps saved-accept visitors' mount-time requests working now that they are caught before persistence hydrates. - **Vue** had the same defect (the blocker is installed in the root's `mounted`, after every child's). The hold now starts in `createVueConsentKernelContext`. - **`createConsentRuntime()`** (used by `@c15t/svelte` and the `c15t` browser client) installs the blocker in `start()`, which Svelte calls from the provider's `onMount` after its children. The hold now starts at construction. `@c15t/solid` doesn't expose the network blocker. Apps that don't pass `networkBlocker` still never download the blocker chunk. The hold code is in first-load JavaScript for every provider app. ## What c15t can't cover These are documented on the new Next.js and React network blocker pages: - Code that runs before the provider renders: inline scripts, tags in ``, `beforeInteractive` scripts, and client modules evaluated before the root renders. **Webpack evaluates a route's client component modules when its chunk loads, so module-level requests still leak under webpack builds** (the Next 15 compat cell pins this). Turbopack evaluates a client module when its first element renders, so a module used inside the provider is covered. - Code that saved its own reference to `fetch` before the provider rendered; `sendBeacon`, WebSocket, EventSource, element-initiated requests, and workers. - The standalone `useNetworkBlocker` hook still installs after mount. Its render-purity contract is tested ("abandoned render does not patch fetch"), so I left it alone; the docs point to the provider option. The docs recommend sending tracking calls from effects or event handlers rather than at module top level, loading SDKs through `scripts`, and checking `useConsent()` in your own code, with the blocker as a backstop. ## Before / After Packed tarballs installed into a Next 16.3.4 App Router production consumer (Turbopack) using the documented streaming layout (`resolveConsent` promise → `ConsentRoot`) and a `networkBlocker` rule for `tracker.test`. Requests: (a) at client module evaluation of a page component, (b) in a `useEffect` of a component rendered next to (before) `ConsentRoot`, (c) in a child's mount effect by fetch and by XHR, (d) 1.5 s after mount. Counts are runs where Playwright saw the request leave the browser, with the median send time after navigation. Arms were interleaved. Base `40032552c` (origin/v3), head `390c0f5f3`. | Visit | Runs | Before: (a) (b) (c fetch) (c XHR) | After: (a) (b) (c fetch) (c XHR) | (d) before → after | | --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | | Fresh | 5 | 5/5 each, 48–57 ms | 0/5 | 0 → 0 | | Saved reject | 5 | 5/5 each, 44–50 ms | 0/5 | 0 → 0 | | Saved accept (control) | 5 | 5/5 each, 46–52 ms | 5/5 each, 51–52 ms | 5/5 → 5/5 | | Failing manifest (503), fresh / reject / accept | 3 each | 3/3 each | 0/3 | 0 → 0 | | Hanging manifest, fresh / reject / accept | 3 each | 3/3 each | 0/3 (held, never sent) | 0 → 0 | | Cold manifest (1.5 s, fresh cache), fresh / reject | 3 each | 3/3 each, 84–93 ms | 0/3 | 0 → 0 | | Cold manifest, saved accept | 3 | 3/3 each, 84–88 ms | 3/3 each, 1,565 ms (sent once the policy resolved) | 3/3 → 3/3 | Under webpack (Next 15 compat cell, after): (b) and (c) are blocked on fresh and saved-reject visits, and (a) still leaks for the reason above. First-load JS, route `/docs`, gzip per file (Node zlib), same consumer: | App | Before | After | Delta | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Without `networkBlocker` | 213,296 B (696,966 raw) | 214,064 B (698,763 raw) | +768 B gzip | | With `networkBlocker` | 214,788 B | 215,730 B | +942 B gzip | | Lazy blocker chunk (loaded only with `networkBlocker`) | 1,468 B | 1,641 B | +173 B gzip | FCP and TBT under condition B (4× CPU, 170 ms RTT, 9 Mbit/s down) over HTTP/2 via `h2-proxy.mjs`. Route `/docs`, fresh visit, cold HTTP cache, 9 samples per arm, four arms interleaved. Load average 2.52 / 3.56 / 3.84 at start, 2.32 / 3.01 / 3.57 at end. Median (min–max): | Arm | FCP ms | TBT ms | Banner interactive ms | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Without `networkBlocker`, before | 512 (500–520) | 0 (0–0) | 806 (797–825) | | Without `networkBlocker`, after | 516 (504–520) | 0 (0–0) | 815 (803–832) | | With `networkBlocker`, before | 516 (508–520) | 0 (0–0) | 816 (804–825) | | With `networkBlocker`, after | 516 (508–520) | 0 (0–1) | 814 (803–826) | The FCP and TBT differences are within sample spread. ## Tests - `internals/next-compat`: a `/network-blocker` route and a network-level Playwright suite in the Next 16 (Turbopack) and Next 15 (webpack) cells. It checks that (a)–(c) never leave the browser on fresh and saved-reject visits, and that saved-accept visits send them. Against the origin/v3 packages, the fresh and saved-reject cases fail with all four requests sent. - `@c15t/react`: `network-blocker-early.test.tsx` checks that requests from a child's and a sibling's mount effects are held before the lazy blocker loads, including under StrictMode, and are sent when stored consent allows them. It fails without the hold. - `@c15t/core`: `hold.test.ts` covers the hold, replay, waiting on a pending policy (allow, deny, failure), XHR replay, sync XHR, cleanup, and running with no `window`. A runtime test checks the hold between construction and `start()`. - `@c15t/vue`: child `onMounted` fetch is held until the root mounts the blocker. It fails without the hold. - Package tests and `check-types` for core, react, nextjs, vue, svelte and tanstack-start, plus `bun run lint`, `bun run fmt`, `test:scripts`, and `lint:docs`. ## Conflicts The branch merges cleanly with #1200, with #1201, and with both combined (`git merge-tree`). All three add the same `no-barrel-file` disable line to `packages/react/src/preferences.ts`; the new import pushed that barrel over the threshold here too. ## Follow-ups - `useNetworkBlocker` still installs after mount. - The plain Vue plugin's `C15tVuePluginOptions` type doesn't include `networkBlocker`, even though the plugin reads it at runtime. The Vue test passes a `RuntimeConsentConfig`. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled. ## Review fixes - A provider that unmounts before its blocker loads, a runtime disposed before `start()`, or a Vue context disposed before its root mounts no longer leaves matching requests pending. The requests it held are answered as blocked (451 for `fetch`, a failed XHR), not sent, and requests another caller still holds keep waiting. > [!NOTE] > ### Hold matching network requests before the network blocker loads > - Adds a new `network-hold` module in core that patches `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` early, queueing matching requests until the blocker installs. Matching synchronous XHRs throw a `NetworkError` immediately; nonmatching requests pass through ([hold.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1202/files#diff-27ef55dacaa0e26b1b84ad0d9aac193165960b0653d174f3342ccbfc2b5db43a)). > - `createConsentRuntime` starts the hold at runtime construction and transfers it to the blocker on startup; disposing before startup settles held requests as blocked ([index.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1202/files#diff-3a1fc27e345ff5cfacf0557fc8f132d407202255ba8598557cc44791512b93ff)). > - The React `NetworkBlockerMount` and Vue kernel start the hold during initial render/kernel setup, and answer held requests as blocked (451 fetch, aborted XHR) if the component unmounts before the blocker loads ([provider.tsx](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1202/files#diff-ebad2f84b1dc68cbe0cc36fd742ad550e4d6c3d1dd2b71c0a2e6c12ff07c36bf), [kernel.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1202/files#diff-f1ebcbf60f8f8be12f5cddc6872d9612cd9e919658f96dfc30445783d41be2ba)). > - Patches fetch and XHR in the blocker to also wait while consent policy resolution is pending, then re-evaluate after settlement ([patch-fetch.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1202/files#diff-af1357dbaa557a2d1de6f532b51c2f3fc0132863f08eb86b0e9d0a51f75538e7), [patch-xhr.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1202/files#diff-e85dcd65fcc4014349c847b42fc928d58aca06274f1ad42d28055611120fc286)). > - Adds broad test coverage: core hold tests, React early/unmount browser tests, Vue startup tests, and a shared Playwright compatibility suite for Next 15/16, plus new network-blocker docs for React and Next.js. > - Behavioral Change: requests issued before blocker install are no longer sent to the network while consent is unknown — they resolve as 451 when blocked, replay in order when allowed, and matching sync XHRs throw instead of sending. fix: close consent surfaces without waiting for the backend save (#1205) In v3, Save in the preference dialog kept the dialog open until `POST /subjects` answered. `saveConsentUI` reopened the dialog after the kernel committed the receipt, then closed it only on `result.ok`. Vue's `ConsentManager` and Svelte's `saveConsents` copied the same logic, and the browser client did it for the banner too. v2 closes on the click. The kernel already records the choice, updates permissions, schedules the storage write and queues failed saves for replay before the transport runs. So this PR drops the wait: every save path closes its surface in the click task and leaves the request to finish in the background. The request's outcome never reopens anything. ## Save paths found and what changed | Framework | Path | Before | Change | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | React, Next.js, TanStack Start | `saveConsentUI` (`packages/react/src/ui-save.ts`), used by `ConsentButton` (banner, dialog, set-consent), `useHeadlessConsentUI().performAction` / `saveCustomPreferences`, `useConsentManager().saveConsents` | Reopened the dialog, closed on `ok` | Closes when the save recorded a new receipt or vendor map. A save that recorded nothing closes when it resolves. The navigation guard stays for that case. | | React IAB | stock `IABConsentBanner` / `IABConsentDialog` via `component-hooks/use-headless-iab-consent-ui.ts` | Closed when the IAB commit landed, after TC string encoding, which can wait on the TCF chunk | New `saveIABConsentUI`: closes on the click, restores the surface only if nothing was recorded locally | | React IAB, public hook | `hooks/use-headless-iab-consent-ui.ts` | Already closed on the click | Unchanged | | Next.js, TanStack Start | no own close logic (`root.tsx` only wraps the transport) | | Covered by React | | Vue, Nuxt | `ConsentManager` `onAction` (`manager.vue`) | Reopened the manager, closed on `ok` | Closes on the local record, as React | | Vue IAB | `iab-prompt.vue`, `iab-panel.vue` | Closed on the IAB commit | Close on the click through `utils/save-iab-choice.ts` | | Vue banner | `prompt.vue` | Already closed through the kernel commit | Unchanged | | Svelte | `saveConsents` (`context.svelte.ts`), used by `ConsentButton` and `performAction` | Reopened the dialog, closed on `ok` | Closes on the local record. Bulk actions reset the draft at record time. `ConsentButton` no longer leaks an unhandled rejection when the request fails. | | Svelte IAB | `iab-prompt.svelte`, `iab-panel.svelte` | Closed on the IAB commit | `saveIABChoice`, as React | | Astro | delegated banner handler (`client.ts`) | Already closed through the kernel commit | Unchanged. Dialog islands render the React, Vue or Svelte surfaces, so they get those fixes. | | Browser client / global | `saveSelection` (`client.ts`), used by `acceptAll`, `rejectAll`, `save`, the banner and dialog | Restored the banner or dialog, closed on `ok` | Closes on the local record | | Browser IAB | `saveIAB`, `iab/surface.ts` | Closed after `handle.save()` resolved | Closes on the click, restores only if nothing was recorded. The "Unable to save" message only shows on a restored surface. | | Core kernel | `commands.save` | Commits synchronously, then yields one task before the transport | Unchanged | | `@c15t/ui`, `@c15t/solid` | no close logic | | Unchanged | `ConsentGate`'s button opens the dialog, so it follows the dialog path. ## Failure and retry I kept the existing kernel queue rather than adding one. A failed request emits `command:error`, which reaches `onError` in React, Next.js, TanStack Start and Svelte, and the `error` event on the browser client. Vue has no `onError` option, so there the kernel event is the only signal. The kernel also queues the payload in localStorage (`c15t-v3-pending-consent-saves:v1`). It replays after the next successful init and on `online`, for up to 10 attempts over 7 days. The UI no longer reopens and the choice is not rolled back. Backend contract for late saves: the queued payload keeps `givenAt` from the click and the `policySnapshotToken` from init. The backend records the visitor's time, not the replay time. The consent id covers tenant, subject, domain, policy and `givenAt`, so a retry of a save that did land returns the existing record. One limit I didn't change: the self-hosted backend's snapshot tokens expire after 30 minutes, so a replay after that gets a 422 and the save stays browser-only. This isn't new. The old dialog kept the same choice locally after a failed save. ## Callback timing Unchanged, now documented in `docs/guides/consent-state.mdx`: 1. Click task: receipt commit, `onChoiceRecorded`, `onPermissionsChanged`, script loader, iframe and network blockers, then the surface leaves the active state. 2. Next task: cookie and localStorage write. 3. Then `POST /subjects`. 4. When it settles: `command:save:completed`. The promises from `kernel.commands.save()`, `performAction()`, Svelte's `saveConsents()` and the browser client's `save()` settle here, as before. Svelte's `saveConsents()` still rejects on failure. ## Before / After Next.js 16.3.4 App Router production consumer built from packed tarballs, the `combined-v2-v3` consumer with the v3 guide shape (`ConsentRoot`, `manifestURL`, awaited `resolveConsent`). Arms: v2 = `@c15t/nextjs` 2.2.1; base = packed `40032552c`, whose core/react/nextjs/ui/iab/vue/svelte/browser sources are identical to `origin/v3` `9993ae578` (only Astro changed in between); fix = this branch packed before the last round of comment, lint and typing edits. Its runtime logic matches `2c34648cd`. HTTP/2 through the h2 proxy, `/docs` route. 9 measured samples + 1 warm-up per arm and cell, arms interleaved with rotating order. fix(react): prerender pages that render ConsentGate (#1209) With Next.js 16 `cacheComponents: true`, `next build` fails on any page that renders `ConsentGate` in its prerendered shell: ``` Error: Route "/embed": Next.js encountered the unstable value `Date.now()` in a Client Component. ``` It fails on alpha.2 and on current `v3`. #1195 tells users to wrap the gate in its own `Suspense` as a workaround. This PR removes the need for that. ## Cause `ConsentGate` decided consent with `evaluateConsent({ category }, snapshot)`, whose `now` parameter defaults to `Date.now()`. It ran during render, including the server render. `useVendorAllowed` had the same call. I checked the other gates too. Vue's `ConsentGate` already evaluates at `snapshot.evaluatedAt`. Svelte reads `effectivePermissions` and renders nothing until mount. Astro has no gate component. Nothing else in the React gate's render path reads the clock, `Math.random()`, cookies or storage. ## Change - `hooks.ts` gets an internal `useGateSelector`. Its server snapshot evaluates at the snapshot's own `evaluatedAt`, so server rendering and hydration never read the clock. The browser snapshot still evaluates at `Date.now()`, so a grant that expired before the kernel's deadline timer fired still denies. That is the same enforcement as before. - `ConsentGate` uses it through `useCategoryAllowed`. So does `useVendorAllowed`. - The Next.js `ConsentGate` page says the gate needs no `Suspense` of its own. With the fix, a static page stays `○` and its prerendered HTML contains the placeholder. With the `Suspense` workaround, Next.js bails the gate out to client rendering. The HTML has only the fallback, and the placeholder appears after hydration. ## Tests - `next-16-cache-components` compat cell: two new routes render a marketing `ConsentGate` straight from the page with no `Suspense`. One uses a client-init layout (`/gate`, static) and one uses the promise layout (`/gate-stream`, partial). Without the fix the cell's `next build` fails with the error above. The new test also checks, from browser network requests, that the placeholder is in the first HTML, nothing requests the embed before Accept, Accept loads it once, a returning visitor who accepted loads it once, and one who rejected never loads it. - `consent-gate-placeholder.test.tsx`: server-renders the gate with `Date.now` stubbed to throw, granted and denied. Both fail without the fix. ## Before / After Integration baseline: local merge of the 12 open perf PRs (`integ/all-perf` at `c05270016`, on `v3` `9993ae578`). After: that plus this PR. Consumer: Next.js 16.3.4 production build, `cacheComponents: true`, c15t installed from packed tarballs outside the workspace. Merge the PRs below it first. `c15t setup --ssr` generated `components/consent-manager/index.tsx` as an async Server Component that awaited `resolveConsent`, and the generated layout wraps the whole page in it without a `Suspense` boundary. There is no React reveal delay in that shape, but no byte of the response is sent until consent resolves. The generated app uses hosted mode, so that means a server-side `GET ${backendURL}/init` on every request, not only on a cold cache. `examples/nextjs` awaited the same way in its App Router layout, with a cached manifest. This PR switches both to the form #1195 makes the App Router default: start `resolveConsent`, don't await it, and pass the pending promise to the provider. `ConsentProvider`'s `prefetch` and `ConsentRoot`'s `state` already accept a promise. ## Changes - CLI: the generated `ConsentManager` is synchronous and passes the promise. Its doc comment explains the alternative: make it async, await `resolveConsent`, and wrap it in `` to get the banner in the server HTML at the cost of holding the page. The generated provider's `state` prop is typed `ConsentState | Promise` (prebuilt and expanded templates), so switching back to the awaited form needs no type change. - CLI: the SSR prompt no longer warns that SSR raises TTFB. It says pages render without waiting and the banner appears after hydration. - `examples/nextjs`: the App Router layout passes the promise. The README describes the awaited form as the alternative. - Example acceptance test: the App Router route's server HTML still has the `ConsentGate` placeholder and no iframe, but no longer has the banner. The Pages Router route still renders the banner on the server. - `docs/cli/commands/setup.mdx`: the `--ssr` row describes the new behavior. - Tegami patch note for `@c15t/cli`. Files that earlier `setup` runs generated are not touched. Not changed: the TanStack Start boilerplate and `examples/tanstack-start` await consent in the root loader, which also holds the response. `@c15t/tanstack-start`'s `ConsentRoot` only accepts a resolved `state`, so moving TanStack to a streamed form needs an SDK change first. ## Relation to #1195 This does not depend on #1195's code. The generated comment links to `/docs/frameworks/next/app-router`. On `v3` today that page leads with the awaited layout and documents the promise form under "Stream the page while consent resolves". #1195 makes the promise form the default there and moves the awaited layout to "Render the banner in the server HTML", which is the framing this template follows. Merging #1195 first makes the link read consistently. ## Before / After An app generated with `c15t setup hosted --backend-url http://127.0.0.1:5470 --ssr --apply --skip-install` from this branch's CLI, in a minimal Next.js 16.3.4 App Router project (React 19.2.8), production build, `next start`. feat(react)!: remove useConsentManager (#1197) ## Summary Removes the v2-compatible `useConsentManager()` hook from `@c15t/react` and everything that re-exports it (`@c15t/nextjs`, `@c15t/tanstack-start`, their `/headless` entries, and the `c15t/react`, `c15t/next`, `c15t/tanstack-start` umbrella entries). This is an intended breaking change for the v3 alpha. The hook read the whole consent snapshot plus the draft, so every caller re-rendered on every change. With 50 components subscribed to a category that never changes, one saved toggle re-rendered all 50. c15t's own dialog, preference rows, vendor lists, dialog trigger, overlay and `ConsentGate` used it too, so they paid the same cost. - **Stock components** now read only the values they render. The two fields no public hook exposed in the right shape (`has()` with gate-clock semantics, the translation language, the displayed categories) get narrow internal selectors in `kernel-selector.ts`. Draft state is read through an internal slice selector (`useConsentDraftSlice`), and the accordion renders one row component per category, so a staged toggle re-renders only that category's row and vendor list. - **Removed:** `useConsentManager` and the undocumented `useConsentManagerDraft` on `@c15t/react/draft`, which existed only for it. - **Added to the main entries:** `useSubscribeToConsentChanges()` and `useRegisterConsentCategories()`, already public on `@c15t/react/hooks`. Without them two fields had no replacement outside that subpath. - **CLI:** new `c15t codemods use-consent-manager-to-hooks`. It rewrites destructuring to one hook per field, turns `has('literal')` calls into `useConsent('literal')`, maps literal `saveConsents('all' | 'necessary' | 'custom')` calls to `useHeadlessConsentUI().saveCustomPreferences()`, and moves draft fields to `useConsentDraft()`. Fields it cannot rewrite stay on a `useConsentManager()` call under a `TODO(c15t v3)` comment naming the replacement, so the build fails at each spot that needs manual work. It runs only when named: `--all` and the menu still select the v1 to v2 transforms only, and `--to 3.0.0` is still rejected. - **Docs:** the upgrade guide gains a "Replace `useConsentManager()`" section with the full mapping. The React and Next.js hooks page moves from `hooks/use-consent-manager/overview` to `hooks/overview`, since it documents the selector hooks. The retired routes are recorded in the writing-docs route inventory. perf!: stop a slow or failing consent backend from holding server renders (#1212) > **Stack:** layer 20 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1210, above #1195; the `timeoutMs` wording is applied to #1195's restructured `app-router.mdx`. Server-side consent resolution waited for the manifest cache's 10 second fetch timeout when the backend hung, and every request after a cold failure went back to the backend. This PR gives server rendering a 500 ms budget, caches cold failures with a short backoff, and reads the manifest in Next.js `resolveConsent` through the in-process cache. ## Cause - `resolveConsent` (Next.js, TanStack Start) and Nuxt's server render had no budget of their own. With the awaited layout, a hanging backend on a cold cache kept the page blank until `MANIFEST_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (10 s) fired. - The manifest cache remembered nothing after a failed fill with nothing cached. Stale entries had a 5 s retry floor; cold keys had none, so sequential requests each hit the backend. - Next.js `resolveConsent` fetched `manifestURL` with a plain `fetch`. Pointed at the manifest route it paid a loopback hop on every render; pointed at the backend it skipped both caches. ## Changes - `@c15t/core` manifest cache: - `timeoutMs` bounds how long a call waits, counted from the start of the upstream request, so a call joining a slow request gives up at once. The request keeps running, fills the cache, and goes to `onBackgroundRevalidate`. - A failed fill with nothing usable cached is recorded. That key is not retried for 1 s, doubling to 5 s. Calls in between reject with `ManifestUnavailableError` (`reason: 'backoff'`, `retryAfterMs`, `cause`). Coalescing and stale-while-revalidate are unchanged. A stale copy is still never served past its window. - The upstream request timeout drops from 10 s to 5 s, so the cache notices a recovered backend sooner after a hang. - Non-2xx errors carry `status`. - New exports: `withResolutionBudget` and `DEFAULT_RESOLVE_TIMEOUT_MS`. - `@c15t/nextjs` `resolveConsent`: new `timeoutMs` option (default 500, `false` to disable). It covers the manifest read, the backend `/init` call (`AbortSignal.timeout`) and local resolution. The manifest is read through the in-process cache for any `manifestURL`. `waitUntil` also receives the request that the render stopped waiting for. - `@c15t/tanstack-start` `resolveConsent`: same `timeoutMs`. - `@c15t/vue` (Nuxt): - New `timeoutMs` config. The server render sends it to the in-process init route as `x-c15t-timeout-ms`, because an abort signal does not reach Nitro's local fetch. It also passes `timeout` to `useFetch` for an absolute backend `/init`. - The init route no longer falls back to backend `/init` on every request while the manifest backs off. It still falls back when the backend has no `/manifest` (404). - The awaited and streamed layouts behave the same way. The awaited one paints after at most the budget. The streamed promise resolves to the baseline within the budget. Neither renders consent UI without a policy. - Docs: App Router guide, Next.js fetching reference (new "Slow or unavailable backends" section), TanStack Start and Nuxt quickstarts. Tegami note with a migration section. - The seven-day CDN TTL is unchanged. A `manifestURL` pointing at the backend is now routed through the cache rather than rejected. The manifest route stays the documented setup because it adds the Data Cache and a CDN-cacheable response. ## Before / After Baseline: the integration of the 12 open perf PRs (`integ/all-perf` at `c05270016`, on `origin/v3` `9993ae578`). After: that plus this change (`465e2cbe5`, same code as this PR). Both arms use packed tarballs installed into the same Next.js 16.3.4 production consumer. The consumer has a same-origin manifest route, a `/c15t/init` route, hosted mode, a gated `/tracker.js` (measurement) and a `ConsentGate` iframe (marketing). It has an awaited layout (`` around `await resolveConsent`) and a streamed layout (promise passed as `state`). The external mock backend serves the alpha.2 gateway's manifest and headers. Each sample uses its own manifest key (cold cache, warm process). Arms are interleaved and alternate order each round. Headless Chromium, Apple silicon, other benchmarks running; load averages 3.1 to 9.5. fix(react)!: hold useNetworkBlocker requests from the first render (#1216) > **Stack:** layer 23 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1214 (#1202 is further down), so its diff now shows only this PR's commit. Stacked on #1202 (`fix/react-network-blocker-early-install`), which adds `@c15t/core/modules/network-hold`. This PR changes that module and uses it from the hook, so it can't land without #1202. Review only the top commit. ## Cause #1202 made `ConsentProvider`'s `networkBlocker` option hold matching requests from its first render. The standalone `useNetworkBlocker` hook still installed the blocker from a mount effect. React runs children's effects before their parent's, and earlier siblings' effects before later ones, so every matching `fetch` or XHR sent from those effects went out before the hook did anything. #1202 left the hook alone because a test required that "abandoned render does not patch fetch". ## Fix - `useNetworkBlocker` now starts a hold during its first render in the browser, as the provider does. Nothing runs on the server. - **Holds are tracked per caller.** `holdNetworkRequests(rules)` now returns a `NetworkHold`, and `createNetworkBlocker({ hold })` takes over only that caller's requests. Before, the first blocker to load (or the first unmount) ended every hold, so on a page using both the provider option and the hook, the provider's blocker loading would release the hook's held requests unchecked. `createNetworkBlocker()` without `hold` still ends every hold; Vue and `createConsentRuntime()` use that. - **Renders React throws away.** A render that never commits has no effect cleanup to end its hold, so each render-time hold expires after 10 s unless its component commits. A component that commits also ends any uncommitted hold for the same rules. That covers a retry after suspending: without it, the discarded attempt's hold made requests that consent allows wait 10 s. When a hold expires, its requests are sent, as they would have been without the hook, because its rules never took effect. - The provider's `NetworkBlockerMount` uses the same helper (`module-hooks/network-hold.ts`), so it gets per-caller release and the expiry too. StrictMode's effect re-run is still handled: the cleanup defers the release and a re-mount cancels it. ### Breaking change: the hook's render has a side effect The test "abandoned render does not patch fetch" is removed. It required the hook's render to leave `window.fetch` alone, and that is why requests leaked: nothing can be held before the effect if the render may not patch anything. The new contract, tested in `use-network-blocker-early.test.tsx`, is that a discarded render's hold ends on its own and sends what it held. Tests that assert `window.fetch` is untouched after rendering a component that calls the hook need updating. App code needs no changes. The tegami note has a migration section. ## Before / After The network-level harness from #1202 (Playwright records what leaves the browser), with the provider's `networkBlocker` option removed and `useNetworkBlocker({ rules })` called by a component inside `ConsentRoot` that wraps the page. Packed tarballs installed into a Next 16.3.4 App Router production consumer (Turbopack, `reactStrictMode: true`), rule `{ category: 'measurement', domain: 'tracker.test' }`. Requests: `module` at client module evaluation of the page component; `sibling` from an effect of a component rendered before `ConsentRoot`; `provider-sibling` from an effect of a component inside `ConsentRoot` rendered before the hook's component; `mount` / `mount-xhr` from a child's mount effect; `late` 1.5 s after mount. Before = #1202 head `400decc31`. After = this branch's working tree before the final lint-only edits (runtime logic matches `23e2e7299`). Arms interleaved; load average 6.99 at start, 3.93 at end. Cells: runs in which the request left the browser, with the median send time after navigation. | Condition | Visit | Runs | Before: module, sibling, provider-sibling, mount, mount-xhr | After | `late` before → after | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | | Healthy | Fresh | 5 | 5/5 each, 52–61 ms | 0/5 each | 0/5 → 0/5 | | Healthy | Saved reject | 5 | 5/5 each, 50–58 ms | 0/5 each | 0/5 → 0/5 | | Healthy | Saved accept (control) | 5 | 5/5 each, 50–57 ms | 5/5 each, 54–56 ms | 5/5 → 5/5 | | Manifest 503 | Fresh, reject, accept | 3 each | 3/3 each, 48–63 ms | 0/3 each | 0 → 0 | | Manifest hangs | Fresh, reject, accept | 3 each | 3/3 each, 47–55 ms | 0/3 each (held, never sent) | 0 → 0 | | Cold manifest (1.5 s) | Fresh, reject | 3 each | 3/3 each, 90–100 ms | 0/3 each | 0 → 0 | | Cold manifest (1.5 s) | Saved accept | 3 | 3/3 each, 89–94 ms | 3/3 each, 1,564 ms (sent once the policy resolved) | 3/3 → 3/3 | `module` is covered because Turbopack evaluates the page's client module when its first element renders, which is inside the hook's component. Under webpack it would still leak, as #1202 documents for the provider. ## Tests - `@c15t/react` `use-network-blocker-early.test.tsx`: - requests from a child's and an earlier sibling's mount effects are held and blocked (fails on #1202: both are sent), and the same under StrictMode (fails); - held requests are sent when stored consent allows them; - after a retry following a suspend, an allowed request doesn't wait (fails with the same-rules cleanup disabled: it waits for the 10 s expiry); - a discarded render's hold ends on its own and sends its request (fails on #1202). - `@c15t/core` `hold.test.ts`: releasing one caller sends only what no other caller holds; a blocker given one caller's hold leaves the other hold in place; releasing after the blocker took over does nothing. - Package tests for core, react, vue, svelte, nextjs and tanstack-start (browser tests headless), `check-types` for core and react, `bun run lint`, `bun run fmt`. ## Docs `docs/shared/react/network-blocker.mdx` now covers when blocking starts with the hook, what happens to a discarded render's hold, and the narrower limit (requests sent before the calling component renders). ## Review fixes - A blocker with `enabled: false` no longer ends other callers' holds, and `createConsentRuntime()` and the Vue plugin now hold per caller too, so disposing one before it starts ends only its own hold and answers the requests it held as blocked instead of sending them (`@c15t/vue` added to the release note). - A render hold that ends unclaimed (a discarded render after 10 seconds, or an unmount before the blocker loads) now fails its requests as blocked instead of sending them. > [!NOTE] > ### Make `useNetworkBlocker` hold requests from first render with per-caller holds > - `useNetworkBlocker` now patches `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` during its component's first render, so requests from earlier effects are held before the blocker loads. The loaded blocker takes over the hold; an uncommitted or prematurely unmounted hold expires after 10 seconds (`UNCOMMITTED_HOLD_MS`) and fails its unchecked requests as blocked. > - `holdNetworkRequests` now returns a `NetworkHold` handle. Each caller owns its own rules and queue, so blocking or releasing one caller no longer affects another caller's held requests. A `NOT_HELD` sentinel covers disabled and server-side callers. > - `createNetworkBlocker` accepts an internal `hold` option on `NetworkBlockerOptions`; a supplied hold is released and replayed through the blocker's patches, while omitting it keeps the whole-active-hold takeover. Runtime and Vue kernel code ([index.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1216/files#diff-3a1fc27e345ff5cfacf0557fc8f132d407202255ba8598557cc44791512b93ff), [kernel.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1216/files#diff-f1ebcbf60f8f8be12f5cddc6872d9612cd9e919658f96dfc30445783d41be2ba)) now create, claim, and dispose per-context holds. > - Risk: breaking change — callers of `holdNetworkRequests` and `blockHeldRequests` ([hold.ts](https://github.com/c15t/c15t/pull/1216/files#diff-27ef55dacaa0e26b1b84ad0d9aac193165960b0653d174f3342ccbfc2b5db43a)) get new per-owner semantics; requests matched by a removed caller now fail as blocked instead of replaying, and only requests sent before the hook's component renders remain uncovered. > > > > Macroscope summarized 7409b74. > > ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Matching network requests are now held from the first browser render when using the React network blocker, helping prevent requests from being sent before consent checks run. - Holds are isolated per caller: disabling or disposing one blocker no longer releases another caller’s requests. Requests released without a consent check are blocked. - If a render is discarded before the blocker takes over, held requests are sent after 10 seconds. - **Documentation** - Updated network-blocker guidance to describe early request holding and its limitations.

fix(backend,core)!: record consent saves replayed after the policy token expired (#1219) > **Stack:** layer 24 of 25 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1216, above #1205 and #1206; the `saveFailure` change moved into `hosted-records.ts`, where #1206 put the hosted save. Follow-up from #1205. Based on `v3` (`9993ae578`): the save queue and snapshot tokens are both on `v3`, so this doesn't depend on #1205, but #1205 makes the queue the normal path for a failed save. ## Cause When a save fails, the kernel queues it in localStorage and replays it after the next successful init and on `online`, for up to 10 attempts over 7 days. The replay keeps the click time as `givenAt` and the `policySnapshotToken` from the `/init` the visitor saw. The self-hosted backend's tokens expire 30 minutes after `/init`, and `POST /subjects` verified them against the arrival time, so any replay after that got `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID` and the choice stayed browser-only. The client couldn't tell that refusal from a transient one and retried it until its attempts ran out. Only hosted mode is affected. Manifest mode asserts decision inputs, which the backend recomputes against the current manifest at any time. ## Fix **Backend** (`policy-snapshot.ts`, `consent-submission.ts`): a token that expired before the request arrived is verified again with `givenAt` as the clock. The late save is accepted when: - signature, issuer and tenant audience verify (jose only reports expiry after the signature checks out); - `givenAt` is within the token's `iat`…`exp`, with 10 minutes of slack for the visitor's clock; - the request arrives within `policySnapshot.replayWindowSeconds` of `exp` (new option, default 7 days to match the client queue, `0` turns late acceptance off); - the manifest still has the policy the token names under the same fingerprint and model. The record keeps `givenAt` as sent, `createdAt` is the arrival, and `runtimePolicySource` is `snapshot_token_replayed`. The wide event gets `consent.decisionSource`. Saves that arrive while their token is valid take the same path as before. I picked this over refreshing the token on the client before replay. A refreshed token reflects the visitor's location and the manifest at replay time, not at the click, so it can name a different policy for reasons that have nothing to do with the policy changing, and it costs an `/init` per replay. The original token already is the evidence of what was shown; the question is only how long to honour it. **Refusals are now specific:** | Case | Response | | --- | --- | | Choice made after the token expired, or replay after the window | `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRED` (the code already existed in `@c15t/schema` but was never sent) | | Token names a policy that changed since | `422 STALE_POLICY`, reason `policy-changed` (was `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID`), live or late | | Token doesn't verify | `409 POLICY_SNAPSHOT_INVALID`, unchanged | **Client** (`@c15t/core`): `saveFailure()` turns those four codes (plus `POLICY_SNAPSHOT_REQUIRED`) into a `ConsentSaveRejectedError`, thrown by the hosted and manifest transports (the browser package reuses `hosted.save`). The kernel doesn't queue a live save refused that way, and the replay queue drops such an entry at once instead of spending its 10 attempts. `save:replayed` carries `rejected: `, and devtools shows it. Other failures (network, 5xx, 400) stay retryable. The TanStack Start quickstart awaits the consent server function in the root loader. TanStack Start runs every matched loader before it renders, so no byte of the response goes out until `resolveConsent()` returns. With a warm manifest cache that is a few milliseconds. On a cold cache (the first request after a server starts) it adds the backend's latency to TTFB and first paint, and when the backend stops answering it holds the page until the manifest cache's request timeout fires (10 s on `v3`). #1195 and #1215 moved Next.js to the streamed form, where `ConsentRoot` gets the pending `resolveConsent` promise. The server-state decision seed for the same-origin init route is only built from a resolved state; after a streamed state resolves, saves carry the decision the kernel applied, so the route's assertion still accepts them. - The quickstart gets a "Stream the page while consent resolves" section with the loader (`loader: () => ({ consent: getConsentState() })`), the banner trade-off and when to pick which. perf(vue): keep all-locale translations out of the Nuxt first load (#1235) > **Stack:** layer 33 of 36 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1233. Merge the PRs below it first. Every page of a Nuxt 4 app with the c15t module downloaded the all-locale translations chunk in its first load: 56,646 B gzip, 205,873 B raw, 29% of the page's first-load JS. That happened in every manifest mode, including the documented server manifest setup, where the browser never resolves a manifest and never reads those translations. Found while checking whether #1194 (manifest resolver kept off the first save) and #1192 (offline presets kept out of the initial bundle) apply to Vue. The Vue save path already avoids the resolver in server manifest mode, so #1194 itself does not apply. This is a different way for the same chunk to reach the page. ## Cause `kernel.ts` loads client manifest mode's resources with two calls, `import('@c15t/core/transports/manifest')` and `import('@c15t/translations/all')`. Both are dynamic, and neither module is imported statically anywhere in the client. In a Nuxt 4.5.1 build (Vite 8.3.1, Rolldown 1.2.11) the translations chunk ends with: ```js var t=Object.defineProperty,n=(e,n)=>{...},r=n({baseTranslations:()=>i}),i={bg:{...}} export{i as n,n as r,r as t}; ``` `n` is Rolldown's `__export` namespace helper. Rolldown placed it in the translations chunk, and the app entry needs the same helper, so the entry imports it from there: `import{r as e}from"./ujZdANZs.js"`. That static import pulls the whole chunk in, and Nuxt preloads it with the page. A plain Vue app built with Vite 8 (`@c15t/vue/vite`, the `examples/vue` shape) does not get this chunk graph. Its first load is unchanged by this PR (see below). ## Change - `runtime/client-manifest.ts` re-exports `createManifestTransport` and `baseTranslations`. The kernel imports that one module. Its chunk exports the bindings directly, so no namespace helper is built for it and nothing else imports from it. - Client manifest mode resolves the manifest as the page starts. With a dynamic import only, its resolver was fetched after the entry ran, and the banner appeared 49 ms later under condition B over HTTP/2 (865 ms against 816 ms, first fix build). The Nuxt module now adds `plugin-client-manifest.nuxt` in that mode only. It imports the module statically and hands it to the kernel through the internal `registerClientManifest()`, so the resolver is in the entry and preloads with the page, as before. - No public API change. The server routes are untouched. ## Before / After Consumer outside the workspace, built from packed tarballs (`bun pm pack` of core, ui, vue, schema, translations, iab, dev-tools): Nuxt 4.5.1, the Nuxt quickstart setup (`manifest: true`, `showTrigger: true`, footer "Privacy settings" button), a mock backend serving the alpha.2 gateway manifest, `nitro.compressPublicAssets` so JS is served brotli-compressed as from a CDN. perf(vue): re-render composable subscribers only when their value changes (#1236) > **Stack:** layer 34 of 36 in stack #1225 on `v3`, based on #1235. Merge the PRs below it first. Checking whether the cause behind #1197 exists in Vue. #1197 removes React's `useConsentManager()` because it read the whole state and re-rendered every caller on every change. Vue's field composables mostly avoid that already, but three of them don't: `useHasConsent()`, `useConsentInit()` and `useConsentPolicyActions()` built a new array or object on every kernel update. Vue 3.4+ only skips a computed's dependents when its value is identical, so every component reading one of them re-rendered whenever anything in the snapshot changed, including opening or closing the dialog. ## Measured Nuxt 4.5.1 consumer built from packed tarballs (quickstart setup, server manifest mode), `/subscribers` page with 50 components per composable. Each renders one value from its composable and counts its own `onUpdated` calls. Headless Chromium. Counts were identical in 3 interleaved runs per arm. fix(core): isolate consent listeners and keep nested transitions ordered (#1221) ## Problem Checked against `9993ae578`, the current `v3` head. Snapshot notification called subscribers without isolation and passed the live snapshot cell. - A throwing subscriber stopped the subscribers after it. The exception rejected `commands.save()` before `choice:recorded`, so persistence never wrote the denial, even though the in-memory permission had already changed. - A subscriber that saved a grant while being notified of a denial ran a nested notification. The outer loop then resumed with the new snapshot, so later subscribers saw `[true, true]` and missed the denial. `permissions:changed` arrived newest first, and the outer save's `choice:recorded` carried the nested snapshot. ## Change Snapshot subscribers and the event bus now share one dispatcher (`packages/core/src/kernel/dispatch.ts`). - Each listener call is isolated. Errors go to `reportError` where the platform has it, and to `console.error` otherwise. The reporter's own failures are swallowed, so reporting cannot recurse into delivery. - `commit()` delivers the frozen snapshot it produced, not the live cell. - Delivery stays synchronous and reentrant, but deliveries share cursors. When a listener commits, the deliveries in progress first finish for their remaining listeners, then the new one runs, all before the nested commit returns. Every listener sees commits in order. A listener that is mid-work, such as the script loader mounting a script, still learns about a revocation it caused. - Commands and setters batch a commit together with its follow-up event (`choice:recorded`, `init:applied`, `overrides:set` and so on). The event carries its own snapshot and is delivered before any transition a listener starts. `save()` builds its payload and records generation from its own commit. - A listener added during delivery first receives the next change. A listener removed during delivery is skipped. - Feedback loops stop after 100 nested deliveries and report an error. Before, they overflowed the stack. I first tried a FIFO queue that deferred nested deliveries. It broke `@c15t/dev-tools`' "does not insert a later target after synchronous consent revocation" test: the loader mounted a body script after the visitor had revoked consent. Reentrant delivery with shared cursors keeps that guarantee. Docs: added "How listeners are notified" to the kernel API overview. Release note: `.tegami/2026-09-27-isolate-consent-listeners.md` (`@c15t/core`, `c15t` patch). ## Tests - `kernel/__tests__/listener-isolation.test.ts`: throwing subscribers before, between and after the others; throwing event listeners; `reportError` and a throwing reporter; setters; nested regrant with each registration order; event order and snapshots; synchronous nested delivery; subscribing and unsubscribing during delivery; the feedback cutoff; frozen committed snapshots. - `modules/persistence/__tests__/listener-failure.test.ts`: real `createPersistence` with throwing consumers registered before and after it, and a nested regrant. - Before the fix, 11 kernel cases and both throwing-consumer persistence cases failed. - `bun run --cwd packages/core test`: 1,313 tests pass. Core `check-types` and `lint` pass. - `TURBO_SCM_BASE=origin/v3 bun run test --continue`: every affected package passed except these: - `@c15t/svelte` `iab-lazy` timed out once under full parallel load, and the full Svelte suite passes on its own. - The `example-nextjs` and `next-compat-16-static-export` builds need `NEXT_PUBLIC_C15T_BACKEND_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_COMPAT_BACKEND_URL`, which aren't set locally. - Not verified locally: Playwright browser groups. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? fix(core): reconcile consent that other tabs store (#1223) ## Problem A running runtime kept a grant after another runtime stored a denial in the same browser. `kernel.refresh()` only re-evaluates records already in memory, and `runtime.reinit()` only reruns transport init. Neither reads storage again, and the runtime did not expose its persistence handle. I reproduced this in jsdom through `createConsentRuntime`: grant, start a second runtime, deny from a third, then refresh and reinit the second. It still reported the grant. ## Change **API.** `createPersistence` gets `reconcile()`, `ConsentRuntime` gets `reconcileStorage()`, and React's `usePersistence()` handle gets `reconcile()`. Each returns whether any in-memory record changed. The new persistence option `sync` defaults to `true`. With it on, the module schedules one coalesced reconciliation on a `storage` event for its own keys (including custom `storageKey`s and `localStorage.clear()`), on `visibilitychange` to visible, and on window `focus`. Reconnecting does not trigger a read, since going online changes nothing in storage. `dispose()` removes the listeners and cancels a scheduled run. Every adapter that mounts persistence (React, Next.js, TanStack Start, Vue, Svelte, Astro, the script tag and the runtime) gets this without code changes. **What a reconciliation applies.** Only records whose stored value changed since this runtime last read or wrote them are considered. A record held only in memory is not touched, for example a receipt merged from the server after `identify()`. Each changed record is then handled as follows: - A stored record at least as new as the one in memory replaces it. The comparison uses the record's own times: category `confirmedAt`, `dismissedAt`, vendor `confirmedAt` and directive `recordedAt`. - An older stored record is ignored. - A record removed from readable storage is cleared, so the active policy decides again. - Blocked storage and bytes that do not decode change nothing. There is a new `readStoredRecordsForReconcile`, because the existing read treats undecodable bytes as absent, which under an opt-out policy would turn a denial into a grant. Changes go through `kernel.hydrate()`, so they are validated and never written back. The existing evaluator decides expiry at read time. Subscribers and `permissions:changed` fire once. **Ordering.** Reconciliation first flushes this runtime's queued writes, so it never reverts the visitor's latest action in this tab. Writes are now guarded: a queued write skips when storage holds a newer record. The rewrite triggered by `subject:resolved` only lands on a record that still holds this runtime's decisions. That also fixes a pre-existing race where a slow save response could overwrite another tab's newer denial or recreate records another tab had cleared. As with any hydration, a save still in flight when another tab's choice is applied is fenced by the records generation, so this tab neither sends it nor queues it for retry. I didn't restructure `notify()` or `commit()` in `kernel/runtime.ts`. ## Tests - `packages/core/src/runtime/__tests__/storage-reconciliation.test.ts` (jsdom, public runtime API) covers the reproduction plus notification, clearing under opt-in and opt-out, a custom storage key, blocked and undecodable storage, memory-only records, the queued-write-first order, an older queued write versus a newer stored denial, a late subject acknowledgement versus a newer denial or a clear, the event triggers and key filtering, `sync: false`, and disposal. I checked that the ordering tests fail when the write guards, the flush-before-read, the undecodable-read handling or the change fingerprints are removed. - `packages/browser/src/__tests__/storage-sync.browser.test.ts` runs in real Chromium through the existing Vitest browser project. It opens two pages with `window.open` against a fixture page served by the Vitest server. A denial saved in one page reaches the other and notifies it, and clearing in one returns the other to the opt-in default. It fails without the listeners and passed six times in a row with them. Commands run: - `TURBO_SCM_BASE=origin/v3 bun run test --continue`: every package test task passed (core 1307, react 719, browser 206, vue 345, svelte 480, astro 318, nextjs 283, tanstack-start 299, and the rest). That file is unchanged here, and the count stays at 104 with the new module removed from `dist`. ## Not verified - Cross-origin iframes, Safari and Firefox. Only Chromium was exercised. - Whether Chromium ever delivers the `storage` event before another renderer can read the new cookie. The cookie is read first. If it lags, the next event, focus or visibility change picks the record up. I did not see this in six runs. - IAB/TCF state across tabs. fix(iab): encode, decode and enforce publisher restrictions (#1222) Publisher restrictions were declared in the public types (`TCFConsentData.publisherRestrictions`, `TCData.publisher.restrictions`) but dropped at every stage of the TCF pipeline. ## What was broken I reproduced this with hand-built TC strings before changing anything. `packages/iab/src/__tests__/fixtures/publisher-restrictions.ts` writes and reads the core segment from the field table in the IAB spec, including NumPubRestrictions, PurposeId(6), RestrictionType(2), NumEntries(12) and the range entries. It shares no code with `@iabtechlabtcf/core`, so it can check the encoder's bit layout independently. Against `9993ae57`: - **Encode:** `generateTCString` ignored `publisherRestrictions`. The PubRestrictions section was always `[]`. - **Decode:** `decodeTCString` had no restrictions field. It returned `undefined` for the type 0, 1 and 2 fixtures. - **CMP API:** `getTCData().publisher.restrictions` was always `{}`. - **Authority and gates:** `KernelIABAuthority` had nowhere to put restrictions, and `hasIABConsent` granted a vendor whose purpose was prohibited. - **Unsupported input:** the codec already rejects type 3, purpose ID 0 and inverted ranges on decode. Vendor ID 0, LI required for purpose 3 and conflicting types for one vendor decoded without error. On encode, the library silently drops any restriction its vendor list does not allow. ## Contract `publisherRestrictions` is accepted by `createIAB`, `IABProvider` and the runtime's `iab` options. It is documented in a shared include used by the JavaScript, React and Next.js IAB pages. | Type | Meaning | Allowed when the vendor | | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | Purpose not allowed | declares the purpose for consent or LI | | 1 | Consent required | declares it for LI and lists it in `flexiblePurposes` | | 2 | LI required | declares it for consent and lists it in `flexiblePurposes`, and the purpose is not 1, 3, 4, 5 or 6 | Restrictions require a service-specific string. Unsupported input throws `PublisherRestrictionError`, a subclass of `TypeError`. This covers reserved type 3, IDs out of range, a vendor or purpose missing from the list, a restriction that does not match the vendor's declarations, conflicting types for one vendor and purpose, and a non-service-specific string. `whenReady()` rejects, `save()` and `generateTCString()` reject, and no TC string or consent is written. ## Change - `tc-string.ts` validates restrictions against the vendor list, then encodes them. It checks that the library kept each one, and decodes and validates them on read. - `cmp-api.ts` reports restrictions decoded from the current TC string as `{ [purposeId]: { [vendorId]: type } }`. - `authority.ts` puts decoded restrictions on `KernelIABAuthority`. A stored string whose restrictions differ from the configuration for listed vendors is not restored, so the visitor is asked again. - `has.ts`: in `hasIABConsent`, type 0 denies. Type 1 moves an LI purpose to consent, and type 2 moves a consent purpose to LI. A move only applies when the vendor list marks the purpose flexible for that vendor; otherwise the vendor is denied. - `acceptAll` sets the vendor signal a restriction moves a purpose to, such as LI for a vendor that declares no LI purposes. - Core threads the option through `IABConfig`, the runtime factory options and the save-authority guard. ## Tests - `publisher-restrictions.test.ts`: decodes the spec fixtures and rejects invalid ones. Checks the encoder's bit layout with the independent reader and round-trips through decode. Covers 14 encode rejection cases and the CMP API map. - `authority.test.ts`: full save flow with configured restrictions (gating, the `getTCData` map, the LI signal from accept all). Unsupported restrictions reject `whenReady` and `save`. Stored authority must match the configuration. A malformed restriction on authority passed to `commands.save` is rejected. - Core `has.test.ts` and `effective-gates.test.ts`: evaluation for each type, flexibility, consent-only purposes and a gate through `evaluateConsent`. These fail on the old evaluator. Commands run: `bun turbo run check-types test` for core and iab, `check-types` for react, nextjs, astro and c15t, core `check-types:test`, `bun run lint`, `bun run fmt`, `bun run lint:docs`, `bun run fmt:docs`, `leadtype lint --src docs` (only the existing framework-picker errors remain), `bun run test:scripts scripts/docs-validation.test.ts`, and `TURBO_SCM_BASE=origin/v3 bun run test --continue`. In the affected run, `@c15t/example-nextjs` and `@c15t/next-compat-16-static-export` builds failed because they need backend URL env vars. An Astro browser test and a Svelte lazy-IAB test hit 5 s timeouts under full-suite load; both packages pass when run on their own. ## For review - Types 1 and 2 on a purpose that isn't flexible, and type 0 on a purpose the vendor doesn't declare, are rejected. The spec gives them vendor-side meanings, such as "don't process" or "ignore", but `@iabtechlabtcf/core` drops them on encode, so c15t cannot write them. - Validation depends on the current vendor list. A vendor that drops a declaration or its flexibility makes the configuration fail loudly until it is updated. - Decoded ranges may cover IDs missing from the list, since the spec allows a range to span gaps. `getTCData` reports the string as encoded, and the authority comparison only looks at listed vendors. - Not covered: the Astro `C15tIABOptions` type does not declare `publisherRestrictions`, and the IAB dialog UI does not reflect restrictions. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? fix(core,react): keep v3 iframe blocker running past unreadable nodes and invalid categories (#1249) ## Overview This is the v3 counterpart to #1248, which fixes the same bug on canary. The v3 iframe blocker was rewritten, so the fix is separate. One bad node can make the blocker let consent-gated iframes load. On v3 this happens in two ways: 1. **A node page script can't read.** The observer in `modules/iframe-blocker` reads `node.nodeType` without a guard, for both added and removed nodes. Firefox throws `Permission denied to access property "nodeType"` for some nodes, most likely ones inserted by extensions. v3 collects every iframe in a batch before reconciling any, so the throw skips all of them, including iframes added before the bad node. The on-demand watcher in `@c15t/react` (`isIframe` / `collectIframes`) has the same unguarded read. 2. **An iframe with an invalid `data-category`.** `determineCategory` throws. `registerIframes` reads every gated iframe's category before any iframe is reconciled, so one invalid category: - makes `createIframeBlocker` throw on startup, and no observer is attached; - stops every later pass early. Revoking consent updates the permissions but leaves the other gated iframes loaded. The kernel catches subscriber errors, so consent saves still work on v3. The damage is limited to iframes. ## Related Issue Fixes #1168 for v3. #1248 fixes it on canary. ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) ## Implementation Details ### Key Changes 1. `isIframe` and `addIframes` in `modules/iframe-blocker/index.ts` read each node inside a try/catch, for added nodes, removed nodes, and attribute targets. An unreadable node is skipped, and the rest of the batch is gated. 2. `determineCategory` returns `null` for an unknown category instead of throwing. `reconcileIframe` keeps that iframe blocked and logs a console warning. `registerIframes` already skipped falsy categories, so it needs no change. 3. The React on-demand watcher gets the same guard in `isIframe` and `collectIframes`. 4. The sentence in `docs/integrations/granular-consent.mdx` that said an unknown category always throws now names the iframe blocker as the exception. 5. A Tegami note bumps `@c15t/core` and `@c15t/react` (patch). ### Technical Notes - An iframe with an invalid category is kept **blocked**. The React on-demand watcher already does this (`isClearlyAllowed` returns `false` for a category it can't read), so the watcher and the loaded blocker now agree. The canary fix in #1248 leaves such an iframe unchanged, to avoid changing behavior on the stable line. - Behavior change: `createIframeBlocker` no longer throws for an invalid `data-category`, and the on-demand path no longer produces an unhandled rejection. The tests that asserted those errors now assert the iframe stays blocked and a warning is logged. ## Testing ### Test Plan - [x] Core (`iframe-blocker.test.ts`, `reconcile.test.ts`) covers: - an invalid category at startup, and during a revoke; - an unreadable node between two iframes in one batch; - an invalid-category iframe inside a batch; - `determineCategory` returning `null`; - an invalid-category iframe staying blocked even with every category granted. All 6 new tests fail on `v3` and pass with the fix. The full core suite passes (1490 tests). - [x] React (`iframe-blocker-on-demand.test.tsx`, real Chromium) covers an iframe added in the same batch as an unreadable node, and an invalid category staying blocked with a warning. Both fail on `v3` and pass with the fix; all 11 tests in the file pass. - [x] I ran a browser repro against `v3`, before and after the fix. Chromium 149 and Firefox 151 gave identical results: | Scenario | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | Unreadable node, then marketing iframe, in one batch | iframe loads, uncaught error | blocked | | Marketing iframe, then unreadable node, in one batch | iframe loads, uncaught error | blocked | | Invalid category + marketing iframe in one batch | iframe loads, uncaught error | blocked | | Invalid-category iframe on the page at startup | `createIframeBlocker` throws; later iframes load | blocked | | Accept all, invalid-category iframe appears, then revoke | marketing iframe keeps loading | `src` cleared | ### Edge Cases - [x] Error handling: unreadable nodes are skipped silently, and invalid categories log a warning and stay blocked. - [x] Performance: no extra DOM work. The try/catch wraps reads that were already happening. - [x] Security: this closes a gap where consent-gated iframes loaded, or stayed loaded, without consent. feat: share consent and script controls across frameworks (#1204)

Blume needs c15t to own script loading and consent lifecycle while
allowing an existing CMP to remain the consent authority. This adds that
support to c15t's shared core and native framework APIs, plus
consent-aware application event dispatch in the scripts SDK.

`consentSource` works through React (including Next.js and TanStack
Start), Vue/Nuxt, Svelte/SvelteKit, the browser client, and Astro.
Headless JavaScript and Solid use the same core runtime. No framework
depends on Astro for these controls. React uses a lightweight controls
entrypoint to preserve lazy script loading. When the source withdraws a
granted category, the page reloads through the existing
`reloadOnConsentRevoked` option and `onBeforeConsentRevocationReload`
callback.

External permissions start denied and follow the provider's current
decisions. c15t skips its backend initialization, persistence, and IAB
setup, and never turns provider booleans into choice receipts. Save
commands reject before recording. Native preference controls delegate
through a shared kernel event while c15t's own choice surfaces stay
hidden. Preference failures reach lifecycle error callbacks. Nuxt skips
consent prefetch and record hydration for an external source and
subscribes after mount.

`createEventDispatcher` delivers only to configured integrations whose
current gates permit analytics, discards denied events, isolates vendor
errors, and deduplicates explicitly configured SPA pageviews. The SDK
additions preserve Google tag config, custom GTM queues with denied
defaults before container initialization, and Segment load options. The
scripts package declares its core dependency.

Validation:
- 4,018 tests passed across core (1,297), React (720), Vue/Nuxt (347),
Svelte (481), browser (205), Astro (319), Next.js (283), TanStack Start
(299), and DevTools (67). Applicable coverage gates passed.
- The scripts SDK's 434 tests passed for the initial SDK changes; this
follow-up changes the framework wiring and shared controls.
- Builds, typechecks, and lint passed for all affected runtime/framework
packages and the umbrella package, using Node 24.
- Framework regressions cover external grants, withdrawal, preference
delegation, listener disposal, React StrictMode, lazy script loading,
and Nuxt initialization boundaries.
- Canonical shared documentation added, package docs regenerated, and
umbrella exports regenerated.
- Blume refreshed local packages passed targeted consent/analytics
tests, uncached workspace typechecks, and production browser checks for
both offline GTM and Osano external consent, including events,
preferences, navigation, and withdrawal/reload. The initial integration
also verified Fides and ejected sites. Vendor requests were intercepted.

Draft companion to https://github.com/BurnedChris/blume/pull/1. The
external CMP remains responsible for records, expiration, privacy
signals, and category mapping; the bridge does not certify compliance.
Blume's temporary file dependencies must be replaced with the published
v3 alpha before release.

test(release): stop the version PR body test depending on pending notes (#1255) The alpha.3 release run after #1254 failed in **Repository and docs**, before anything was published: ``` FAIL tegami.test.ts > renders a version PR body for the real workspace that GitHub accepts AssertionError: expected 0 to be greater than 0 ``` The test from #1253 rendered the body from the repository's own `.tegami` notes and required at least one pending note. Merging a version PR consumes every note, so the test fails on v3 right after each version PR merges, which blocks that release's publish. This replaces it with two fixture tests that don't read repository state: - **lists each bumped version and release note:** two notes on two packages, checks the version table row and one line per note. - **drops note lines past GitHub's size limit:** 300 notes with 200-character titles, checks the body stays within 65,536 characters and ends with the "…and N more release notes" line. Nothing tested the trimming path before; disabling the trim loop makes this test fail. `scripts/tegami.ts` is unchanged, and the real-workspace draft test stays as it was. Once this merges, the v3 release run should publish alpha.3 from the lock #1254 committed. ## Testing - `bun run test:scripts tegami.test.ts`: 35 passed. - `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the changed file are clean. - `browser-process.test.ts` fails locally on Node 26 but passes in CI; this PR doesn't touch it. --- Need help on this PR?
